sermons.title: NIGHT 1: CONFESSION AND FORGIVENESS
sermons.speaker: Trent Cornwell
sermons.notesHtml:
Commitment

We will give ourselves to a regular lifestyle of confession and forgiveness.

THE HOUR AT A GLANCE

:00 to :05 Welcome and Introduction :05 to :12 Table Warm-Up :12 to :38 The Lesson :38 to :45 Couple’s Exercise :45 to :55 Table Talk :55 to 1:00 Review and Closing Prayer

TABLE WARM-UP

Have you ever paid off a debt or had one canceled? How did that release feel?

When you were a child and got caught doing something wrong, were you a confessor, a blamer, or a hider?

THE LESSON

Every marriage is the union of two sinners.

That is not pessimism. It is the doorway to hope because sinners are exactly who Jesus came to save.

This commitment is first on purpose. Nothing else in this series will work in a home where sin is hidden, excused, or weaponized.

“God decided to leave you in this fallen world to live, love, and work, because he intended to use the difficulties you face to do something in you that couldn’t be done any other way.” Paul David Tripp, Marriage

Transition: Before we can fix what is between us, we must face what is within us.

1. CONFESSION BEGINS VERTICALLY WITH GOD

Scripture

“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” 1 John 1:8–9

Exposition

John removes the middle ground.

Either we deceive ourselves, or we confess.

Notice the ground of forgiveness. It is not the depth of our emotion or the sincerity of our apology. It is the character of God.

“He is faithful and just.”

God is faithful to His promise, and He is just because the penalty for our sin was already paid at the cross.

A spouse who lives under the truth of this verse has nothing left to protect and nothing left to hide.

Self-deception is the first enemy of every marriage. We edit our own story until we become the hero and our spouse becomes the problem.

Illustration

A man disputes a charge on his credit card for months. He insists that the charge cannot possibly be his.

Then he finds the receipt in his own coat pocket.

Many marital disputes end the same way. The evidence was in our pocket all along.

2. UNCONFESSED SIN IS HEAVY, BUT CONFESSION BRINGS RELEASE

Scripture

“When I kept silence, my bones waxed old through my roaring all the day long. For day and night thy hand was heavy upon me: my moisture is turned into the drought of summer. Selah. I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid. I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the LORD; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin.” Psalm 32:3–5

Exposition

David describes silence as physical decay.

“My bones waxed old.”

Hidden sin never remains hidden. It dries out a soul and a marriage like the drought of summer.

Then notice the speed of grace.

The moment David says, “I will confess,” the verse concludes, “and thou forgavest.”

God forgives faster than we confess.

Question for the Room

What has silence been costing your home?

Illustration

A splinter left in a finger does not remain a small splinter. It festers.

The pain of pulling it out lasts only seconds. The pain of leaving it there can last for weeks.

Confession is the pulling out of the splinter.

3. CONFESSION IS ALSO HORIZONTAL

Scripture

“Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.” James 5:16

Exposition

James will not allow confession to remain private.

“One to another.”

Confession must be spoken. It must be specific. It must be made to the person who was wronged.

Notice that confession is coupled with prayer.

“Pray one for another.”

The goal of confession is not humiliation. The goal is healing.

“That ye may be healed.”

Two of the most powerful sentences in a marriage are:

“I was wrong.”

“I am praying for you.”

Those two sentences often travel together.

Illustration

Many couples have never heard their spouse say the plain, unedited words, “I was wrong.”

There is usually a qualification:

“I was wrong, but you…”

“I am sorry if you were offended.”

“I should not have done that, but you need to understand…”

That is not confession. That is explanation disguised as confession.

Question for the Room

When did your spouse last hear you say, plainly and without qualification, “I was wrong”?

4. FORGIVEN PEOPLE FORGIVE

Scripture

“And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you.” Ephesians 4:32

Exposition

The standard is not, “Forgive your spouse as much as your spouse deserves.”

The standard is:

“Even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you.”

Paul David Tripp describes forgiveness as the vertical commitment that makes the horizontal transaction possible.

I settle forgiveness before God first. Therefore, I am ready to grant forgiveness when my spouse confesses the wrong.

Forgiveness in marriage is not merely a feeling for which we wait.

Forgiveness is a debt we cancel because our debt was canceled.

Illustration

People frame mortgage payoff letters. Nobody frames a monthly bill.

Ephesians 4:32 teaches that your spouse should live with a framed payoff letter, not under a running invoice.

KEY TRUTH

Confession and forgiveness are not occasional events in a healthy marriage. They are a lifestyle.

“Hopelessness is a way of seeing, not a state of being.” Paul David Tripp, Marriage

No marriage represented at these tables is beyond the reach of grace.

Hopelessness is a lens, not a fact.

Tonight, we exchange that lens for the cross.

COUPLE’S EXERCISE: SHORT ACCOUNTS

Time: 7 minutes

Alone: 2 Minutes

Each spouse should privately complete these two sentences on a card:

“One thing I need to confess to you is…”

“One way I may have made confession feel unsafe for you is…”

Together: 5 Minutes

Exchange your answers one at a time.

The listening spouse may respond with only these two statements:

“Thank you.”

“I forgive you.”

Do not explain.

Do not defend yourself.

Do not introduce another accusation.

Do not respond with a cross-charge.

Leader Note

Tell the room:

“If something surfaces tonight that is too serious or complicated to address through this exercise, do not force the conversation. Come speak with me or one of the pastors this week.”

TABLE TALK

When your sin is exposed at home, what is your first instinct: to confess or to explain and defend yourself? Why?

Tonight we said that your greatest marriage problem is your own sin. What makes that difficult to believe? What would change in your home if you truly believed it?

Which is more difficult for you: confessing or forgiving? What does your answer reveal?

Does your marriage have both the humility of approachability and the courage of loving honesty? Which one is weaker? What is one step you can take to strengthen it?

REVIEW AND CLOSING

Review

My greatest marriage problem is my own sin, and Christ has already answered it. 1 John 1:9

Silence dries out a marriage, but confession brings release. Psalm 32:3–5

Confession must go one to another and must be coupled with prayer. James 5:16

I forgive because I have been forgiven. Ephesians 4:32

This Week at Home

Repeat the Short Accounts exercise once during the week without being prompted.

Make the confession specific.

Speak forgiveness clearly.

Closing Prayer

Close in prayer at the tables.

Ask God to make your home a place where confession is safe and forgiveness is quick.

sermons.title: NIGHT 2: Growth & Change
sermons.speaker: Trent Cornwell
sermons.notesHtml:
Six Gospel Commitments

Underlined words are the blanks in the couple's workbook. Bracketed tags mark which slide to be on.

[SLIDE 1 — Growth & Change — Title Slide]

Night 2

We will make growth and change our daily agenda.

[SLIDE 2 — The Second Gospel Commitment]

Opening Prayer for the Night

Lord, we confess that we drift. We coast on old habits and call it normal.

Tonight, give us eyes to see the weeds we have let grow in our marriages — selfishness, busyness, inattention, self-righteousness, fear, and laziness — and courage to pull them.

Plant in us the fruit of Your Spirit, and make us couples who work at our marriage every day, not just on hard days.

Do in us what only Your grace can do. In Jesus' name, Amen.

Table Warm-Up

If your marriage were a garden, what would passersby see growing in it right now? What is one habit you fought hard to break in life — and what finally worked?

The Lesson

[SLIDE 4 — Start Here]

Start here: no marriage stands still. It is either being cultivated or it is going to weeds. Tripp pictures marriage as a garden — and gardens are ruled by daily work, not annual events. Nobody drifts into a great marriage; couples drift only one direction.

[SLIDE 5 — Transition — What We Don't Tend]

Transition: God's Word warns us what unattended sin does to a relationship.

[SLIDE 6 — Little Bites Become Big Destruction]

1. Little bites become big <u>destruction</u>.

But if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another. — Galatians 5:15 (KJV)

[SLIDE 7 — What Paul Forces Us to Face]

Exposition: Paul chooses animal words on purpose — "bite… devour… consumed." Sharp words, sarcasm, and score-keeping feel small in the moment, but Paul says they escalate: biting becomes devouring becomes consuming. "Take heed" means watch the little moments — that is where marriages are lost, and where they are won. No couple ever consumed each other in one bite.

Illustration cue: Termites do more property damage each year than house fires — and nobody ever hears a termite. Ask the room which their marriage should fear more: the blow-up fight, or the quiet daily chewing.

[SLIDE 8 — Growth Is the Spirit's Fruit]

2. Growth is the Spirit's <u>fruit</u>, cultivated <u>daily</u>.

But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance: against such there is no law. — Galatians 5:22–23 (KJV)

[SLIDE 9 — Fruit Takes a Whole Season]

Exposition: Fruit is not manufactured; it is grown — slowly, in season, by the Spirit's power and not our willpower. Every quality in this list is a marriage quality: longsuffering with a spouse's weakness, gentleness in correction, meekness in conflict, temperance with the tongue. And fruit grows in cultivated soil — the daily habits of the Word, prayer, and confession we committed to last week are the tilling.

Illustration cue: You can buy plastic fruit that looks right across the room and fools nobody at the table. Manufactured niceness is plastic fruit; the Spirit grows the real thing — slower, but alive.
"A healthy marriage is all about knowing what to say <u>no</u> to." — Paul David Tripp, Marriage

Growth is as much about pulling weeds as planting seeds. Saying yes to your marriage will mean saying no to lesser things — the schedule, the screen, the self. Tripp names six weeds by name:

  • selfishness
  • busyness
  • inattention
  • self-righteousness
  • fear
  • laziness

Read the list slowly; every couple in this room owns at least one.

[SLIDE 10 — Change Is a Work of Beholding]

3. Change is a work of <u>beholding</u>, not just behaving.

But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord. — 2 Corinthians 3:18 (KJV)

[SLIDE 11 — We Become What We Behold]

Exposition: "Beholding… we are changed." Paul's word order matters: transformation follows attention. We become what we steadily look at — which is why a marriage fed on comparison, screens, and grievance is being changed by them, "from glory to glory" in the wrong direction. The couple that beholds Christ together — in the Word, in worship, in prayer — is being changed together. Change of behavior that lasts always starts as a change of gaze.

Illustration cue: Couples married fifty years start to finish each other's sentences — you become like what you behold. The question is not whether your marriage is being shaped, but by what.

[SLIDE 12 — God Finishes What He Starts]

4. God <u>finishes</u> what He starts.

Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ. — Philippians 1:6 (KJV)

[SLIDE 13 — Patience Is Simply Faith]

Exposition: "Confident" — not wishful. The guarantee of your growth is not your discipline but God's faithfulness: He "will perform it." That frees couples from despair over slow change. You are married to an unfinished person — and so is your spouse — but God does not abandon His projects. Patience with each other is simply faith that God is still working.

Illustration cue: A construction site looks worst mid-project — framing exposed, mud everywhere. If you judge the builder mid-build, you'll misjudge every time. Your spouse is mid-build.

[SLIDE 14 — Key Phrase for the Night]

Key phrase for the night: Growth and change are not the emergency plan for a broken marriage — they are the daily <u>agenda</u> of a healthy one.

[SLIDE 15 — Couple's Exercise — Alone (2 min)]

Couple's Exercise — Weed & Seed (7 min)

Alone (2 min): From Tripp's six weeds — selfishness, busyness, inattention, self-righteousness, fear, laziness — each spouse writes the one that grows fastest in themselves (not in their spouse). Then one seed: a small daily habit to plant.

[SLIDE 16 — Couple's Exercise — Together (5 min)]

Together (5 min): Share your own weed first — never your spouse's. Agree on one shared seed for the week and when it will happen (name the time of day). Leader note: Warn the tables: the exercise fails the moment anyone diagnoses their spouse. Own your own weed.

[SLIDE 17 — Table Talk — Questions 1–2]

Table Talk

Which of the six weeds is most socially acceptable — the one churches let slide? Why is it still deadly? "We become what we behold." What does your marriage spend the most time beholding in a normal week?

[SLIDE 18 — Table Talk — Questions 3–4]

What is one thing your marriage needs to say no to, so growth has room to grow? How does Philippians 1:6 change the way you respond to slow change — in yourself and in your spouse?

[SLIDE 19 — Review & This Week]

Review & Closing

Review: Little moments of biting become seasons of devouring (Galatians 5:15).

Review: The Spirit grows fruit where couples do daily work (Galatians 5:22–23).

Review: We are changed by what we behold (2 Corinthians 3:18).

Review: God finishes what He starts — in you and in your spouse (Philippians 1:6).

This week at home: Work the seed you planted tonight every day, and check in on day three: is the weed shrinking?

Close in prayer at the tables: ask the Spirit for one specific fruit your marriage needs this week.

sermons.title: Night 3: Sturdy Bond Trust
sermons.speaker: Trent Cornwell
sermons.notesHtml:
NIGHT 3 — TRUST Six Gospel Commitments — Commitment #3 "We will work together to build a sturdy bond of trust."

Opening Prayer — confess broken trust and fear of giving it; ask for eyes to see the cracks; ask to trust God first.

INTRODUCTION

  • Trust Fall (volunteers) jk
  • No couple stands at the altar with trust already built — only trust promised
  • Trust = "the fine china of a relationship" (Tripp) — beautiful when present, shattered by one careless drop
  • Two sides of trust: proving trustworthy (honesty, consistency) + entrusting yourself (vulnerability) — a marriage needs both
  • Bridge: the gospel doesn't just forgive our marriages (Night 1) and grow them (Night 2) — it makes them safe enough to trust

I. Trust cracks in small dishonesties. Ephesians 4:25 — "Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another."

  • A. To lie to your spouse is to lie to your own body — "members one of another"
  • B. Dishonesty ≠ only the flat lie — withholding, minimizing, managing the truth all count (Prov. 12:22)
  • C. Application: name the category, not the specific lie
  • D. Illustration: a credit score — years to build, one missed payment to wreck
  • E. Quote: "We simply cannot have a healthy, God-honoring, mutually satisfying marriage without trust." — Tripp

II. Trust is proved in the small, not the grand gesture. Luke 16:10 — "He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much."

  • A. Faithfulness is one fabric — shows up first in the smallest threads (Prov. 31:11)
  • B. Trust isn't rebuilt with one big apology — rebuilt the same way it was worn down
  • C. Illustration: nobody trusts a bridge because of one inspection

III. Trust means taking the armor off. Genesis 2:25 — "And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed."

  • C. Application: where do you still "get dressed" before walking into the room with your spouse?
  • D. Illustration: a soldier only removes armor inside the camp

IV. Trusting God is what frees us to trust each other. Proverbs 3:5–6 — "Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths."

  • A. Every human trust will disappoint somewhere — every spouse is still mid-build (Lam. 3:22–23)
  • B. Not asking a flawed person to become flawless — asking a couple to keep trusting a faithful God
  • C. Illustration: no insurer covers a building it hasn't inspected

KEY PHRASE: Trust is not the wedding gift you're given — it's the fine china you build together, one honest day at a time.

COUPLE'S EXERCISE — Fine China

  • Alone (2 min): name one place you haven't been fully honest; name one small habit to start
  • Together (5 min): share the habit, not necessarily the dishonesty; agree how to notice it this week
  • Leader note: not a confession booth — habit level only

TABLE TALK

  1. Harder to do: be fully honest, or extend trust you don't have to? Why?
  2. Where does trust feel fragile right now, even if nothing's technically broken?
  3. One small, ordinary thing where more consistency would rebuild trust?
  4. How would trusting God more change how much you risk trusting your spouse? (If time: Gen. 2:25 — where do you still "get dressed" emotionally? / Eph. 4:25 — how does a lie work against your own body? / What would it look like to let God rebuild broken trust? / Who modeled trust to you growing up?)

REVIEW

  • Small dishonesties crack trust like fine china (Eph. 4:25)

  • Trust grows where a couple removes the armor (Gen. 2:25)
  • Trusting God frees a couple to trust each other again (Prov. 3:5–6)
  • This week: practice the habit; check in day three

sermons.title: The House that Waited
sermons.speaker: Trent Cornwell
sermons.notesHtml:
Passage: Haggai 1

Big Idea: When God's people put their own comfort above God's house, all their labor comes up empty.

Points

  1. •This is the excuse God would not let stand. (vv. 1–4)
  2. •his is the emptiness God let them feel. (vv. 5–6, 9–11)
  3. •This is the exhortation God still gives to tired builders. (vv. 7–8)

INTRODUCTION

A. Book Overview

1. Starting a short series through one of the smallest, most overlooked books in the Bible

2. Haggai: only 2 chapters — readable in about 5 minutes

3. Don't let the size fool you

4. God packed some of the sharpest, most personal words in Scripture into these two chapters

B. Where Haggai Fits

1. Sits near the end of the Old Testament, among the 12 Minor Prophets

2. “Minor” = shorter, not less important

3. Memory pattern: 5, 12, 5, 5, 12 — Law, History, Poetry, Major Prophets, Minor Prophets (39 books total)

4. Haggai = 10th of the Minor Prophets

5. One of the last three prophetic voices before 400 years of silence

6. Silence broken when the angel told Zacharias God was speaking again

C. Historical Background

1. About 70 years earlier: Judah carried into Babylon, exactly as God's prophets warned

2. Jerusalem destroyed

3. The temple — God's dwelling among His people — burned to the ground

4. God promised through Jeremiah: exile is not the end

5. After 70 years, Cyrus decrees a remnant may go home and rebuild

6. Ezra 1 and 3 — the return: altar rebuilt, temple foundation laid

7. Old men wept, remembering Solomon's temple

8. Young men shouted for joy — so loud you couldn't tell the weeping from the rejoicing

9. Ezra 4 — everything stops: surrounding peoples hire counselors against the builders

10. Persian government issues a stop-work order

11. The order stands for years; delay becomes normal — nobody expects it to move again

D. Where Haggai Opens

1. Sixteen years later

E. One Detail Before We Read

1. This message worked

2. God sends Haggai and Zechariah together

3. Temple finished in about 4 years (Ezra 6)

4. One prophet's obedience — and a nation's — turned 16 years of nothing into 4 years of building

F. Transition and Reading

1. Same sequential walk through Scripture tonight as any other night

2. Before looking closely, read the whole book aloud together — let it wash over us as a whole

3. Read Haggai 1:1–2:23 aloud in its entirety

G. The Thought of Things Unfinished

1. Every fall the calendar fills fast — new school year, new AWANA year, new activities, new sign-up sheets

2. I'm good at starting things. Not always as good at finishing them

3. The kitchen table going to refinish — walk past it, don't think about it — it just waits

4. You have one too: a Bible reading plan, a conversation you need to have, an apology

5. Started with real intention, life got busy, it started waiting

6. The truth none of us likes to say: we're good at finishing what we care about most

7. We're just as good at finding reasons the things God cares about most can wait

8. We all have an unfinished house somewhere

9. A habit of prayer you dropped

10. Your involvement in this church — sitting exactly where it was a year ago

11. Your own walk with Christ

H. Big Idea Transition

1. When God's people put their own comfort above God's work in our lives (house), all their labor comes up empty

2. Let's see it together

I. This is the excuse God would not let stand. (Haggai 1:1–4)

“In the second year of Darius the king, in the sixth month, in the first day of the month, came the word of the LORD by Haggai the prophet unto Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest, saying, Thus speaketh the LORD of hosts, saying, This people say, The time is not come, the time that the LORD's house should be built. Then came the word of the LORD by Haggai the prophet, saying, Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?” (Haggai 1:1–4)

A. God speaks first to the leaders. (v. 1)

1. The word comes to Zerubbabel, the governor, a descendant of David

2. The word comes to Joshua, the high priest

3. Both civil and spiritual leadership are held responsible for sixteen years of stalled obedience

4. Leadership does not wait on the people to change first — leadership goes first

B. The people's excuse sounds reasonable. (v. 2)

1. “The time is not come” is not open refusal — it sounds careful, wise, patient

2. Isn't it wise to wait for the right time instead of rushing in?

3. God is about to show us this was never really about timing

C. God exposes the real reason with one question. (vv. 3–4)

1. God does not argue about calendars — He asks about houses

2. A cieled house was a finished house: paneled, comfortable, complete

3. Their own homes were done while the temple sat in ruins — not half done, finished

4. The issue was never the calendar. The issue was the order of their priorities

Illustration

  • 1. The project in my garage is not there because I lack time
  • 2. I found time to finish other things this year — I found time for what I decided mattered
  • 3. Your bank statement tells the truth faster than your calendar will
  • 4. Judah said “the time is not come” with their mouths, while their cieled houses said something else entirely

Application

1. What is the honest reason your unfinished thing with God is still unfinished?

2. Not the reason you'd say out loud — the real one

3. For parents: family devotions, prayer at the table, a steady seat in church can quietly become the unfinished house

4. AWANA is a wonderful tool, but it was never meant to replace what happens in your home

When God's people put their own comfort above God's house, all their labor comes up empty. Judah's excuse was the first crack. Watch what it grew into.

II. This is the emptiness God let them feel. (Haggai 1:5–6, 9–11)

“Now therefore thus saith the LORD of hosts; Consider your ways. Ye have sown much, and bring in little; ye eat, but ye have not enough; ye drink, but ye are not filled with drink; ye clothe you, but there is none warm; and he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes.” (Haggai 1:5–6)

“Ye looked for much, and, lo, it came to little; and when ye brought it home, I did blow upon it. Why? saith the LORD of hosts. Because of mine house that is waste, and ye run every man unto his own house. Therefore the heaven over you is stayed from dew, and the earth is stayed from her fruit. And I called for a drought upon the land, and upon the mountains, and upon the corn, and upon the new wine, and upon the oil, and upon that which the ground bringeth forth, and upon men, and upon cattle, and upon all the labour of the hands.” (Haggai 1:9–11)

A. “Consider your ways” — a command to stop and examine the road you are actually walking. (v. 5)

B. God names the exhaustion they already felt. (v. 6)

1. Sow much, bring in little

2. Eat, and stay hungry

3. Drink, and stay thirsty

4. Clothe yourself, and stay cold

5. Earn wages that vanish, like a bag with holes in the bottom

6. This mirrors the old covenant warning of Deuteronomy 28

7. God was not improvising a punishment — He was keeping His word

C. God says this emptiness was not an accident. (vv. 9–11)

1. “I did blow upon it” — this was not bad luck

2. This was God speaking directly

3. “Because of mine house that is waste, and ye run every man unto his own house”

4. He called for the drought. He stopped the dew. He stopped the harvest. On purpose

5. “Ye run every man unto his own house” pictures a scattered community

6. Everyone chasing his own project instead of gathering to build one house together

D. Does this mean every hard season is God punishing me for something I've neglected?

1. No — Scripture never lets us say that about every hardship

2. But here, in this specific moment, God tells us plainly what the connection was Illustration

  • Think about a bag with a hole in the bottom
  • You can keep pouring more in, but it will never fill up until someone fixes the hole

Application

1. Where do you feel that bag-with-holes feeling right now?

2. Tired but not rested. Busy but not satisfied

3. Before you assume the answer is do more, consider whether the answer is go back

4. Go back and finish what you already started with God

This is a description of the bag with holes so many of us are living out of right now. But God is not done talking — He does not leave them in the emptiness.

III. This is the exhortation God still gives to tired builders. (Haggai 1:7–8)

“Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Consider your ways. Go up to the mountain, and bring wood, and build the house; and I will take pleasure in it, and I will be glorified, saith the LORD.” (Haggai 1:7–8)

A. God repeats Himself on purpose. (v. 7)

1. “Consider your ways,” again

2. Some things are worth saying twice

B. God's next step is small enough to obey today. (v. 8)

1. Go up to the mountain

2. Bring wood

3. Build the house

4. Three simple, physical, doable actions, after sixteen years of nothing

5. God did not ask for a finished masterpiece — He asked for the next step

C. God attaches the outcome to Himself, not to them. (v. 8)

1. “I will take pleasure in it, and I will be glorified”

2. He puts the weight of the outcome on Himself

3. Their job was to go get the wood. His job was everything the wood became

D. What if I start again and fail again?

1. You will be in good company with every believer who has ever obeyed God one imperfect step at a time

2. God did not ask this tired, discouraged, sixteen-years-behind people for a guarantee of success

3. He asked for wood

Illustration

  • The project in my garage does not need me to finish the whole room tonight
  • It needs me to pick up the first piece and start

Application

1. What is the one small, doable, physical next step God is asking of you?

2. Not the whole rebuild — just the first piece of wood

3. Maybe your mountain is a regular seat with your family this year instead of an occasional one

4. Maybe it's signing up to help with these kids instead of just dropping them off

5. Maybe it has nothing to do with this building at all, and everything to do with a phone call you've been putting off

Whatever it is, God is not asking for the whole mountain tonight. He is asking for the first log.

CONCLUSION

1. God spoke first to the leaders, then to the people

2. He exposed an excuse that had been hiding behind sixteen years of finished houses and an unfinished temple

3. He let them feel the emptiness of chasing everything except the one thing He had asked for

4. In mercy, He did not walk away from them

5. He gave them a doable next step and a promise that the outcome was His to carry, not theirs

Good News

1. This ancient, unfinished building points somewhere you might not expect

2. Later in this book, God promises this same temple would one day be filled with a glory greater than Solomon's house ever held

3. That promise found its answer when Jesus walked into that rebuilt temple and stood there in the flesh

4. God's own glory dwelling among His people again

5. When religious leaders demanded a sign, Jesus pointed to Himself: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up”

6. John tells us plainly, “he spake of the temple of his body” (John 2:19, 21)

7. The house Zerubbabel's generation built was never the final house — it was a signpost

8. Pointing forward to a greater house God Himself would build with His own body, and raise on the third day

9. Israel was told: consider your ways, go build, and I will be pleased

10. You and I are not saved by finally getting our priorities perfectly ordered

11. Jesus is the house we could never finish building

12. He lived the perfectly obedient life we could not live

13. He never once let His Father's business wait for His own comfort

14. On the cross He said, “It is finished” — not “consider your ways and try harder forever”

15. Your standing with God does not rest on how well you rebuild

16. It rests on what Christ already completed in your place

Questions for You

1. What is your unfinished house?

2. Not the whole list — just the one thing God brought to mind while we read this together

3. Name it honestly

4. This week, go get one piece of wood

5. One prayer. One conversation. One step back toward the thing you started with God and quietly let sit

We

1. As a church family, especially tonight, as we launch a new year with these kids and families

2. Let's not let AWANA, school, or any good and busy thing become one more finished house

3. That quietly crowds out what God actually asked us to build together

4. Let's go up to the mountain. Let's bring the wood. Let's build

Invitation

1. If tonight you realize the real issue is bigger than a stalled project

2. If you have never trusted Jesus Christ, the One who finished what none of us could

3. I want to give you the chance to respond to Him right now

The project in my garage does not need me to finish the whole room tonight

It needs me to pick up the first piece and start

Application

1. What is the one small, doable, physical next step God is asking of you?

2. Not the whole rebuild — just the first piece of wood

3. Maybe your mountain is a regular seat with your family this year instead of an occasional one

4. Maybe it's signing up to help with these kids instead of just dropping them off

5. Maybe it has nothing to do with this building at all, and everything to do with a phone call you've been putting off

Whatever it is, God is not asking for the whole mountain tonight. He is asking for the first log.

CONCLUSION

1. God spoke first to the leaders, then to the people

2. He exposed an excuse that had been hiding behind sixteen years of finished houses and an unfinished temple

3. He let them feel the emptiness of chasing everything except the one thing He had asked for

4. In mercy, He did not walk away from them

5. He gave them a doable next step and a promise that the outcome was His to carry, not theirs

Good News

1. This ancient, unfinished building points somewhere you might not expect

2. Later in this book, God promises this same temple would one day be filled with a glory greater than Solomon's house ever held

3. That promise found its answer when Jesus walked into that rebuilt temple and stood there in the flesh

4. God's own glory dwelling among His people again

5. When religious leaders demanded a sign, Jesus pointed to Himself: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up”

6. John tells us plainly, “he spake of the temple of his body” (John 2:19, 21)

7. The house Zerubbabel's generation built was never the final house — it was a signpost

8. Pointing forward to a greater house God Himself would build with His own body, and raise on the third day

9. Israel was told: consider your ways, go build, and I will be pleased

10. You and I are not saved by finally getting our priorities perfectly ordered

11. Jesus is the house we could never finish building

12. He lived the perfectly obedient life we could not live

13. He never once let His Father's business wait for His own comfort

14. On the cross He said, “It is finished” — not “consider your ways and try harder forever”

15. Your standing with God does not rest on how well you rebuild

16. It rests on what Christ already completed in your place

Questions for You

1. What is your unfinished house?

2. Not the whole list — just the one thing God brought to mind while we read this together

3. Name it honestly

4. This week, go get one piece of wood

5. One prayer. One conversation. One step back toward the thing you started with God and quietly let sit

We

1. As a church family, especially tonight, as we launch a new year with these kids and families

2. Let's not let AWANA, school, or any good and busy thing become one more finished house

3. That quietly crowds out what God actually asked us to build together

4. Let's go up to the mountain. Let's bring the wood. Let's build

Invitation

1. If tonight you realize the real issue is bigger than a stalled project

2. If you have never trusted Jesus Christ, the One who finished what none of us could

3. I want to give you the chance to respond to Him right now

Bible Reading

Proverbs 29:18 “18 Where there is no vision, the people perish: but he that keepeth the law, happy is he.”

18 Where there is no vision, the people perish: but he that keepeth the law, happy is he.

  • The word ‘vision’ here is — divine revelation.
  • The Word of God. The vision and the law are the same thing.
  • Without Scripture, people do not just struggle. They perish.

As we approach the Bible

  1. This Book is not our to edit.
  2. We come as humble students.

“Wrong I may be — but a heretic I am not. If I err, correct me with the Word.”

  1. Obedience is our guiding hermeneutic.

We cannot seek to comprehend what we have already decided to ignore.

Prayer by Chuck Littlefield (importance of protecting the ministry of God’s Word)

Sermon Introduction

The question every human being eventually asks: where did we come from, and how did this all start?

Not merely an academic question.

The answer runs the operating system of everything else — worth, meaning, identity, what you do with your life.

Every culture answers this question.

  • Every answer carries assumptions about who you are and what you are worth.
  • Egyptian religion was not primitive superstition. It was a complete worldview — a total account of reality, meaning, worth, and what happens when you die.
  • It answered every question Genesis 1 answers. It just answered them differently.

1 In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. 2 And the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters. 3 And God said, Let there be light: and there was light. 4 And God saw the light, that it was good: and God divided the light from the darkness. 5 And God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And the evening and the morning were the first day. 6 And God said, Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters. 7 And God made the firmament, and divided the waters which were under the firmament from the waters which were above the firmament: and it was so. 8 And God called the firmament Heaven. And the evening and the morning were the second day. 9 And God said, Let the waters under the heaven be gathered together unto one place, and let the dry land appear: and it was so. 10 And God called the dry land Earth; and the gathering together of the waters called he Seas: and God saw that it was good. 11 And God said, Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind, whose seed is in itself, upon the earth: and it was so. 12 And the earth brought forth grass, and herb yielding seed after his kind, and the tree yielding fruit, whose seed was in itself, after his kind: and God saw that it was good. 13 And the evening and the morning were the third day. 14 And God said, Let there be lights in the firmament of the heaven to divide the day from the night; and let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years: 15 And let them be for lights in the firmament of the heaven to give light upon the earth: and it was so. 16 And God made two great lights; the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night: he made the stars also. 17 And God set them in the firmament of the heaven to give light upon the earth, 18 And to rule over the day and over the night, and to divide the light from the darkness: and God saw that it was good. 19 And the evening and the morning were the fourth day. 20 And God said, Let the waters bring forth abundantly the moving creature that hath life, and fowl that may fly above the earth in the open firmament of heaven. 21 And God created great whales, and every living creature that moveth, which the waters brought forth abundantly, after their kind, and every winged fowl after his kind: and God saw that it was good. 22 And God blessed them, saying, Be fruitful, and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas, and let fowl multiply in the earth. 23 And the evening and the morning were the fifth day. 24 And God said, Let the earth bring forth the living creature after his kind, cattle, and creeping thing, and beast of the earth after his kind: and it was so. 25 And God made the beast of the earth after his kind, and cattle after their kind, and every thing that creepeth upon the earth after his kind: and God saw that it was good. 26 And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth. 27 So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them. 28 And God blessed them, and God said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it: and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over every living thing that moveth upon the earth. 29 And God said, Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed, which is upon the face of all the earth, and every tree, in the which is the fruit of a tree yielding seed; to you it shall be for meat. 30 And to every beast of the earth, and to every fowl of the air, and to every thing that creepeth upon the earth, wherein there is life, I have given every green herb for meat: and it was so. 31 And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. And the evening and the morning were the sixth day.

What Egypt said about God:

  • No single God. Dozens of gods.
  • The universe was not the work of one Creator. It was the product of divine conflict and negotiation.
  • The gods were not all-powerful.
  • Ra (the sun god) fought the giant serpent Apep every night in the underworld.
  • If he lost, the sun would not rise.
  • Priests performed elaborate rituals before dawn to help him win.
  • The cosmic order was fragile and required human effort to sustain.

The gods had backstories.

  • They were born, they died, they were restored.
  • They were players in a story that preceded them.
  • None of them was ultimate.

What Egypt said about the world:

  1. The Nile flooding on schedule meant Hapi the river god was pleased.
  2. A poor flood meant the gods were angry.
  3. Every harvest, every drought, every birth was a divine cause requiring ritual response.
  4. Nothing in nature was ordinary. Everything was a god.

What Egypt said about you:

  1. Human beings were created to serve the gods through labor.
  2. You existed to meet the needs of beings more powerful than you.
  3. Worth equals output.
  4. A slave who could not work had no standing.
  5. Only Pharaoh bore the divine image — the son of Ra. No one else had that standing.
  6. Your eternal fate depended on your ritual performance in this life.

What our world says:

  1. No author. No design. The universe appeared from nothing by chance. You are a product of an unguided process.
  2. Your worth is your output. Your value is your productivity, your appearance, your platform, your salary. A person who cannot produce has diminishing standing.
  3. You construct your own identity. You decide who you are. No one has the authority to tell you otherwise.
  4. When you die, nothing was lost except chemistry.

Same story. Updated vocabulary. Different gods, same slavery.

  • Israel did not observe this from a distance.
  • They breathed it for four hundred years.
  • Ten generations of children raised inside that story.
  • It does not just change what you think. It changes what feels true.
  • Genesis 1 was written for people coming out of Egypt. Every sentence is a direct answer to what Egypt said.

The God who made everything by his word declared it finished and very good — which means he alone has the authority to tell you who he is, what the world is, and who you are.

If the God of Genesis 1 is who he says he is — why we look to anyone else to tell us your reason for living.

Sermon Introduction

The question every human being eventually asks: where did we come from, and how did this all start?

Not merely an academic question. 

The answer runs the operating system of everything else — worth, meaning, identity, what you do with your life.

Every culture answers this question. 

Every answer carries assumptions about who you are and what you are worth.

Egyptian religion was not primitive superstition. It was a complete worldview — a total account of reality, meaning, worth, and what happens when you die. 

It answered every question Genesis 1 answers. It just answered them differently.

1 In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.

What Egypt said about God:

No single God. Dozens of gods. 

The universe was not the work of one Creator. It was the product of divine conflict and negotiation.

The gods were not all-powerful. 

Ra (the sun god) fought the giant serpent Apep every night in the underworld. 

If he lost, the sun would not rise. 

Priests performed elaborate rituals before dawn to help him win. 

The cosmic order was fragile and required human effort to sustain.

The gods had backstories. 

They were born, they died, they were restored. 

They were players in a story that preceded them. 

None of them was ultimate.

What Egypt said about the world:

The Nile flooding on schedule meant Hapi the river god was pleased. 

A poor flood meant the gods were angry. 

Every harvest, every drought, every birth was a divine cause requiring ritual response. 

Nothing in nature was ordinary. Everything was a god.

Human beings were created to serve the gods through labor. 

You existed to meet the needs of beings more powerful than you. 

Worth equals output. 

A slave who could not work had no standing.

Your eternal fate depended on your ritual performance in this life.

No author. No design. The universe appeared from nothing by chance. You are a product of an unguided process.

Your worth is your output. Your value is your productivity, your appearance, your platform, your salary. A person who cannot produce has diminishing standing.

You construct your own identity. You decide who you are. No one has the authority to tell you otherwise.

When you die, nothing was lost except chemistry.

Same story. Updated vocabulary. Different gods, same slavery.

Ten generations of children raised inside that story.

The slave woman making bricks bore it as fully as the man whose face was on the coins. 

Everything in six days was preparation for you. 

The light, the sky, the land, the fruit trees, the fish, the cattle — all of it set and waiting before you arrived. 

You are not the universe’s afterthought. We are why God created the world as He did.

B. Your worth was declared before you did anything.

Ancient kings placed statues in conquered territory to declare ownership. 

God placed his image in creation. 

Every human being is a living declaration that this world belongs to him.

This dignity arrives before achievement, before failure, before a diagnosis or a bank balance or a report card. It precedes everything you have ever done.

Read the verdict pattern aloud. 

Light — good. 

Sky — good. 

Land — good. 

Sun — good. 

Fish — good. 

Animals — good. Then you. 

Everything he had made — very good. 

Your presence changed the evaluation. 

Both male and female — explicitly. 

In every surrounding culture, women were property. 

Genesis 1:27 gives the full image to both. Equally. 

27 So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.

This was almost incomprehensible in the ancient world.

In Egypt, a woman’s standing depended on her husband’s rank. Genesis 1:27 gives her the same image as Pharaoh claim to have. 

27 So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.

The galaxies are unimaginably larger than you. 

But you know they exist. 

They do not know you exist. 

Size is not the measure of value. You bear the image of God. A galaxy does not. 

C. The damaged image is being restored and God invites you into his rest.

Someone is thinking: but we are fallen. 

We are broken. How can God say very good? He is not saying it about what we became. He is saying it about what he made. Genesis 1 is before the fall. Genesis 3 is the fall. The distance between them — between what he made and what we chose — is exactly what Christ came to close.

26 And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth. 

27 So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them. 

28 And God blessed them, and God said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it: and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over every living thing that moveth upon the earth. 

29 And God said, Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed, which is upon the face of all the earth, and every tree, in the which is the fruit of a tree yielding seed; to you it shall be for meat. 

30 And to every beast of the earth, and to every fowl of the air, and to every thing that creepeth upon the earth, wherein there is life, I have given every green herb for meat: and it was so. 

31 And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. And the evening and the morning were the sixth day.

The only question Genesis 1 leaves you with is this: whose voice are you going to believe?

1 In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. 

2 And the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters. 

3 And God said, Let there be light: and there was light. 

4 And God saw the light, that it was good: and God divided the light from the darkness. 

5 And God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And the evening and the morning were the first day. 

6 And God said, Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters. 

7 And God made the firmament, and divided the waters which were under the firmament from the waters which were above the firmament: and it was so. 

8 And God called the firmament Heaven. And the evening and the morning were the second day. 

9 And God said, Let the waters under the heaven be gathered together unto one place, and let the dry land appear: and it was so. 

10 And God called the dry land Earth; and the gathering together of the waters called he Seas: and God saw that it was good. 

11 And God said, Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind, whose seed is in itself, upon the earth: and it was so. 

12 And the earth brought forth grass, and herb yielding seed after his kind, and the tree yielding fruit, whose seed was in itself, after his kind: and God saw that it was good. 

13 And the evening and the morning were the third day. 

14 And God said, Let there be lights in the firmament of the heaven to divide the day from the night; and let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years: 

15 And let them be for lights in the firmament of the heaven to give light upon the earth: and it was so. 

16 And God made two great lights; the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night: he made the stars also. 

17 And God set them in the firmament of the heaven to give light upon the earth, 

18 And to rule over the day and over the night, and to divide the light from the darkness: and God saw that it was good. 

19 And the evening and the morning were the fourth day. 

20 And God said, Let the waters bring forth abundantly the moving creature that hath life, and fowl that may fly above the earth in the open firmament of heaven. 

21 And God created great whales, and every living creature that moveth, which the waters brought forth abundantly, after their kind, and every winged fowl after his kind: and God saw that it was good. 

22 And God blessed them, saying, Be fruitful, and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas, and let fowl multiply in the earth. 

23 And the evening and the morning were the fifth day. 

24 And God said, Let the earth bring forth the living creature after his kind, cattle, and creeping thing, and beast of the earth after his kind: and it was so. 

25 And God made the beast of the earth after his kind, and cattle after their kind, and every thing that creepeth upon the earth after his kind: and God saw that it was good. 

26 And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth. 

27 So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them. 

28 And God blessed them, and God said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it: and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over every living thing that moveth upon the earth. 

29 And God said, Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed, which is upon the face of all the earth, and every tree, in the which is the fruit of a tree yielding seed; to you it shall be for meat. 

30 And to every beast of the earth, and to every fowl of the air, and to every thing that creepeth upon the earth, wherein there is life, I have given every green herb for meat: and it was so. 

31 And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. And the evening and the morning were the sixth day.

The culture’s answer says: you are an accident, your worth is your output, and you define yourself. That answer has been running for four thousand years and it has never once set anyone free.

God’s answer says: I made you, I declared you very good, my Son died to restore what was broken, and the work is finished. Enter the rest.

Ancient list 

The Nile is not a god. 

The sun is not a god. 

Pharaoh is not a god.

Modern list 

Your bank account is not a god. 

Your reputation is not a god. 

Your body is not a god. 

Your political party is not a god. 

Technology is not a god. 

The algorithm that tells you whether you matter today is not a god.

You are not a slave created to serve any of them. You bear the image of the one true God who made everything by his word.

Revelation 4:11 “11 Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they are and were created.” 

11 Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they are and were created.

In the beginning, God. That is what Egypt never told you. But today we have been to told and this changes everything about what we think about this world and why we are here.

sermons.title: THE WAY LIFE WAS MEANT TO BE
sermons.speaker: Trent Cornwell
sermons.notesHtml:
Before Adam ever acted, God had already finished His work, formed him personally, and entrusted him with a choice — making grateful obedience the only fitting response to all that God is and all that God gives.

REVIEW

[What Egypt Never Told You — Dr. Wise]

Genesis 1 — Who made the world?

Genesis 2 — What kind of world did God make for man to live in?

Today: Work as a gift. Rest as a rhythm. Boundaries as blessings.

INTRODUCTION

Library / Britannica entry on “week” — seven days, artificially devised, no astronomical basis — traced to the ancient Jews and Genesis.

The day = earth spinning. The year = earth circling the sun. The week? Nothing in the heavens runs on a seven-day count. And yet the whole world does.

When God builds something into His world, it works. Structurally. You cannot engineer your way around it.

But the week is just one instruction. Genesis 2 shows us the whole design.

“Is God’s design a cage to you?”

Somewhere in this room someone is feeling exactly that — His Word pointing one way, everything in you pointing another.

That is the oldest question in the world. Genesis 2 is the last record of a world before anyone answered it badly.

His design is not the condition of His love. It is the expression of it.

TRANSITION: Walk with me into the garden. Three things God did before Adam did anything. Each one comes with an invitation.

1. A WORLD WHERE GOD’S PROVISION MEETS US BEFORE OUR WORK BEGINS.

Genesis 2:1–3

Adam’s first full day was not a workday. He woke into a world already finished, furnished, called very good. He did not earn it. He received it.

God provides before man arrives.

A. God’s work was complete. (v. 1–2a)

  1. The piling up of completion words:
  2. finished,
  3. ended,
  4. all the host of them.
  5. Nothing missing. Nothing needs improvement.
  6. Why “heavens” (pl.) in 2:1 vs. “heaven” in 1:1? Grammar, not theology. Collective summary of all above the earth.

[Illustration: David Rackley’s roof — shingles, nails, flashing, every piece in place before anyone moves in.]

B. God’s rest was exemplary. (v. 2b)

  1. Rhythm built into the week for man’s good. Mark 2:27 “27 And he said unto them, The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath:”
  2. Sabbath at Sinai extended to sons, daughters, servants, strangers, cattle (Exod 20:10). Built-in dignity for every worker.
  3. Did God need a nap? No. Isaiah 40:28 “28 Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary? there is no searching of his understanding.”

He rested because the work was finished.

C. God’s blessing made the day holy. (v. 3)

  1. First thing called holy in Scripture — not a mountain, nation, or building.
  2. A day. Before God sanctifies a place, He sanctifies time. This verse is why that Britannica entry exists.

“When God established man’s week, He pointed back to His own. The pattern has force because the days are the same kind of days.” —

[More on this Wednesday night — the sabbath deserves more time.]

TRANSITION: God hands Adam a finished world. But if everything is done, why am I here? Verses 4–15 answer that. Provision is not the whole gift. There is also purpose.

2. A WORLD WHERE GOD’S PURPOSE, NOT IDLENESS, DEFINES OUR WORK.

Genesis 2:4–15

Not general. Personal. A specific man, specific garden, specific work. Before Adam made a choice, God had already invested everything.

A. God formed man intimately. (v. 4–7)

  1. New name: Genesis 1 = Elohim (power, ×35).
  2. Genesis 2:4 = LORD God (Jehovah Elohim).
  3. The God of galaxies introduces Himself by His personal name the moment He deals personally with man.
  4. Verse 7 — the verb is a potter shaping clay.
  5. Dust = dependence.
  6. God’s breath = unlike anything else He made.

Q: Is Genesis 2 a contradictory creation account? No. Ch. 1 = wide angle. Ch. 2 = zoom on day six. Same design, closer lens, closer name.

B. God placed man intentionally. (v. 8–14)

God plants, then places the man. Adam did not design or stock the garden. Provision comes before assignment. Two named trees (v. 9): tree of life — freely available. Mark it. It will not appear again until the last chapter of the Bible. Real geography: Tigris, Euphrates. The Bible makes a historical claim.

C. God employed man meaningfully. (v. 15)

“To dress it and to keep it.”

  1. Work existed before the fall.
  2. Meaningful labor is part of paradise. Verse 5: “no man to till the ground.”
  3. The world was waiting for its worker. Purpose was woven in before Adam drew breath.
  4. Fascinating fact: abad (serve) + shamar (guard) reappear in Num 3:7–8 for priestly tabernacle service.
  5. Eden = first sanctuary.
  6. Adam = first priest-gardener. Work under God is worship.

Numbers 3:7–8 “7 And they shall keep his charge, and the charge of the whole congregation before the tabernacle of the congregation, to do the service of the tabernacle. 8 And they shall keep all the instruments of the tabernacle of the congregation, and the charge of the children of Israel, to do the service of the tabernacle.”

  • “We were none of us sent into the world to be idle.” — Matthew Henry

Commencement Speeches: AI and jobs — blue, white, no collar — work matters and should not be seen as a disease to eradicate.

TRANSITION: A finished world. A man formed with purpose. One more thing — and it is the one we least expect. For the first time in this chapter, God speaks directly to the man.

3. A WORLD WHERE EVERY CHOICE CARRIES MORAL WEIGHT.

Genesis 2:16–17

A. The permission was wide. (v. 16)

  1. “Of every tree thou mayest freely eat.”
  2. One restriction in a world of generosity.
  3. People fixate on the no.
  4. The text shouts a thousand yeses.
  5. God’s default posture is generosity. “Freely eat” = emphatic Hebrew doubling: eating thou mayest eat. Hold onto that grammar. You will hear it again.

B. The prohibition was singular. (v. 17a)

  1. One tree. One boundary.
  2. One question underneath it all.
  3. The tree completed the garden.
  4. Without it, Eden was a cage. With it, Eden was a covenant.
  5. Without the tree Adam obeys — but has no choice.
  6. A robot cannot worship.
  7. A puppet cannot love.
  8. Every morning he passed it without eating = an act of worship: I trust You. You are God. I am not.

Q: Why put the tree there? Love that cannot choose is not love. Not danger. Dignity.

Q: “Knowledge of good and evil”? Not information — authority. Claiming the right to define good and evil for oneself. Who gets to be God?

C. The penalty was honest. (v. 17b)

  1. Grace tells the truth in advance. God did not hide the stakes.
  2. Q: “Thou shalt surely die”? Dying thou shalt die — emphatic. Death in every dimension. Same doubling as “freely eat” — as extravagant in warning as in permission.
  3. Adam could not see what God could see. He only needed to trust the heart of the One who gave him everything.

“When you cannot trace His hand, you can trust His heart.” — Charles Spurgeon

TRANSITION: That tree is not the last tree in the Bible. It is only the first.

GOOD NEWS — WHAT GENESIS 2 SETS IN MOTION

Every thread Moses planted here runs straight to the cross.

The rest points forward —

Hebrews 4:9 “9 There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God.”

We receive it the same way Adam did — not by what we achieve but by what God has already finished.

The forming points forward —

The God who made you personally has not stopped caring personally about what happens to you.

The tree in this story will wait, but there is another we must not wait for

The tree points forward most of all —

1 Corinthians 15:45 “45 And so it is written, The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit.”

Both men stood before a tree. Both carried the destiny of many.

Luke 22:42 “42 Saying, Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.”

He answered Adam’s question — correctly, completely, on behalf of all who trust Him.

And then He was nailed to a tree.

1 Peter 2:24 “24 Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed.”

Romans 5:19 “19 For as by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.”

Genesis 2 began with a garden and a tree of life. The Bible ends the same way.

Revelation 22:2

There is a perfect Savior — and through Him, the world God always intended is coming back.

APPLICATION

Most of us live as if provision is something we produce, purpose is something we find, and boundaries are something we endure. Genesis 2 says all three are backwards.

On rest: Adam’s first day was a gift before any work began. If you can’t sit down without feeling behind, you haven’t believed Point 1. This week — one evening, received, not earned.

On work: Whatever your garden is — desk, classroom, job site, kitchen — tend it like someone placed there, not stuck there.

On generosity: Count the yeses before you resent the no. Most of us have never taken a full inventory of the yes column.

OUR CHURCH TOGETHER

A people who rest without guilt, work without idolatry, and obey without resentment become a preview of Eden — a small green garden in a weary world.one.

CONCLUSION

Before Adam drew his first breath, the world was already finished. He woke into a world he did not build, could not earn, did nothing to deserve.

THAT IS POINT 1. God’s provision came before Adam’s performance — and before yours.

God gave him a name, a garden, a job. Formed him personally. Placed him intentionally. Employed him meaningfully.

THAT IS POINT 2. You were made on purpose, for a purpose.

God gave him a choice. Not to test him — to honor him. Every morning he passed that tree was an act of worship.

THAT IS POINT 3. Every choice carries moral weight.

1. You can trust this God with your rest — He finished the work before you began.

2. You can trust this God with your work — He made you on purpose, for a purpose.

3. You can trust this God with your choices — He told you the truth before you ever faced the tree.

Every morning Adam walked past that tree.

Every afternoon Adam walked past that tree.

Every evening Adam walked past that tree.

And every time he passed it he was answering the question Genesis 2 has been asking from verse one:

Do I trust the God who gave me everything?

What Adam did at his tree is a story for another Sunday.

What Jesus did at His tree cannot wait.

The Last Adam received no finished world. He stepped into a broken one, took the curse, and answered the question correctly on behalf of everyone who would trust Him.

Romans 5:19 “19 For as by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.”

Some of you need to trust Christ for the first time today.

Some of you need to surrender the area where you know God’s Word but have been resisting it.

Some of you came in feeling like God’s design is a cage. I hope you are leaving knowing it is a gift.

Trust His Word. Trust His wisdom. Trust His heart.

Life works best God’s way.

Next week: For the first time in the Bible, God looks at something and says it is not good. What was it? Genesis 2:18–25 — the creation of woman, the first marriage, and God’s blueprint for men, women, and family.

sermons.speaker: Trent Cornwell
sermons.notesHtml:
Text: Genesis 2:18–25

Big Idea: God saw what we couldn't do alone and built exactly what we needed before we knew to ask.

Review of Part 1

Two weeks ago we walked through Genesis 2:1–17 and established the first three points of a six-part picture of the world God designed —

  1. a world where God's provision meets us before our performance begins
  2. where God's purpose defines our work
  3. where every choice carries moral weight.

Today we pick up at verse 18 and see the rest of what He designed.

Sermon Introduction

I was travelling — promoting missions, visiting churches, living out of a suitcase. Thanksgiving came and I was too far from Kentucky to make it home. So I did what any reasonable person does when they are alone on a national holiday: I went to Golden Corral. By myself. On Thanksgiving…

When we think of Genesis 2, we think of man and woman. But before it is a passage about marriage, it is a passage about us — about what human beings cannot do alone and what God does about it.

Every generation tries to solve loneliness with more connection. And the ache persists because we keep treating the symptom while the disease goes undiagnosed. We are not just lonely. We are attempting a life God never designed a single person to carry. FThe mandate of Genesis 1:28 — given to them, plural — was never private.

We are trying to do alone what was built for more than one.

Transition: Three things God did in these eight verses. Each one is a window into the world He designed.

1. A world where God Himself named what was missing.

Genesis 2:18 “18 And the LORD God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him.”

This is the only thing God has ever called not good in the original creation. Six times in Genesis 1 — good. End of day six — very good. Now, inside that very good world: not good.

A. The not good is a Trinitarian diagnosis.

  1. God did not say Adam was sad. He said Adam was alone — and a solitary image cannot display a relational God.
  2. The God who made Adam is Trinity — Father, Son, Holy Spirit in eternal self-giving communion. Adam's relational incompleteness is not incidental. It is iconic. One person cannot mirror the community of the Godhead.
  3. The not good is not a deficiency in God's provision. It is a feature of the image. God built Adam to need what God Himself has always been — love in relationship.

B. The not good is a missional diagnosis.

  1. Genesis 1:28 was given to them — plural. The mandate to fill and subdue the earth requires two. One man could not do it.
  2. What Adam literally could not do alone: reflect the full image of God, reproduce, fill the earth, subdue the earth, exercise dominion across time, or model covenant love. A covenant requires two parties. Faithful love needs both a giver and a receiver.
  3. Adam was not simply lonely. He was unable. God is not designing a remedy for feelings. He is completing the team for the mission.

C. God announced the answer before He delivered it.

  1. "I will make him a helper corresponding to him." The word for helper is used sixteen times in the Old Testament to describe God Himself coming to Israel's aid in battle, in crisis, against enemies too strong to face alone. Psalm 121:2. It is not a word of lesser status. It is a word for the one who arrives when the odds are impossible.
  2. Corresponding to him means his counterpart — facing him, matching him, perfectly complementary.
  3. Differentiated role within equal dignity, for a purpose larger than either of them.
Transition: God named the not good and announced what He would build. But before He provided it, He made Adam feel the full weight of the gap before He filled it. What God is about to take from Adam's side in verse 21 is already a portrait of what He will one day take from the Last Adam's side on Calvary. The pattern is already in the text.

2. A world where God built what the whole world couldn't provide.

Genesis 2:21–22 “21 And the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept: and he took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh instead thereof; 22 And the rib, which the LORD God had taken from man, made he a woman, and brought her unto the man.”

God did not improvise. The Hebrew word translated made in verse 22 is the architectural word — the same word used for building the tabernacle and the temple. Deliberate, purposeful construction. The word you use when the builder knows exactly what he is doing and why.

God built the woman. He built her the way He builds everything He intends to last.

A. God first showed Adam what nothing else could be. (v. 19–20)

  1. God brings every creature to Adam to name — not a biology lesson, but a surgical preparation. Adam catalogued all of creation. Nothing corresponded.
  2. "But for Adam there was not found a helper corresponding to him." The search was exhaustive. And empty.
  3. God was not surprised. He was teaching Adam to understand the shape of his need before He filled it. When the woman arrives, Adam receives the answer to a need he has just spent all of creation learning he has.
  4. 1 Timothy 2:13 — Paul draws a theological principle directly from this order. Not cultural accommodation. He is doing theology from the creation account.

B. What the building word tells us about how God builds.

  1. Proverbs 14:1 uses the same architectural word: "Every wise woman builds her house." The wise woman and the God who made her share the same verb. What God built into her, she now does in her household. The architect's instinct passes to the one He architected.
  2. Proverbs 31 is the fullest portrait of that word in motion.
  3. She considers a field and buys it.
  4. She opens her mouth with wisdom.
  5. She looks well to the ways of her household.
  6. Not a list of virtues — a description of someone built for purposeful, intelligent, load-bearing work. The helper of Genesis 2 and the woman of Proverbs 31 are the same design — one in blueprint, one in operation.

C. Passive man, active God — the grammar of grace. (v. 21–22)

  1. Every verb in verses 21–22 has God as the subject. Adam contributes nothing. He is asleep.
  2. This is the shape of every covenant God makes.
  3. In Genesis 15:12 God put Abraham into a deep sleep and cut the covenant alone — while Abraham lay unconscious.
  4. Israel contributed nothing to the Exodus. Grace, by definition, acts on the passive.
  5. The creation of the woman is the first sermon on grace: the gift arrives while the recipient sleeps.
  6. God took from Adam's side — the same word used for the sides of the ark, the tabernacle, the temple. Not spare parts. His own substance. The gift cost him something.

"The woman was made of a rib out of the side of Adam; not made out of his head to rule over him, nor out of his feet to be trampled upon by him, but out of his side to be equal with him, under his arm to be protected, and near his heart to be beloved." — Matthew Henry

  1. God brought her to the man.
  2. The language is that of presenting an offering.
  3. God is the Father of the bride at the first wedding.
  4. Adam woke up to a gift he did not search for, could not have designed, and did nothing to deserve.
Transition: Adam was asleep when God did His most important work. Moses wrote these words for a nation about to enter Canaan a land full of competing definitions of family and marriage. God's word before they crossed the Jordan: the pattern was not invented by a culture. It was built before any culture existed.

3. A world where love was designed for total belonging.

Genesis 2:24 “24 Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”

Most quoted verse from Genesis in the New Testament. Jesus cites it. Paul cites it. Not law design. Predates every nation, every law code, every cultural definition of marriage. Creation architecture built for permanence.

A. The first human words in Scripture were a wedding poem. (v. 23)

  1. Adam has been silent until now. The first recorded speech of any human being in all of Scripture is a poem about his wife.
  2. "This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh." Recognition and delight — emphatic, total, joyful.
  3. He gives her a name that carries his own name inside it. Covenant language: she bears his identity in her identity and is therefore fit to stand with him in his calling.

B. Verse 24 is a hermeneutical key, not merely a marriage text. (v. 24)

  1. "Therefore" — not cultural observation. Foundational principle grounded in the act of creation.
  2. Matthew 19:4–5 — when the Pharisees ask about divorce, Jesus does not go to Mosaic law first. He goes to creation. "What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder." The authority is the Creator's, not the culture's.
  3. Moses wrote one sentence that both Jesus and Paul needed, centuries apart, for different arguments. Jesus uses it to establish the permanence of marriage. Paul uses it in Ephesians 5:31–32 to ground the mystery of the church. That verse carried more meaning than any single reading exhausts — because it was designed to.
  4. Three covenant movements in verse 24:
  • Leave — forsake the prior primary loyalty. Marriage creates a new primary family unit.
  • Cleave — cling, hold fast. The same word used in Ruth 1:14 when Ruth clung to Naomi. Not casual attachment. Covenant binding.
  • One flesh — the same word used in the Shema in Deuteronomy 6:4: "the LORD our God is one LORD." Unity that contains complexity, not uniformity. Two persons, one entity. The oneness of marriage echoes the oneness of God.
  1. The Trinity models this: equal in substance, distinct in role.

"The Son is equal to the Father in all his divine attributes, but in the internal relationship of the Trinity he has a role that is in some ways subordinate to the Father… This is not an inequality of being but a difference in role." — Wayne Grudem, Systematic Theology, ch. 14

  1. Equal in dignity. Different in design. I do not envy women what I cannot be — a mother. They should not envy me what I cannot be — a father, a pastor. That is not loss. That is the image.

This is the last thing Moses wrote before everything broke.

  1. One sentence. Two people, fully known, fully belonging, nothing to hide, nothing to protect themselves from.
  2. Naked and not ashamed is not about clothing. It is about the interior life of a covenant: fully seen — the substance and the shadow, the strength and the lack — and what the other person does when they see all of it is not recoil. It is hold.

I am not saying we will be naked in eternity. Revelation 19:8

  1. Genesis 3:7 — the first thing after the Fall: they knew that they were naked, and they sewed fig leaves together.
  2. Everything verse 25 describes, Genesis 3 kills.
  3. In one chapter. In one choice.
  4. This is the paradise we have lost. You have felt the absence of it; in a marriage, in a friendship, in a room full of people who don't actually know you.
  5. That ache is the ache of a world meant to look like verse 25.
  6. And it is the paradise we are promised back.
  7. Genesis 2:25 to Genesis 3:7 to Revelation 19:8. Not a memory. A direction. That is where the whole story is going.
