Good News — The God Who Saw, and Came

God said “not good” in a nearly perfect world.

  • Adam had no sin. No shame.
  • He walked with God in an unbroken garden. And God looked at him and said: not good.

Since Genesis 3, the not good runs deeper than anything Adam ever felt. We are broken. Ashamed. Alienated from each other, from ourselves, from God.

"It was our sorry case that caused the Word to come down, our transgression that called out His love for us, so that He made haste to help us and to appear among us. It is we who were the cause of His taking human form, and for our salvation that in His great love He was both born and manifested in a human body." — Athanasius, On the Incarnation

The Incarnation is God's answer to the “not good” of the human condition. Not a hard reset. God Himself, taking on the dust and flesh of Genesis 2 and entering the world He made, in the state we broke it into.

Transition: The question is not whether He sees your not good. He does. The question is whether you will bring it to the One who became flesh to meet it.

Application

For the single person:

  • You are not incomplete. The text does not say singleness is not good it says aloneness is not good. They are not the same.
  • God named Adam's aloneness before Adam felt it. He has not been inattentive to yours.
  • The Bridegroom is coming. No one who trusts Him will be left alone.

For the married:

  • Your marriage is a participation in the work God assigned at creation. The mandate of Genesis 1:28 was given to both of you. You were designed to do together what neither of you can do alone.
  • Every time you cleave when leaving would be easier — you are carrying the mission. Handle it accordingly.
  • The covenant you made was not built on feelings. It was built on design. There is a Redeemer. Bring your marriage to Him.

For everyone:

  • God looked at a man in paradise and said: not good. He sees you.
  • Whatever loneliness persists even in the company of people who love you that unnamed ache is not a mistake in the design. It is the design pointing you toward its Maker.
  • The One who became flesh to meet human need is still saying: come. That is why He came.

Our Church Together

A church that takes Genesis 2:18–25 seriously will take loneliness seriously not just marriage. Because verse 18 comes before verse 24. We are not a collection of individual spiritual transactions. We are a body. One flesh together in Christ.

Our community does not need just need a church with the proper doctrinal position on marriage. They need a church that models what covenant love looks like and when we do that, we become a living argument for the design God built into creation.

Good News

The Last Adam woke up in a garden.

The same kind of place the first Adam woke up in — a garden, early in the morning, with everything about to change. But where Adam woke up to a bride who was given, Jesus woke up to a bride who was purchased. Every person in this room who trusts Him is part of what He woke up for.

Ephesians 5:25 “25 Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it;”

He gave Himself for it. That is the marriage. That is the covenant. That is what all of Genesis 2 was always pointing at.

  • If you do not know Christ the Bridegroom is calling. Not religion. Not rules. A Savior who became flesh so you could be brought to Him as a gift. Come to Him today.
  • If your marriage is under strain bring it to the One who invented the covenant. His design is still good even when what we have made of it is not.
  • If you are single and wondering whether God sees you He named Adam's aloneness before Adam felt it. He is building something. Trust the Builder.

Nothing God has built was designed to be left unfinished.

Next week: Genesis 3 — The Fall. The world God designed meets the choice that broke it.

sermons.title: Humanity’s Declaration of Independence
sermons.speaker: Trent Cornwell
sermons.notesHtml:
Humanity’s Declaration of Independence

Big Idea

We declared independence from God, and Genesis 3:15 was His answer.

Before Bible Reading

July 4, 1776. Fifty‑six men stepped forward, one at a time, to sign a document that would either free a nation or hang every one of them. Signing the Declaration of Independence was treason against the Crown, and the penalty for treason was death.

They were signing away their safety, their land, and in more than one case, their lives. They knew it going in. And they signed anyway.

They closed the document with these words:

“We mutually pledge to each other our lives, our fortunes, and our sacred honor.” — Declaration of Independence, 1776

Benjamin Franklin reportedly told the signers:

“We must all hang together, or assuredly we shall all hang separately.” — Benjamin Franklin

That is not a slogan. That is a decision.

Fifty‑six men risked the gallows with one signature. Some of us pray about it for a week before signing up to bring donuts.

Let me say something plainly.

• It has become unfashionable in many pulpits for a pastor to say that he loves his country. I do not believe that.

• I am deeply grateful to God for this country — for the freedoms we enjoy, and for those who paid a price so we could gather in this room today without fear.

• That gratitude does not compete with the gospel. It flows from it.

• God has given the church the commission to take the gospel to the nations.

• God has used the government to provide a place where we can do so freely and give us freedom and access to many places in the world as an American Citizen.

• To all of you and all you loved ones God used to make this possible. I say thank you.

But the passage we are about to read records a decision that came long before Philadelphia. The Founders declared independence from a government while still appealing to “the Laws of Nature and of Nature’s God.” Adam and Eve declared independence from God Himself. That declaration did not win us freedom. It cost us everything.

Listen for the signing as we read. Hear the Word of God — Genesis 3, beginning at verse 1.

Scripture Reading · Genesis 3:1–15

Sermon Introduction

Have you ever played the desert island game with the Bible? You are stranded. You get one page. Not one book — one page. Which page do you take?

Be honest. Some of you are negotiating already. “What if I fold it really small? Front and back counts as one, right?”

Most people reach for the comfort passages. Psalm 23. John 3. Philippians 4. Nobody picks Genesis 3. But I want to argue this morning that Genesis 3 has to make the list.

Here is why. Genesis 3 is the only chapter in the Bible that explains the world you actually live in. Why work is hard. Why marriage is hard. Why your body breaks down. Why you hide things. Why there is a cemetery in every town. Take away this chapter and nothing else in your Bible makes sense — because you no longer know what went wrong, or why anyone needed saving.

• And he exaggerates. God had forbidden one tree out of a garden full of them. The serpent frames it as if God forbade every tree.

And the serpent said unto the woman, Ye shall not surely die. (Genesis 3:4)

• The first flat denial of judgment ever spoken.

• Still the most popular lie in the world. Nobody plans to reap what they sow.

• The serpent did not need to make sin look good — Eve could see that herself. He only needed to make judgment look uncertain.

C. He Promised a Better God (vv. 5–6)

For God doth know that in the day ye eat thereof, then your eyes shall be opened, and ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil. (Genesis 3:5)

• He did not say there was no God. He said there is potential for a better one but it will require your help.

• This is the very sin that ruined him. Isaiah 14: I will ascend into heaven… I will be like the most High. He tempted Eve with the sin that had already cost him everything.

  1. Good for food — a physical appeal. The lust of the flesh.
  2. Pleasant to the eyes — an aesthetic appeal. The lust of the eyes.
  3. Desired to make one wise — an intellectual appeal. The pride of life.

  2. For the one who has never trusted Him: the God who came looking in the garden is still asking, “Where art thou?” — not because He cannot find you, but because He wants you to stop hiding.

Big Idea

Before Bible Reading

July 4, 1776. Fifty‑six men stepped forward, one at a time, to sign a document that would either free a nation or hang every one of them. Signing the Declaration of Independence was treason against the Crown, and the penalty for treason was death.

They were signing away their safety, their land, and in more than one case, their lives. They knew it going in. And they signed anyway.

They closed the document with these words:

“We mutually pledge to each other our lives, our fortunes, and our sacred honor.” — Declaration of Independence, 1776

Benjamin Franklin reportedly told the signers:

“We must all hang together, or assuredly we shall all hang separately.” — Benjamin Franklin

Fifty‑six men risked the gallows with one signature. Some of us pray about it for a week before signing up to bring donuts.

sermons.title: The Great Dilemma
sermons.speaker: Trent Cornwell
sermons.notesHtml:
Bible Reading

Genesis 1:26–31

Genesis 2:7, 15–17

Genesis 3:1–7

Illustration — Two Chairs:

  1. Rule One: always sitting in this chair.
  2. Rule Two: always sitting in that chair, at the same time.

The moment is named: that is what we call a dilemma.

Hold onto those two chairs. We are going to come back to them more than once this morning.

Genesis 3 tells us that on the day sin entered the world, something in God's own creation broke — not something small, the single most valuable thing God had ever made. This morning's question: did God decide it was worth saving, and what did that actually require of Him? Four points. It gets heavier before it gets good.

1. God Made Us to Show Him

God made man in His own image and likeness so that man could know Him and reflect Him to the world.

Genesis 1:27 “27 So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.”

A. Made by Deliberate Pattern

  1. The rest of creation is spoken into being — "let there be..." Man is patterned on purpose, not just spoken.
  2. "Let us make man" is one of the earliest suggestive hints in Scripture of more than one Person within the one God.

B. Made to Represent God, Not Resemble Him Physically

  1. "Image" is representation of His authority. "Likeness" is resemblance of His character. The two are closely connected, not separate categories — you were given both together, not just the job.
  2. Illustration — The Ambassador: An embassy flies a flag for a king who isn't in the room. Everything inside represents him. Eden was the same — not gods themselves, God's flag planted in the garden.
  3. Dominion is a representative's job. Adam functioned as God's vice-regent over creation — ruling the earth not autonomously, but under God's authority and on His behalf.

C. This Gives Every Human Life Inherent Worth

  1. Not based on usefulness — based on being made after God's pattern. This is the foundation under every later Bible teaching on human dignity.
  2. Application — NIL: College sports now runs on Name, Image, and Likeness deals. One player's image is worth millions; the guy next to him, same roster, same work, gets nothing — the market decides. Genesis 1:26 is the opposite: worth already infinite before you earned a thing.
  3. This dignity holds from conception until death. The image is not something a person grows into, or can lose through weakness, age, or dependency.

D. This Set Humanity Apart From Every Other Creature God Made

Genesis 1:31 “31 And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. And the evening and the morning were the sixth day.”

  1. "Very good" appears only after man — every earlier day is just "good." No fish, bird, or beast is ever called God's image. Humanity alone.
  2. Psalm 8:4–5 “4 What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him? 5 For thou hast made him a little lower than the angels, and hast crowned him with glory and honour.”
  3. Man is the climax of the creation week. Everything in Genesis 1 builds toward, and culminates in, the making of man.

Transition: That's what we were made for. But the reflection didn't stay intact — and what happened to it runs deeper than most of us are comfortable admitting. So what was God going to do?

2. Sin Broke What We Were Made to Show

Sin was not merely a broken rule but an assault on the image itself, and it corrupted man so completely that Scripture calls him not wounded, but dead.

Genesis 3:4–5 “4 And the serpent said unto the woman, Ye shall not surely die: 5 For God doth know that in the day ye eat thereof, then your eyes shall be opened, and ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil.”

A. Sin Has a Precise Biblical Definition

  1. 1 John 3:4 “4 Whosoever committeth sin transgresseth also the law: for sin is the transgression of the law.”
  2. Sin is rebellion against God's spoken word specifically, not just a vague moral failure.
  3. Romans 3:23 “23 For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God;”
  4. James 4:17 “17 Therefore to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin.”

At its root, in the simplest terms: sin is refusing God's rule so that we can rule ourselves.

B. Eden's Temptation Targeted the Image Directly

  1. "Ye shall be as gods" — not a rule broken, an attempt to stop reflecting God and start replacing Him.
  2. The serpent's lie directly contradicted God's own word — "ye shall not surely die" set squarely against "thou shalt surely die".
  3. Genesis 2:17 “17 But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.”

The very first sin was a dispute over whether God's word could be trusted — the exact tension Point 3 is built on.

C. God Did NOT Erase the Image When Man Fell — He Reaffirmed It

Observation: If you break something ordinary, you throw it away. If you break something precious, someone has to decide whether it's worth saving — and what they're willing to pay. (Garage Floor Test)

  1. Genesis 9:6 “6 Whoso sheddeth man’s blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man.”
  2. After the fall. After the flood — the closest thing to a divine "start over." Still called "the image of God." Present tense. Not erased.

D. The Corruption Ran Deeper Than Surface Damage

  1. Romans 1:21 “21 Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened.”
  2. Ephesians 2:1 “1 And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins;”
  3. Not dying. Dead.
  4. Isaiah 59:2 “2 But your iniquities have separated between you and your God, and your sins have hid his face from you, that he will not hear.”
  5. Separated — God's face hidden. A dead man does not feel dead — not always miserable, not always aware, but genuinely dead, genuinely separated, unable on his own to do a thing about it.

"Genesis 3 teaches that sin is not merely breaking a rule. It is rebellion that makes us guilty, corruption that makes us sick, slavery that binds us, death that claims us, and separation that keeps us from the God we were created to know. That's why the gospel had to be so much more than a pardon. We needed a Redeemer, a Physician, a Liberator, a Resurrection, and a Reconciler."

E. Left Alone, Sin Didn't Just Corrupt the Image — It Inverted It Into Idolatry

  1. Romans 1:22–23 “22 Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools, 23 And changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and fourfooted beasts, and creeping things.”
  2. Man made to reflect God outward — fallen man reverses the current, manufacturing gods in the image of the creature instead. The reflection doesn't dim. It runs backward.
  3. Exodus 20:4 “4 Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:”
  4. Not arbitrary — God protecting the one thing sin most wants to corrupt.

Transition: A dead man cannot revive himself, and if his worship runs backward, he cannot even want to be revived rightly on his own. But the deeper problem isn't only what happened to man. It's what this now demanded of God. So what was God going to do?

3. The Great Dilemma

Man's corruption placed God Himself in a genuine dilemma, because His unchanging truth required death to follow sin exactly as He had said, while His unchanging goodness would not allow His own image-bearers to be lost forever.

Genesis 2:17 “17 But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.”

A. God's TRUTH Was on One Side of the Tension

  1. Disobedience brings death, exactly as stated above — overlooking sin means God breaking His own word.
  2. Numbers 23:19 “19 God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good?”

B. God's GOODNESS Was on the Other Side of the Same Tension

  1. Letting His image-bearers be lost forever, deceived by an enemy with no right to claim them — equally unthinkable. What would it say about God if His handiwork could be undone by a liar in a garden?
  2. Illustration — Remember the Two Chairs. Who will sit in that chair?

C. Neither Option Alone Could Resolve the Tension — No Human Could Resolve It for Him

  1. Man had no currency to pay a debt he was already inside of.
  2. Future obedience can't erase a debt already owed. Only God's own character could satisfy both truths without either giving way.

D. Silence Was Never a Real Third Option

  1. Inaction isn't neutral when the One deciding is perfectly good. Doing nothing while His image-bearers stayed dead forever would itself be a failure of goodness.
  2. Question: Someone here is probably thinking: couldn't God just forgive us?
  • A forgiveness with no cost isn't forgiveness — it's permission. Throughout the New Testament we learn that forgiveness is never the ignoring of sin, but the bearing of sin.
  • 1 Peter 2:24 “24 Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed.”
  • This is what we learn about forgiveness throughout Scripture. God never denies justice. He satisfies justice through Christ. Someone was always going to carry what sin cost — us, forever, or Him, once.

Transition: No human problem before or since ever required God to answer to His own nature. If the tension was inside God, only God could resolve it — but resolving it would cost Him everything. So what was God going to do?

4. Jesus Sat in Both Chairs

Because no angel and no other human being could resolve a conflict within God's own character, God the Son took on a body capable of dying, so that His one death — carrying infinite worth — could pay the debt owed by all and rise again to prove the debt was paid.

Genesis 3:15 “15 And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.”

Even in the middle of pronouncing the curse, God had already planted His answer. The rest of this point is that promise unfolding.

Observation: Was Jesus truly God, truly man, both at once? At the Council of Nicaea, AD 325, this was wildly debted and settled. Settled centuries ago — but settled doesn't mean remembered.

That debate is where the two chairs finally get their answer. Jesus didn't send someone else to sit in the chair we couldn't sit in. He became human — sat down in our chair Himself — while never once leaving the chair marked "fully God." That's the doctrine Nicaea was fighting to protect.

Explanation: A pastor named Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, gave nearly his entire life to teaching exactly this — that the incarnation, God becoming man, was the only solution to our dilemma. He wrote the argument as a young man, around AD 318, and spent forty-five years refusing to soften it. Exiled five times by four emperors. Fleeing one who wanted him dead, he escaped down the Nile in a small boat — when pursuers asked how far off Athanasius was, he answered, "Not far," and kept rowing. History calls him Athanasius contra mundum — "against the world." Never martyred, but willing to be, for forty-five years, over this exact truth.

"Is the world against Athanasius? Then Athanasius is against the world."

"You know what happens when a portrait that has been painted on a panel becomes obliterated through external stains. The artist does not throw away the panel, but the subject of the portrait has to come and sit for it again, and then the likeness is re-drawn on the same material. Even so was it with the All-holy Son of God. He, the Image of the Father, came and dwelt in our midst, in order that He might renew mankind made after Himself, and seek out His lost sheep."

Athanasius, On the Incarnation

God did not throw the picture away. He sent the only One who bore the resemblance — to sit in the wreckage with us.

A. No Angel and No Other Human Being Was Qualified to Solve This

Hebrews 2:16–17 “16 For verily he took not on him the nature of angels; but he took on him the seed of Abraham. 17 Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people.”

  1. He had to take on OUR nature specifically, because the debt was ours.
  2. Another human was already inside the corruption — no untainted currency to offer.

B. Only the Eternal Word, Made Flesh, Was Sufficient

John 1:14 “14 And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.”

  1. As God, the Son cannot die — He is life itself. He took a body specifically so death would finally have something real to touch.
  2. Because that body belonged to the eternal Word, His death = the Life entering death on behalf of ALL.

C. This Is What the Entire Old Testament Sacrificial System Had Been Pointing Toward

  1. Once a year, on the Day of Atonement, Israel's high priest carried blood into the Most Holy Place — and had to bring blood for his own sin first.
  2. Leviticus 17:11 “11 For the life of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul.”
  3. Hebrews 9:22 “22 And almost all things are by the law purged with blood; and without shedding of blood is no remission.”
  4. Every lamb, goat, bull = a receipt. Proof the debt was real, not yet paid.
  5. Colossians 1:15 “15 Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature:”

Only He was worth enough.

D. Because Death Could Not Hold the Source of Life Itself, He Rose

  1. The resurrection is the receipt marked PAID IN FULL.
  2. 1 Corinthians 15:22 “22 For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.”
  3. Romans 1:4 “4 And declared to be the Son of God with power, according to the spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead:”
  4. This also settled, publicly, the very question Nicaea would later defend. Full circle to Point 1: the image broken in the first Adam is remade in the last Adam.

Observation: No other worldview offers this. Islam denies Christ died at all. Naturalism has no God to be truthful or good in the first place. Only this account gives a God who is both the offended party and the substitute, fully just and fully merciful in the same act.

The Just and the Justifier

Let’s turn to Romans 3.

Everything we've traced this morning — the image, the fall, the dilemma, the cross — Paul writes down in a few dense verses near the beginning of his letter to the Romans.

Romans 3:21–26 “21 But now the righteousness of God without the law is manifested, being witnessed by the law and the prophets; 22 Even the righteousness of God which is by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe: for there is no difference: 23 For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God; 24 Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus: 25 Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins that are past, through the forbearance of God; 26 To declare, I say, at this time his righteousness: that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus.”

Notice what most people miss on a first pass. Paul does not say Christ was set forth primarily to save you. Look at verses 25 and 26 — he says it happened "to declare his righteousness," twice, back to back. Your salvation is real and glorious. But according to Paul's own logic, it is not the center of this passage. God's own righteousness is.

Explaining the passage:

• Verses 21–23 restate Point 2: no one has righteousness of their own.

• Verses 24–25: God set Christ forth as a "propitiation" — the actual means by which God's wrath against sin was fully satisfied.

• The problem underneath verse 25: God, in His forbearance, had passed over sins committed in ages past without yet fully punishing them.

• Verse 26 is why the cross had to happen when it did, publicly, decisively — that He might be just, and the justifier.

Mankind is not the centerpiece of Romans 3. God's righteousness is.

Our instinct is to assume the gospel exists mainly to solve humanity's problem. But Paul's own logic runs the other direction. Our rescue is real and wonderful — but it is the by-product of God vindicating Himself, not the main event.

That is the Great Dilemma, in Paul's own words, from the heart of the New Testament. God's justice on one side, God's mercy on the other. The resolution — not God choosing one over the other, but God, in Christ, being both at once. Just, and the justifier.

Approaching the Table

Which brings us, finally, to this morning.

Jesus Christ is not another marred reflection trying to repair Himself. He is the perfect Image of the invisible God — the Original, wearing our flesh, walking where Adam failed to walk, obeying where Adam disobeyed, and finally bearing in His own body the death God's truth required, so that God's goodness could be free to save without contradiction.

Application — Who This Table Is For: Before we come to the bread and the cup, a word about who this Table is for, because it does not belong to us to open or close by our own preference — it belongs to the Lord. This morning we observe close communion: this Table is for those who have been born again by grace through faith in Jesus Christ alone, and who have publicly professed that faith by believer's baptism. If that describes you, we welcome you to the Table with us this morning.

1. Gospel Invitation

Remember where we've been this morning. Dead in trespasses and sins. Separated, with God's face hidden. But Ephesians 2 does not end at verse 1:

Ephesians 2:4–5 “4 But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us, 5 Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ, (by grace ye are saved;)”

God did not start over. He sent the true Image to sit again for the portrait — to bleed in our place.

2. Time of Prayer

Invite the church to bow in silent prayer, examining their own hearts.

1 Corinthians 11:28 “28 But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup.”

3. Song During Distribution

5. The Meaning of the Elements

• The bread reminds us that the eternal Son truly became man.

• The broken body reminds us that God Himself entered our dilemma.

• The cup reminds us that without the shedding of blood there is no remission.

• The resurrection proves the payment was accepted.

6. Prayer Read Before the Bread and Cup Are Taken

  1. Bread
  • 1 Corinthians 11:23–24 “23 For I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you, That the Lord Jesus the same night in which he was betrayed took bread: 24 And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me.”
  1. Cup
  • 1 Corinthians 11:25–26 “25 After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me. 26 For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord’s death till he come.”

Thanks be to God, who is both just, and the justifier.

Bible Reading

Genesis 1:26–31

Genesis 2:7, 15–17

Genesis 3:1–7

Illustration — Two Chairs: 

Rule One: always sitting in this chair. 

Rule Two: always sitting in that chair, at the same time. 

The moment is named: that is what we call a dilemma.

Hold onto those two chairs. We are going to come back to them more than once this morning.

Genesis 3 tells us that on the day sin entered the world, something in God's own creation broke — not something small, the single most valuable thing God had ever made. This morning's question: did God decide it was worth saving, and what did that actually require of Him? Four points. It gets heavier before it gets good.

1. God Made Us to Show Him

God made man in His own image and likeness so that man could know Him and reflect Him to the world.

Genesis 1:27 “27 So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.”  

A. Made by Deliberate Pattern

The rest of creation is spoken into being — "let there be..." Man is patterned on purpose, not just spoken. 

"Let us make man" is one of the earliest suggestive hints in Scripture of more than one Person within the one God. 

B. Made to Represent God, Not Resemble Him Physically

"Image" is representation of His authority. "Likeness" is resemblance of His character. The two are closely connected, not separate categories — you were given both together, not just the job.

Illustration — The Ambassador: An embassy flies a flag for a king who isn't in the room. Everything inside represents him. Eden was the same — not gods themselves, God's flag planted in the garden.

Dominion is a representative's job. Adam functioned as God's vice-regent over creation — ruling the earth not autonomously, but under God's authority and on His behalf.

C. This Gives Every Human Life Inherent Worth

Not based on usefulness — based on being made after God's pattern. This is the foundation under every later Bible teaching on human dignity.

Application — NIL: College sports now runs on Name, Image, and Likeness deals. One player's image is worth millions; the guy next to him, same roster, same work, gets nothing — the market decides. Genesis 1:26 is the opposite: worth already infinite before you earned a thing.

This dignity holds from conception until death. The image is not something a person grows into, or can lose through weakness, age, or dependency.

D. This Set Humanity Apart From Every Other Creature God Made

Genesis 1:31 “31 And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. And the evening and the morning were the sixth day.”  

"Very good" appears only after man — every earlier day is just "good." No fish, bird, or beast is ever called God's image. Humanity alone.

Psalm 8:4–5 “4 What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him? 5 For thou hast made him a little lower than the angels, and hast crowned him with glory and honour.”  

Man is the climax of the creation week. Everything in Genesis 1 builds toward, and culminates in, the making of man.

Transition: That's what we were made for. But the reflection didn't stay intact — and what happened to it runs deeper than most of us are comfortable admitting. So what was God going to do?

2. Sin Broke What We Were Made to Show

Sin was not merely a broken rule but an assault on the image itself, and it corrupted man so completely that Scripture calls him not wounded, but dead.

Genesis 3:4–5 “4 And the serpent said unto the woman, Ye shall not surely die: 5 For God doth know that in the day ye eat thereof, then your eyes shall be opened, and ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil.”  

A. Sin Has a Precise Biblical Definition

1 John 3:4 “4 Whosoever committeth sin transgresseth also the law: for sin is the transgression of the law.”  

Sin is rebellion against God's spoken word specifically, not just a vague moral failure.

Romans 3:23 “23 For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God;”  

James 4:17 “17 Therefore to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin.”  

At its root, in the simplest terms: sin is refusing God's rule so that we can rule ourselves.

B. Eden's Temptation Targeted the Image Directly

"Ye shall be as gods" — not a rule broken, an attempt to stop reflecting God and start replacing Him. 

The serpent's lie directly contradicted God's own word — "ye shall not surely die" set squarely against "thou shalt surely die".

Genesis 2:17 “17 But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.”  

The very first sin was a dispute over whether God's word could be trusted — the exact tension Point 3 is built on.

C. God Did NOT Erase the Image When Man Fell — He Reaffirmed It

Observation: If you break something ordinary, you throw it away. If you break something precious, someone has to decide whether it's worth saving — and what they're willing to pay. (Garage Floor Test)

Genesis 9:6 “6 Whoso sheddeth man’s blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man.”  

After the fall. After the flood — the closest thing to a divine "start over." Still called "the image of God." Present tense. Not erased.

D. The Corruption Ran Deeper Than Surface Damage

Romans 1:21 “21 Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened.”  

Ephesians 2:1 “1 And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins;”  

Not dying. Dead.

Isaiah 59:2 “2 But your iniquities have separated between you and your God, and your sins have hid his face from you, that he will not hear.”  

Separated — God's face hidden. A dead man does not feel dead — not always miserable, not always aware, but genuinely dead, genuinely separated, unable on his own to do a thing about it.

"Genesis 3 teaches that sin is not merely breaking a rule. It is rebellion that makes us guilty, corruption that makes us sick, slavery that binds us, death that claims us, and separation that keeps us from the God we were created to know. That's why the gospel had to be so much more than a pardon. We needed a Redeemer, a Physician, a Liberator, a Resurrection, and a Reconciler."

Romans 1:22–23 “22 Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools, 23 And changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and fourfooted beasts, and creeping things.”  

Man made to reflect God outward — fallen man reverses the current, manufacturing gods in the image of the creature instead. The reflection doesn't dim. It runs backward.

Exodus 20:4 “4 Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:”  

Not arbitrary — God protecting the one thing sin most wants to corrupt.

Transition: A dead man cannot revive himself, and if his worship runs backward, he cannot even want to be revived rightly on his own. But the deeper problem isn't only what happened to man. It's what this now demanded of God. So what was God going to do?

3. The Great Dilemma

Man's corruption placed God Himself in a genuine dilemma, because His unchanging truth required death to follow sin exactly as He had said, while His unchanging goodness would not allow His own image-bearers to be lost forever.

Genesis 2:17 “17 But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.”  

A. God's TRUTH Was on One Side of the Tension

Disobedience brings death, exactly as stated above — overlooking sin means God breaking His own word.

Numbers 23:19 “19 God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good?”  

B. God's GOODNESS Was on the Other Side of the Same Tension

Letting His image-bearers be lost forever, deceived by an enemy with no right to claim them — equally unthinkable. What would it say about God if His handiwork could be undone by a liar in a garden?

Illustration — Remember the Two Chairs. Who will sit in that chair?

C. Neither Option Alone Could Resolve the Tension — No Human Could Resolve It for Him

Man had no currency to pay a debt he was already inside of. 

Future obedience can't erase a debt already owed. Only God's own character could satisfy both truths without either giving way.

D. Silence Was Never a Real Third Option

Inaction isn't neutral when the One deciding is perfectly good. Doing nothing while His image-bearers stayed dead forever would itself be a failure of goodness.

Question: Someone here is probably thinking: couldn't God just forgive us?

A forgiveness with no cost isn't forgiveness — it's permission. Throughout the New Testament we learn that forgiveness is never the ignoring of sin, but the bearing of sin.

1 Peter 2:24 “24 Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed.”  

This is what we learn about forgiveness throughout Scripture. God never denies justice. He satisfies justice through Christ. Someone was always going to carry what sin cost — us, forever, or Him, once.

Transition: No human problem before or since ever required God to answer to His own nature. If the tension was inside God, only God could resolve it — but resolving it would cost Him everything. So what was God going to do?

Because no angel and no other human being could resolve a conflict within God's own character, God the Son took on a body capable of dying, so that His one death — carrying infinite worth — could pay the debt owed by all and rise again to prove the debt was paid.

Genesis 3:15 “15 And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.”  

Even in the middle of pronouncing the curse, God had already planted His answer. The rest of this point is that promise unfolding.

Observation: Was Jesus truly God, truly man, both at once? At the Council of Nicaea, AD 325, this was wildly debted and settled. Settled centuries ago — but settled doesn't mean remembered.

That debate is where the two chairs finally get their answer. Jesus didn't send someone else to sit in the chair we couldn't sit in. He became human — sat down in our chair Himself — while never once leaving the chair marked "fully God." That's the doctrine Nicaea was fighting to protect.

Explanation: A pastor named Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, gave nearly his entire life to teaching exactly this — that the incarnation, God becoming man, was the only solution to our dilemma. He wrote the argument as a young man, around AD 318, and spent forty-five years refusing to soften it. Exiled five times by four emperors. Fleeing one who wanted him dead, he escaped down the Nile in a small boat — when pursuers asked how far off Athanasius was, he answered, "Not far," and kept rowing. History calls him Athanasius contra mundum — "against the world." Never martyred, but willing to be, for forty-five years, over this exact truth.

"Is the world against Athanasius? Then Athanasius is against the world."

"You know what happens when a portrait that has been painted on a panel becomes obliterated through external stains. The artist does not throw away the panel, but the subject of the portrait has to come and sit for it again, and then the likeness is re-drawn on the same material. Even so was it with the All-holy Son of God. He, the Image of the Father, came and dwelt in our midst, in order that He might renew mankind made after Himself, and seek out His lost sheep."

Athanasius, On the Incarnation

God did not throw the picture away. He sent the only One who bore the resemblance — to sit in the wreckage with us.

A. No Angel and No Other Human Being Was Qualified to Solve This

Hebrews 2:16–17 “16 For verily he took not on him the nature of angels; but he took on him the seed of Abraham. 17 Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people.”  

He had to take on OUR nature specifically, because the debt was ours. 

Another human was already inside the corruption — no untainted currency to offer.

B. Only the Eternal Word, Made Flesh, Was Sufficient

John 1:14 “14 And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.”  

As God, the Son cannot die — He is life itself. He took a body specifically so death would finally have something real to touch. 

Because that body belonged to the eternal Word, His death = the Life entering death on behalf of ALL.

C. This Is What the Entire Old Testament Sacrificial System Had Been Pointing Toward

Once a year, on the Day of Atonement, Israel's high priest carried blood into the Most Holy Place — and had to bring blood for his own sin first.

Leviticus 17:11 “11 For the life of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul.”  

Hebrews 9:22 “22 And almost all things are by the law purged with blood; and without shedding of blood is no remission.”  

Every lamb, goat, bull = a receipt. Proof the debt was real, not yet paid.

Colossians 1:15 “15 Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature:”  

Only He was worth enough.

D. Because Death Could Not Hold the Source of Life Itself, He Rose

The resurrection is the receipt marked PAID IN FULL.

1 Corinthians 15:22 “22 For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.”  

Romans 1:4 “4 And declared to be the Son of God with power, according to the spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead:”  

This also settled, publicly, the very question Nicaea would later defend. Full circle to Point 1: the image broken in the first Adam is remade in the last Adam.

Observation: No other worldview offers this. Islam denies Christ died at all. Naturalism has no God to be truthful or good in the first place. Only this account gives a God who is both the offended party and the substitute, fully just and fully merciful in the same act.

The Just and the Justifier

Let’s turn to Romans 3.

Everything we've traced this morning — the image, the fall, the dilemma, the cross — Paul writes down in a few dense verses near the beginning of his letter to the Romans.

Romans 3:21–26 “21 But now the righteousness of God without the law is manifested, being witnessed by the law and the prophets; 22 Even the righteousness of God which is by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe: for there is no difference: 23 For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God; 24 Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus: 25 Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins that are past, through the forbearance of God; 26 To declare, I say, at this time his righteousness: that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus.”  

Notice what most people miss on a first pass. Paul does not say Christ was set forth primarily to save you. Look at verses 25 and 26 — he says it happened "to declare his righteousness," twice, back to back. Your salvation is real and glorious. But according to Paul's own logic, it is not the center of this passage. God's own righteousness is.

Explaining the passage:

• Verses 21–23 restate Point 2: no one has righteousness of their own.

• Verses 24–25: God set Christ forth as a "propitiation" — the actual means by which God's wrath against sin was fully satisfied.

• The problem underneath verse 25: God, in His forbearance, had passed over sins committed in ages past without yet fully punishing them.

• Verse 26 is why the cross had to happen when it did, publicly, decisively — that He might be just, and the justifier.

Mankind is not the centerpiece of Romans 3. God's righteousness is.

Our instinct is to assume the gospel exists mainly to solve humanity's problem. But Paul's own logic runs the other direction. Our rescue is real and wonderful — but it is the by-product of God vindicating Himself, not the main event.

That is the Great Dilemma, in Paul's own words, from the heart of the New Testament. God's justice on one side, God's mercy on the other. The resolution — not God choosing one over the other, but God, in Christ, being both at once. Just, and the justifier.

Approaching the Table

Which brings us, finally, to this morning.

Jesus Christ is not another marred reflection trying to repair Himself. He is the perfect Image of the invisible God — the Original, wearing our flesh, walking where Adam failed to walk, obeying where Adam disobeyed, and finally bearing in His own body the death God's truth required, so that God's goodness could be free to save without contradiction.

Application — Who This Table Is For: Before we come to the bread and the cup, a word about who this Table is for, because it does not belong to us to open or close by our own preference — it belongs to the Lord. This morning we observe close communion: this Table is for those who have been born again by grace through faith in Jesus Christ alone, and who have publicly professed that faith by believer's baptism. If that describes you, we welcome you to the Table with us this morning. 

1. Gospel Invitation

Remember where we've been this morning. Dead in trespasses and sins. Separated, with God's face hidden. But Ephesians 2 does not end at verse 1:

Ephesians 2:4–5 “4 But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us, 5 Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ, (by grace ye are saved;)”  

God did not start over. He sent the true Image to sit again for the portrait — to bleed in our place.

2. Time of Prayer

Invite the church to bow in silent prayer, examining their own hearts.

1 Corinthians 11:28 “28 But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup.”  

3. Song During Distribution

5. The Meaning of the Elements

• The bread reminds us that the eternal Son truly became man.

• The broken body reminds us that God Himself entered our dilemma.

• The cup reminds us that without the shedding of blood there is no remission.

• The resurrection proves the payment was accepted.

6. Prayer Read Before the Bread and Cup Are Taken

Bread

1 Corinthians 11:23–24 “23 For I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you, That the Lord Jesus the same night in which he was betrayed took bread: 24 And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me.”   

Cup

1 Corinthians 11:25–26 “25 After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me. 26 For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord’s death till he come.”   

Thanks be to God, who is both just, and the justifier.

sermons.title: Not On Your Terms
sermons.speaker: Trent Cornwell
sermons.notesHtml:
Scripture Reading

Read Genesis 4:1–16 aloud from your Bible — 

  • Read the remainder section after we look at the story. 
  • Take a glance at ch 5. / reason 1 of 2 we wont be here next week

Pray: We will see that we do not come to God on our own terms but he is willing and desirous to tell us how to worship Him.

Introduction — Flushing, NY

There's a door in every life we pretend isn't there.

The scene

  1. Storefront church, Queens 
  2. With Kanon Bloom. Service ends — a small group.

I was not following the argument.

What was actually said

Walking to the car, Kanon explains: a woman was arguing God has no right to turn away a gift — sincere should be enough, form shouldn't matter.

I'd heard that argument before. Just not in Chinese. I heard it in Genesis 4. C. Common thought

1. We live inside a culture with one rule for anything sacred: if it's authentic, it's valid — nobody gets to tell you your sincerity isn't enough.

2. That woman wasn't fringe. She was fluent in a language we speak.

That woman was standing exactly where Cain stood. Let's go stand there too.

Big Idea

This chapter refuses — again and again — to let Cain, or you, set the terms on which you come to God.

1. Not a grid I'm laying on the text.

2. Watch it happen, verse by verse.

NOT ON YOUR TERMS. HIS.

1. Cain's offering revealed what he actually trusted (vv. 1–5).

Cain wasn't a bad man having a bad day. He was a religious man bringing a real offering — and God still said no.

A. What Moses tells us — and doesn't

1. Cain: “of the fruit of the ground.” One clause.

2. Abel: “firstlings of his flock — and of the fat thereof.” Two extra details.

3. Not just an animal — the first one.

4. Not just the first one — its richest part.

B. The text's own verdict follows that asymmetry

“The LORD had respect unto Abel and to his offering... unto Cain and to his offering he had not respect.” (v.4-5)

1. “Unto Abel” comes first. Then “the offering.” Twice.

2. God regards the worshiper. The gift follows the man.

C. Later Scripture reads it the same way

“By faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain.” (Hebrews 11:4 )

1. Not the right category. A more excellent sacrifice.

2. Rooted in faith. Visible in what was brought.

“Cain brought... any thing that came next to hand... Abel was curious in the choice of his offering: the firstlings — the best he had, and the fat thereof — the best of those best.” — Matthew Henry

D. So this was never grain versus meat

1. Leftover versus best.

2. Convenient versus costly.

E. Jude names the pattern

“Woe unto them! for they have gone in the way of Cain...” (Jude 1:11)

1. “The way of Cain” — outward motion, inward negotiation.

2. A woman in Flushing walked it.

3. So, if we're honest, do we.

HEART Q → What have you decided God should accept — just because it's sincere, or because it's yours?

TRANSITION → God doesn't answer Cain's rejected offering with silence. He answers with questions — and this isn't the first time.

II. Cain's anger revealed what he actually worshiped (vv. 6–7).

A. God's method — the same one as Genesis 3

1. “Where art thou?” found a hiding Adam (Genesis 3:9).

2. “Why art thou wroth?” finds an angry Cain.

3. Not because He doesn't know — because Cain needs to say it.

B. The imagined inner voice

1. “I brought something. I showed up.”

2. “Shouldn't that count for more than this?”

“If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted? and if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door. And unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him.” (Genesis 4:7)

The lunch

1. I once had the chance to sit at lunch with Dr. Don Sisk.

2. I asked him a question I'd been carrying: how do I stay faithful — to the Lord, to my family, to this church — for an entire lifetime, the way he has?

3. He didn't philosophize. He gave me one sentence.

“The sin that desires to destroy you, your marriage, and your ministry is already at the door. How you identify it and respond to it will determine whether you live in victory.” — Don Sisk

A lifetime of faithfulness isn't decided in one dramatic moment. It's decided at the door, over and over, in ordinary weeks like this one.

D. Whichever reading is right, Cain does neither

Some commentators say the sin offering was at the door, I do not see that being it mirrors the language of Gen 3. However..

1. Masters nothing.

2. Takes up nothing.

3. Goes and finds his brother instead.

HEART Q → What's genuinely unresolved for you this week — and what would it look like to actually act, instead of waiting for it to resolve itself?

TRANSITION → Cain doesn't master what's crouching, doesn't take up what's offered. What he does instead — one sentence, no lingering.

III. Cain's silence toward God revealed itself in violence toward his brother (v. 8).

A. The word this chapter won't let go of

1. “Brother” — seven times in sixteen verses.

2. Not a story about worship in the abstract.

3. A story about what happens between brothers.

[camera on the field — watch how fast this goes]

“And Cain talked with Abel his brother: and it came to pass, when they were in the field, that Cain rose up against Abel his brother, and slew him.” (Genesis 4:8, KJV)

B. Watch the pace

1. A conversation.

2. A field.

3. A rising.

4. A falling.

5. Two verses on two offerings. One sentence on a murder.

6. That's how fast refusal moves, once it's chosen.

C. John names the motive

“Not as Cain, who was of that wicked one, and slew his brother. And wherefore slew he him? Because his own works were evil, and his brother's righteous.” (1 John 3:12)

1. Cain couldn't bear being outdone by a righteousness he refused to imitate.

2. Abel's obedience didn't provoke repentance.

3. It provoked rage.

HEART Q → Is there a brother or sister whose righteousness has quietly become an accusation to you rather than an invitation?

NOT ON YOUR TERMS.

TRANSITION → Cain doesn't master what's crouching, doesn't take up what's offered. What he does instead — one sentence, no lingering.

IV. Cain's punishment revealed his guilt, and God's mark revealed a grace he never earned (vv. 9–16).

A. Same divine pattern a third time

1. “Where art thou” found a hiding sinner. “Why are you wroth?"

2. “Where is Abel thy brother” finds a missing victim.

“And he said, I know not: Am I my brother's keeper?” (9)

3. “Brother” again — refused, not owned.

B. The ground opens its mouth again

“The voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground.” (Genesis 4:10) [picture it]

1. Once, it received sweat.

2. Now it receives blood.

Hebrews 12:24 — another blood has since been shed which speaks “better things than that of Abel.” Not a cry for vengeance. A word of mercy. / Hold that. Not finished with it.

C. The turn nobody expects

“Therefore whosoever slayeth Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold. And the LORD set a mark upon Cain, lest any finding him should kill him.” (Genesis 4:15)

Remember that number — sevenfold. It's about to get twisted. Then it's about to get answered.

1. The man who protected no one is given protection he never earned.

2. Guesses abound for the mark — a letter of God's name, a skin disease, a horn. Nobody can prove which. Big foot?

3. The text doesn't say. Maybe that's the point — the mark's appearance was never the issue. Its purpose was.

4. Cain doesn't negotiate it. Doesn't earn it.

HEART Q → Where have you assumed mercy is something you can arrange for yourself, rather than receive on terms you didn't set?

TRANSITION → Cain gets a mark he never earned, and the chapter still isn't over. Watch where that mercy actually leads — because the rest of this story is the best part.

Conclusion— Genesis 4:17–26

A. Cain’s Line

  1. Cain’s descendants built a city. They made real cultural progress. Music. Metalwork. Civilization.
  2. But five generations later we meet Lamech.
  3. “If Cain shall be avenged sevenfold, truly Lamech seventy and sevenfold.” (Genesis 4:24)
  4. There is that number again, but completely twisted.
  5. God’s promise of restraint becomes Lamech’s excuse for revenge.

Cain’s family is still doing what Cain did at the altar. They have decided for themselves what God’s words mean, reshaping them to fit their own desires

God said, “sevenfold,” to restrain vengeance.

Lamech answered, “seventy-sevenfold,” to justify more vengeance.

That is not misunderstanding God’s Word. That is rewriting God’s Word.

  1. Every generation of Cain’s family kept trying to negotiate better terms with God than the ones He had already given.
  2. It never led to freedom.
  3. It only led them farther from Him.

Don’t believe you can negotiate a better deal with God than the one He has already offered.

Good News

Seth’s Line

  1. Then the story suddenly changes.
  2. Seth has a son named Enos.
  3. Enos means frail or mortal man.
  4. For the first time, mankind stops boasting about itself.
  5. “Then began men to call upon the name of the LORD.” (Genesis 4:26)
  6. Worship was not renewed because people became stronger.
  7. It was renewed because someone finally admitted they were weak.
  8. There are still only two ways to live.
  9. You can spend your life building, boasting, and trying to set your own terms with God.
  10. Or you can admit your need and call on the name of the Lord.

C. Where the Story Leads

Then Jesus brings that number back one more time.

Peter asks,

“Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?”

Jesus answers,

“I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven.”

The very number Lamech used to magnify revenge becomes the number Jesus uses to magnify mercy.

  • Lamech multiplied vengeance.
  • Jesus multiplied forgiveness.
  • Lamech’s kingdom was built on retaliation.
  • Christ’s kingdom is built on grace.

Then Hebrews tells us where all of Genesis has been leading.

“Ye are come…to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel.” (Hebrews 12:22–24)

  • Abel’s blood cried out for justice.
  • Jesus’ blood proclaims mercy.
  • The woman in Flushing thought her sincerity could be enough.

Cain thought his own sacrifice could be enough.

Lamech thought he could rewrite God’s terms.

None of them could.

The good news is that God never asked us to negotiate our way to Him.

  • Jesus fulfilled every term we never could.
  • His mercy is greater than our rebellion.
  • His grace is greater than our sin.
  • His blood speaks a better word than Abel’s.
  • And His invitation has never changed:
  • Stop bargaining.
  • Stop defending yourself.
  • Stop trying to improve God’s offer.
  • Come to Christ.
  • Call upon His name.
  • Because salvation has never been on our terms.
  • It has always been on His.
  • And thank God for that.

The Appeal

To the unbeliever

Hear this warning plainly: you do not get to come to God your own way.

1. You do not get to decide the terms on which you approach Him and assume that's good enough.

2. Cain thought sincerity would be enough. It wasn't.

3. Yours won't be either — not on your terms. Come on His

To the believer

What's sitting outside your door right now?

1. Left unaddressed, it will not stay contained.

2. It is going to destroy someone — maybe you, maybe someone you love — the moment it finally attacks.

3. Name it before you leave this room.

Your part was only ever to come — and call upon His name.

NOT ON YOUR TERMS. HIS. THANK GOD FOR THAT.

sermons.title: Build what others aren't building
sermons.speaker: Trent Cornwell
sermons.notesHtml:
Text: Genesis 6:5-9

ORDER OF SERVICE

  • Before reading, note that Genesis 6:1-4 is being skipped on purpose. We will come back to it later.
  • Read Genesis 6:1-7 aloud, slowly.
  • Pastoral Prayer.

INTRODUCTION

The Loneliest Man in the Bible

"Who is the loneliest person in the Bible?"

For approximately 100 years, Noah:

A. Built an unwanted boat. B. Preached an unheeded warning. C. Was probably thought insane by the people around him.

  • Whatever loneliness you are carrying into this week, it has never once been that.
  • There is a smaller and more familiar version of that loneliness waiting for many people this week.

The Hallway

It is the first day back. "Do I fit in?"

"Am I alone in wanting something different?"

Illustration: Trying to Be Cool in Middle School

Holly / story about the slip being mistaken for a skirt and the entire outfit being assembled from the church's answers.

So, if you are worried about fitting in this week, don't.

I am saying: Don't fit in.

This week, build what others don't even know to build.

This is not only about school.

A. It happens in the break room. B. It happens in the subdivision. C. It happens in the group chat. D. It happens in retirement.

It is the same pressure at a different address.

We are studying Genesis 6:5-9 today. This is a word for everyone shifting into a new season.

Genesis 6:5 “5 And GOD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.”

The majority was moving in one direction: away from God.

Then we read:

Genesis 6:8 “8 But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD.”

Noah's family built what nobody else understood.

So can yours.

BUILD WHAT OTHERS AREN'T BUILDING

Build what others aren't building, even if they never understand why.

We will answer three questions:

  1. What are you building?
  2. Why are you building?
  3. How are you building?

1. WHAT ARE YOU BUILDING?

Genesis 6:5-7

Left alone, every heart builds the same thing:

A. Corruption. B. Grief. C. Nothing that lasts.

A. Nothing but evil

Genesis 6:5

  1. This was a culture-wide heart problem, not merely a collection of bad actions.
  2. Notice the three-part total verdict:
  3. Every.
  4. Only.
  5. Continually.
  6. This verdict falls on both genealogies recorded in Genesis 4 and Genesis 5.
  7. Bloodline was never enough.

B. Nothing but grief

Genesis 6:6 “6 And it repented the LORD that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him at his heart.”

  1. Sin causes God real relational sorrow.
  2. The words "repented" and "grieved" do not mean that God changed His mind or discovered that He had made a mistake. Numbers 23:19 “19 God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good?”
  3. This is relational language, not a contradiction.

C. Nothing that would last

Genesis 6:7 “7 And the LORD said, I will destroy man whom I have created from the face of the earth; both man, and beast, and the creeping thing, and the fowls of the air; for it repenteth me that I have made them.”

  1. The majority did not decide what God saw.
  2. The majority does not decide what He sees in you either.

2. WHY ARE YOU BUILDING?

Genesis 6:8 “8 But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD.”

  1. The best answers to the question "Why?" always begin with grace.
  2. Grace motivated Noah's life and everything he built.
  3. Notice the precious word: "But."

A. Because grace interrupted

Genesis 6:8 “8 But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD.”

  1. God singled out one man from a corrupt majority.
  2. Verse 8 is not merely comfort. It is proof.
  3. Genesis 6:8 defends the fairness of the judgment described in Genesis 6:5.
  4. The entire flood narrative pivots on one word: "But."

B. Because grace wasn't earned

Genesis 6:8 “8 But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD.”

  1. This is the first use of the word "grace" in the Bible.
  2. Grace is unmerited.
  3. Noah found grace.
  4. He did not earn it.
"Noah did not find favour in the eyes of men... But he found grace in the eyes of the Lord, and this was honour and comfort enough." Matthew Henry

C. Because grace wasn't conditional

  1. Noah was still part of the fallen human race.
  2. He was not sinless.

Genesis 9:20–21 “20 And Noah began to be an husbandman, and he planted a vineyard: 21 And he drank of the wine, and was drunken; and he was uncovered within his tent.”

Noah failed after the flood, but grace still held him.

Illustration: The Foundation

No one builds on empty air.

Grace was the ground beneath everything Noah built.

The crowd never got a vote on Noah's grace.

It does not get a vote on yours either.

3. HOW ARE YOU BUILDING?

Genesis 6:9 “9 These are the generations of Noah: Noah was a just man and perfect in his generations, and Noah walked with God.”

Noah's life was not defined by one isolated decision.

He gave his life to the work.

Genesis 6:8 shows us grace found.

Genesis 6:9 shows us what a life shaped by grace looks like.

Illustration: Building Differently

Everyone else was building:

A. Reputation. B. Comfort. C. Temporary security.

Noah's family was building something that would survive.

A. By right standing

Genesis 6:9 “9 These are the generations of Noah: Noah was a just man and perfect in his generations, and Noah walked with God.”

  1. The word "just" describes legal standing before a judge.
  2. It does not merely mean that Noah was a nice person.
  3. Noah is the first person in the Bible explicitly called righteous.
  4. The doctrine of justification begins to appear here.

B. By undivided integrity

Genesis 6:9 “9 These are the generations of Noah: Noah was a just man and perfect in his generations, and Noah walked with God.”

  1. The word "perfect" means complete or undivided.
  2. It does not mean sinless.
  3. The same word is used to describe an unblemished sacrifice.

Leviticus 1:3 “3 If his offering be a burnt sacrifice of the herd, let him offer a male without blemish: he shall offer it of his own voluntary will at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation before the LORD.”

Noah was the same person in private that he was in public.

C. By actually walking

  • Genesis 6:9 “9 These are the generations of Noah: Noah was a just man and perfect in his generations, and Noah walked with God.”
  • The same phrase is used to describe Enoch.
  • Genesis 5:22 “22 And Enoch walked with God after he begat Methuselah three hundred years, and begat sons and daughters:”
  • Genesis 5:24 “24 And Enoch walked with God: and he was not; for God took him.”
  • Enoch's walk ended quietly.
  • Noah's walk produced a public witness.
  • Noah's obedience was specific and verifiable.

Genesis 6:22 “22 Thus did Noah; according to all that God commanded him, so did he.”

Genesis 7:5 “5 And Noah did according unto all that the LORD commanded him.”

The statement that Noah did according to all that the Lord commanded him is repeated twice.

Psalm 1:1 “1 Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful.”

You cannot walk toward God and walk with the crowd at the same time.

Illustration: More Than a Hammer

Every plank Noah placed was a lesson in trusting God.

The building itself was discipleship.

Noah's Public Witness

2 Peter 2:5 “5 And spared not the old world, but saved Noah the eighth person, a preacher of righteousness, bringing in the flood upon the world of the ungodly;”

  1. Noah was "a preacher of righteousness."
  2. He preached for decades.
  3. The only converts were members of his own household.
  4. Faithfulness was measured by whether Noah kept preaching, not by the visible results of his preaching.
  5. The majority does not get a vote on what you build.
  6. Build it anyway, even if you have to build it alone.

Illustration: An Insane and Lonely Project

Noah had no fellow ark-builders.

Boats are beautiful to us now.

The ark would have looked insane in a world with no rain and no ocean in sight.

People do not understand boat-building families.

They never have.

Being understood was never the goal.

CONCLUSION AND CHALLENGE

Review

  1. What are you building?
  2. The world was building nothing that would last.
  3. Are you building an image, or something God actually sees?
  4. Why are you building?
  5. Grace is the ground.
  6. Grace is not the reward for finishing.
  7. How are you building?
  8. By righteousness.
  9. By integrity.
  10. By daily walking with God.

Look at your calendar.

  • Does your calendar show that you are building what you say matters?
  • This message applies to every person in the room, not only the students.
  • Noah built in a world that had stopped building anything worth keeping.
  • You can build in one too.

1 Peter 3:20–21 “20 Which sometime were disobedient, when once the longsuffering of God waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was a preparing, wherein few, that is, eight souls were saved by water. 21 The like figure whereunto even baptism doth also now save us (not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God,) by the resurrection of Jesus Christ:”

The boat was never just a boat.

What Should You Actually Be Building?

A. A marriage nobody has to convince you to keep faithful. B. Children who know your prayer voice before they know a stranger's voice online. C. A household rhythm that outlasts this cultural moment.

That is not vague.

That is an ark built out of different materials.

One Thing This Message Is Not Saying

None of those things are your ark.

Noah's boat saved him because God shut the door, not because Noah's craftsmanship was sufficient.

Genesis 7:16 “16 And they that went in, went in male and female of all flesh, as God had commanded him: and the LORD shut him in.”

Your good life was never meant to be the boat.

Jesus is.

FINAL TEACHING CHALLENGE

Tell God what you have actually been building this year.

Ask for grace to build something different.

Invite one person to pray with you.

Do not build alone.

One More Thing: You Are Not Alone

Families and students, you may feel alone while building.

You are not.

Illustration: "Me Too"

Story about the teacher emails and Chuck.

"I told him that I loved Jesus, and he said, 'Me too.'"

Go find the other Chucks in your hallway.

You will walk back into that hallway this week and keep building.

Just don't build it alone.

sermons.title: Lament (Short)
sermons.speaker: Trent Cornwell
sermons.notesHtml:
Title: Go back to God and talk to Him about it.

Introduction

Some of us do not spend time alone with God because we are afraid, angry, or confused. Lament is a word we do not often use. Lament: to express sorrow, regret, or unhappiness about something. To learn how to lament, we must resolve to talk to God—to keep praying.

There are seasons were are pains moves us to a point where can no longer be silent 1 I cried unto God with my voice, even unto God with my voice; and he gave ear unto me. 2 In the day of my trouble I sought the Lord: my sore ran in the night, and ceased not: my soul refused to be comforted. Difficult prayers of lament are far better than silent despair. 3 I remembered God, and was troubled: I complained, and my spirit was overwhelmed. Selah. 4 Thou holdest mine eyes waking: I am so troubled that I cannot speak.

Asaph asks six hard questions to God.

1. v.7 Will the Lord cast off for ever?

2. v.7 and will he be favourable no more?

3. v.8 Is his mercy clean gone for ever?

4. v.8 doth his promise fail for evermore?

5. v.9 Hath God forgotten to be gracious?

6. v.9 hath he in anger shut up his tender mercies? Selah.

Meditation on God’s great acts of deliverance will turn lamentation into praise 10 And I said, This is my infirmity: but I will remember the years of the right hand of the most High. 11 I will remember the works of the Lord: surely I will remember thy wonders of old. 12 I will meditate also of all thy work, and talk of thy doings.

Asaph asks a wonderful question that praises God. 13 Thy way, O God, is in the sanctuary: who is so great a God as our God?

Belief in God creates challenging questions and lament provides the opportunity to direct our hearts toward what is truly, true not just what we feel to be true.

You need to talk to God. Tell him about your pain and ask Him your questions.
