sermons.title: What if I don’t think I can move on?
sermons.speaker: Trent Cornwell
sermons.notesHtml:
Service Notes

We start Song of Solomon next week; The love story in the Bible most people skip, and the one we most need to hear.

  1. We skip it because it makes us uncomfortable.
  2. We need it because our culture is discipled by bad love stories.
  3. We need it because it teaches that love is powerful, not casual.

Scripture Reading

1 Samuel 30:1–6 (KJV)
1 And it came to pass, when David and his men were come to Ziklag on the third day, that the Amalekites had invaded the south, and Ziklag, and smitten Ziklag, and burned it with fire;
2 And had taken the women captives, that were therein: they slew not any, either great or small, but carried them away, and went on their way.
3 So David and his men came to the city, and, behold, it was burned with fire; and their wives, and their sons, and their daughters, were taken captives.
4 Then David and the people that were with him lifted up their voice and wept, until they had no more power to weep.
5 And David’s two wives were taken captives, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, and Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite.
6 And David was greatly distressed; for the people spake of stoning him, because the soul of all the people was grieved, every man for his sons and for his daughters....
I am going to wait here. As we read it the space seems small. But the gap is large. Large enough that many of you may be living in it.
but David encouraged himself in the LORD his God.

Premise

When we look to God, a reaction to the past does not have to define the future.

  • Bitterness is not just pain. It is pain that feels unjust and unresolved.
  • Dr. Jim Schettler once said, “Bitterness is an unresolved violation of your justice system.”
  • Scripture does not ignore this. It speaks directly to it. Today we will see four truths about bitterness and one gospel truth that overrules them all.
  • Disappointment itself is not sinful. What becomes destructive is the refusal to release violated expectations.
  • And while injustice explains bitterness, only the gospel cures it.
  • Some of you are tired of being bitter but you do not know where to turn. Let us turn to the Lord now.

Sermon Introduction

Stand in the ashes long enough and you start asking questions you never planned to ask.

The Bible tells us why the moment darkened:

“Because the soul of all the people was grieved.” (1 Samuel 30:6)

That word means bitter.

  • David stood in ashes, surrounded by bitter people, with injustice pressing in on every side.
  • And before anything was fixed, David had a choice.
  • The same choice we all face when something feels wrong and will never be made right.

For a long time, I did not think of myself as bitter.

I knew I had pain. I knew I had disappointment.

But bitterness felt like too strong a word.

Disappointment is part of life, and it is not sinful.

What becomes destructive is the constant inability to move on from unfulfilled expectations.

Anger can be directed in many directions. But bitterness remains and goes deep in our heart.

Some of you might say like I did, “I am not bitter.”

But you might say:

  • “I have pain.”
  • “I have disappointment.”
  • “I have a story that will never resolve.”

And Scripture says: That is exactly where bitterness tries to live.

Now the question becomes: What does God teach us about this moment?

Four Truths About Bitterness from 1 Samuel 30

(With One Gospel Truth That Overrules Them All)

1. Bitterness begins when real pain becomes the lens through which the heart interprets life.

A. Real loss experiences grief before it ever welcomes bitterness.

  1. Ziklag is burned (1 Sam. 30:1).
  2. Families are taken (1 Sam. 30:2–3).
  3. Men weep until strength is gone (1 Sam. 30:4).

B. God names grief without rebuking it.

  1. “All the people were grieved” (1 Sam. 30:6).
  2. God does not silence sorrow.
  3. God records it honestly.

C. Pain becomes dangerous when it starts explaining reality.

  1. Pain tells you God has forgotten you.
  2. Pain tells you waiting means God said no.
  3. Pain tells you silence means God does not care.
  4. Pain tells you hardship means you are being punished.
  5. Pain tells you this is how your story ends.
“I shall now perish one day by the hand of Saul” (1 Sam. 27:1).

David does not lose faith when Ziklag burns. The fire exposes a fear that was already there.

Transition: If bitterness begins when pain becomes the lens, the next danger is what the heart does with justice.

2. Bitterness grows when the heart demands justice but refuses to entrust it to God.

A. Grief begins arguing with what happened.

  1. The word “grieved” comes from the marah family.
  2. It means embittered sorrow.
  3. It says, “This is wrong.”

B. God wired us with a hunger for justice.

  1. We recognize right and wrong instinctively.
  2. We protest unfairness naturally.
  3. Our conscience bears witness.
Romans 2:14–15 “14 For when the Gentiles, which have not the law, do by nature the things contained in the law, these, having not the law, are a law unto themselves: 15 Which shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness, and their thoughts the mean while accusing or else excusing one another;)”

If you have several children it is likely at some point someone will bring you your child and say “this one has a strong sense of justice. They cannot handle when things seem unfair.”

Transition: If we will not release what is unfair to God, the pain has nowhere to go but deeper into us.

3. Bitterness settles in when sorrow is rehearsed instead of surrendered.

A. Unaddressed grief does not remain neutral.

  1. Pain replayed becomes pain reinforced.
  2. Memory becomes narrative.
  3. Narrative reshapes identity.

B. The men remain in their sorrow.

  1. They do not pray.
  2. They do not pause.
  3. They do not wait.
  4. Have you been here?
  5. What story do I keep telling myself.
  6. What moment do I keep living inside.
  7. What loss do I refuse to release.

C. Bitterness is anger that has found its a home.

The life of story has a very vivid picture of a man who let bitterness overtake him.

  1. Ahithophel was not just a counselor, he was a wounded man.
  2. He was David’s chief adviser (2 Sam. 15:12), but he was also the grandfather of Bathsheba (2 Sam. 11:3; 23:34).
  3. David’s sin had torn through his own family.
  4. When Absalom rebelled, Ahithophel joined him against David (2 Sam. 15:31).
  5. This was not just politics.
  6. It was pain looking for justice.
  7. He wanted to be the one to kill David himself. 2 Samuel 17:1–2 “1 Moreover Ahithophel said unto Absalom, Let me now choose out twelve thousand men, and I will arise and pursue after David this night: 2 And I will come upon him while he is weary and weak handed, and will make him afraid: and all the people that are with him shall flee; and I will smite the king only:”
  8. When God frustrated Ahithophel’s counsel through Hushai (2 Sam. 17:1–14), it felt like one more loss he could not bear.
  9. The old wounds rushed back.
  10. Instead of surrendering his sorrow to God, he let it decide his future. 2 Samuel 17:23 “23 And when Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed, he saddled his ass, and arose, and gat him home to his house, to his city, and put his household in order, and hanged himself, and died, and was buried in the sepulchre of his father.”
  11. Ahithophel did not die because one plan failed. He died because unresolved pain had taken up residence in his heart.

That is what bitterness does. What is not surrendered begins to rule.

Transition: When sorrow is rehearsed long enough, bitterness begins to feel normal.

4. Bitterness survives when it is named reasonable instead of named sinful.

A. When everyone hurts, bitterness feels normal.

  1. All the people were grieved.
  2. No one questions it.
  3. Agreement replaces discernment.
  4. Ziklag is not just ancient history. It is every room where hurt people talk each other into staying hurt.
  5. Because we live in a world full of people who are inclined toward bitterness, we must look up to God rather than out to others for our hope.

B. When we refuse to trust God with what is wrong bitterness is our only option.

  1. The men do not seek God.
  2. They seek to take whatever action they can that might bring them some relief.
  3. When fear is loud, discernment grows quiet. “The heart is deceitful above all things” (Jer. 17:9).
  4. Stones become the solution (1 Sam. 30:6).
  5. Bitterness can make good people think, say, and eventually act upon things they never would have considered in their right mind.
  6. Pain changed the conversation.
  7. Sorrow narrowed their vision.
  8. Bitterness made violence feel reasonable.

C. God often uses one faithful person to stop the spread.

  1. David is just as grieved.
  2. David chooses differently.
  3. David encourages himself in the Lord.
Transition: Up to now, everything explains bitterness. Now Scripture gives us the truth that overrules all the others.

Because of the cross, the courtroom in your heart can finally close.

Justice is no longer ours to chase, manage, or demand.

1. The cross defines reality, not your pain. 2. The cross satisfied the justice you keep demanding. 3. The cross is where sorrow can finally be surrendered. 4. The cross exposes and forgives what bitterness tries to justify.

I. Faith refuses to let pain make the decisions.

A. David faces real loss without pretending it is small.

  1. Scripture names the weight of the moment.
  2. Grief quickly looks for someone to punish.
  3. Every condition for bitterness is present.

B. David refuses to let pain decide where he looks.

1 Samuel 30:6 “6 And David was greatly distressed; for the people spake of stoning him, because the soul of all the people was grieved, every man for his sons and for his daughters: but David encouraged himself in the LORD his God.”

  1. He does not defend himself.
  2. He does not redirect the anger.
  3. He deliberately turns inward and upward.

C. David entrusts justice to God instead of demanding it from people.

  1. David remembers who God is when emotions argue otherwise.
  2. He returns the unresolved weight of judgment to the Lord.
  3. By doing so, David is freed from keeping a case open God intends to close.

Psalm 37:5–7 “5 Commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass. 6 And he shall bring forth thy righteousness as the light, and thy judgment as the noonday. 7 Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him: fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way, because of the man who bringeth wicked devices to pass.”

II. God shows us the pattern for dealing with bitterness at Marah.

Exodus 15:23 “23 And when they came to Marah, they could not drink of the waters of Marah, for they were bitter: therefore the name of it was called Marah.”

A. God allowed the reality of bitterness to be felt.

  1. They were thirsty
  2. Drinking bitter water seemed to be on the only option.

B. God does not deny or rename the bitterness.

  1. He does not pretend the water is drinkable.
  2. He does not soften the language of the problem.
  3. He allows the pain to be fully seen.
Grace never requires pretending, what happened or is happening is not a big deal.

C. God transforms what bitterness makes unusable.

Exodus 15:25 “25 And he cried unto the LORD; and the LORD shewed him a tree, which when he had cast into the waters, the waters were made sweet: there he made for them a statute and an ordinance, and there he proved them,”

  1. God introduces something from outside the situation.
  2. The water is not removed; it is changed.
  3. What could not sustain life becomes a source of life.
God does not erase bitterness. He redeems it.
But Marah is not the end of the story. The tree in the water points us forward to a greater tree that would finally deal with bitterness at its root.

III. The Gospel finishes what bitterness keeps demanding.

  1. Bitterness survives on unfinished justice.
  2. At the cross, God closes the case our hearts keep reopening.
  3. Because justice is settled, bitterness loses its authority.
Because the Gospel has settled what feels unresolved, we are now free to respond like David did.

How can we encourage ourselves in the Lord?

1 Samuel 30:6–8 (KJV)
6 And David was greatly distressed; for the people spake of stoning him, because the soul of all the people was grieved, every man for his sons and for his daughters: but David encouraged himself in the LORD his God.
7 And David said to Abiathar the priest, Ahimelech’s son, I pray thee, bring me hither the ephod. And Abiathar brought thither the ephod to David.
8 And David enquired at the LORD, saying, Shall I pursue after this troop? shall I overtake them? And he answered him, Pursue: for thou shalt surely overtake them, and without fail recover all.

1. Let God tell you who you are.

  • We remind ourselves whose we are. 1 Samuel 30:6 — “the LORD his God”
  • When everything turns against us, we anchor our identity in relationship, not circumstance.
  • We turn to God instead of turning on people.
  • Others looked for someone to blame. David looked to God. 1 Samuel 30:6 — “but David encouraged himself in the LORD”

2. Seek God before you solve anything.

  • We do not react first. We draw near first. 1 Samuel 30:7 — “Bring me hither the ephod”
  • The ephod was a priestly garment that represented access to God’s presence and God’s guidance.
  • David was doing something very deliberate.

He was saying, Before I chase. Before I fight. Before I defend myself. Before I answer my critics. I want to stand in God’s presence and hear God’s word.

3. Walk where God leads.

  • We ask God what to do rather than assuming we know. 1 Samuel 30:8 — “And David enquired at the LORD”
  • Encouragement submits our instincts to God’s authority.
  • We act on God’s word even while the pain remains. 1 Samuel 30:8 — “And he answered him, Pursue”
  • Encouragement is complete when obedience begins.
At this point, some of us feel a tension we need to name.

“God told David to chase them down, so maybe I should too.”

We are not David. Our enemies are not the Amalekites. Our calling is not to recover stolen livestock and families by force.

Do not skip steps one through four. The goal is not pursuit. The goal is obedience.

The Gospel does not call us to chase down our enemies. It calls us to entrust justice to God and obey whatever He asks of us next.

Conclusion

Disappointment is inevitable. Injustice is devastating. Bitterness is possible.

But because of the gospel, it is not inevitable.

Invitation

  1. For those who do not know Christ: Bitterness is not your biggest problem. Unforgiven sin is. Today, God is not asking you to clean yourself up. He is offering you a Savior who has already carried the judgment you deserve. You can stop carrying what you were never meant to bear and trust in Christ today.
  2. For those who belong to Christ: Some of you are still holding a case God has already closed. Today is not about forgetting what happened. It is about releasing judgment back to the Lord and returning your heart to Him. Encourage yourself in the Lord. Lay it down. Trust Him again.

Families are taken (1 Sam. 30:2–3).

B. God names grief without rebuking it.

“All the people were grieved” (1 Sam. 30:6).

God does not silence sorrow.

God records it honestly.

C. Pain becomes dangerous when it starts explaining reality.

Pain tells you God has forgotten you.

Pain tells you waiting means God said no.

Pain tells you silence means God does not care.

Pain tells you hardship means you are being punished.

Pain tells you this is how your story ends.

“I shall now perish one day by the hand of Saul” (1 Sam. 27:1).

David does not lose faith when Ziklag burns.
The fire exposes a fear that was already there.

Transition: If bitterness begins when pain becomes the lens, the next danger is what the heart does with justice.

2. Bitterness grows when the heart demands justice but refuses to entrust it to God.

A. Grief begins arguing with what happened.

The word “grieved” comes from the marah family.

It means embittered sorrow.

It says, “This is wrong.”

B. God wired us with a hunger for justice.

We recognize right and wrong instinctively.

We protest unfairness naturally.

Our conscience bears witness.

Romans 2:14–15 “14 For when the Gentiles, which have not the law, do by nature the things contained in the law, these, having not the law, are a law unto themselves: 15 Which shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness, and their thoughts the mean while accusing or else excusing one another;)” 

If you have several children it is likely at some point someone will bring you your child and say “this one has a strong sense of justice. They cannot handle when things seem unfair.”

Transition: If we will not release what is unfair to God, the pain has nowhere to go but deeper into us.

3. Bitterness settles in when sorrow is rehearsed instead of surrendered.

A. Unaddressed grief does not remain neutral.

Pain replayed becomes pain reinforced.

Memory becomes narrative.

Narrative reshapes identity.

B. The men remain in their sorrow.

They do not pray.

They do not pause.

They do not wait.

Have you been here?

What story do I keep telling myself.

What moment do I keep living inside.

What loss do I refuse to release.

C. Bitterness is anger that has found its a home.

The life of story has a very vivid picture of a man who let bitterness overtake him. 

Ahithophel was not just a counselor, he was a wounded man.

He was David’s chief adviser (2 Sam. 15:12), but he was also the grandfather of Bathsheba (2 Sam. 11:3; 23:34).

David’s sin had torn through his own family.

When Absalom rebelled, Ahithophel joined him against David (2 Sam. 15:31).

This was not just politics.

It was pain looking for justice.

He wanted to be the one to kill David himself. 2 Samuel 17:1–2 “1 Moreover Ahithophel said unto Absalom, Let me now choose out twelve thousand men, and I will arise and pursue after David this night: 2 And I will come upon him while he is weary and weak handed, and will make him afraid: and all the people that are with him shall flee; and I will smite the king only:”  

When God frustrated Ahithophel’s counsel through Hushai (2 Sam. 17:1–14), it felt like one more loss he could not bear.

The old wounds rushed back.

Instead of surrendering his sorrow to God, he let it decide his future. 2 Samuel 17:23 “23 And when Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed, he saddled his ass, and arose, and gat him home to his house, to his city, and put his household in order, and hanged himself, and died, and was buried in the sepulchre of his father.” 

Ahithophel did not die because one plan failed. He died because unresolved pain had taken up residence in his heart.

That is what bitterness does.
What is not surrendered begins to rule.

Transition: When sorrow is rehearsed long enough, bitterness begins to feel normal.

4. Bitterness survives when it is named reasonable instead of named sinful.

A. When everyone hurts, bitterness feels normal.

All the people were grieved.

No one questions it.

Agreement replaces discernment.

Ziklag is not just ancient history. It is every room where hurt people talk each other into staying hurt.

Because we live in a world full of people who are inclined toward bitterness, we must look up to God rather than out to others for our hope.

B. When we refuse to trust God with what is wrong bitterness is our only option.

The men do not seek God.

They seek to take whatever action they can that might bring them some relief.

When fear is loud, discernment grows quiet. “The heart is deceitful above all things” (Jer. 17:9).

Stones become the solution (1 Sam. 30:6).

Bitterness can make good people think, say, and eventually act upon things they never would have considered in their right mind.

Pain changed the conversation.

Sorrow narrowed their vision.

Bitterness made violence feel reasonable.

C. God often uses one faithful person to stop the spread.

David is just as grieved.

David chooses differently.

David encourages himself in the Lord.

Transition: Up to now, everything explains bitterness. Now Scripture gives us the truth that overrules all the others.

Because of the cross, the courtroom in your heart can finally close.

Justice is no longer ours to chase, manage, or demand.

1. The cross defines reality, not your pain.
2. The cross satisfied the justice you keep demanding.
3. The cross is where sorrow can finally be surrendered.
4. The cross exposes and forgives what bitterness tries to justify.


I. Faith refuses to let pain make the decisions.

A. David faces real loss without pretending it is small.

Scripture names the weight of the moment.

Grief quickly looks for someone to punish.

Every condition for bitterness is present.

B. David refuses to let pain decide where he looks.

1 Samuel 30:6 “6 And David was greatly distressed; for the people spake of stoning him, because the soul of all the people was grieved, every man for his sons and for his daughters: but David encouraged himself in the LORD his God.” 

He does not defend himself.

He does not redirect the anger.

He deliberately turns inward and upward.

C. David entrusts justice to God instead of demanding it from people.

David remembers who God is when emotions argue otherwise.

He returns the unresolved weight of judgment to the Lord.

By doing so, David is freed from keeping a case open God intends to close.

Psalm 37:5–7 “5 Commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass. 6 And he shall bring forth thy righteousness as the light, and thy judgment as the noonday. 7 Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him: fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way, because of the man who bringeth wicked devices to pass.” 


II. God shows us the pattern for dealing with bitterness at Marah.

Exodus 15:23 “23 And when they came to Marah, they could not drink of the waters of Marah, for they were bitter: therefore the name of it was called Marah.” 

A. God allowed the reality of bitterness to be felt.

They were thirsty

Drinking bitter water seemed to be on the only option.

B. God does not deny or rename the bitterness.

He does not pretend the water is drinkable.

He does not soften the language of the problem.

He allows the pain to be fully seen.

Grace never requires pretending, what happened or is happening is not a big deal. 

C. God transforms what bitterness makes unusable.

Exodus 15:25 “25 And he cried unto the LORD; and the LORD shewed him a tree, which when he had cast into the waters, the waters were made sweet: there he made for them a statute and an ordinance, and there he proved them,” 

God introduces something from outside the situation.

The water is not removed; it is changed.

What could not sustain life becomes a source of life.

God does not erase bitterness. He redeems it.

But Marah is not the end of the story. The tree in the water points us forward to a greater tree that would finally deal with bitterness at its root.


III. The Gospel finishes what bitterness keeps demanding.

Bitterness survives on unfinished justice.

At the cross, God closes the case our hearts keep reopening.

Because justice is settled, bitterness loses its authority.

Because the Gospel has settled what feels unresolved, we are now free to respond like David did.

How can we encourage ourselves in the Lord?

1 Samuel 30:6–8 (KJV)

6 And David was greatly distressed; for the people spake of stoning him, because the soul of all the people was grieved, every man for his sons and for his daughters: but David encouraged himself in the LORD his God. 

7 And David said to Abiathar the priest, Ahimelech’s son, I pray thee, bring me hither the ephod. And Abiathar brought thither the ephod to David. 

8 And David enquired at the LORD, saying, Shall I pursue after this troop? shall I overtake them? And he answered him, Pursue: for thou shalt surely overtake them, and without fail recover all.

1. Let God tell you who you are.

We remind ourselves whose we are. 1 Samuel 30:6 — “the LORD his God”

When everything turns against us, we anchor our identity in relationship, not circumstance.

We turn to God instead of turning on people.

Others looked for someone to blame. David looked to God. 1 Samuel 30:6 — “but David encouraged himself in the LORD”

2. Seek God before you solve anything.

We do not react first. We draw near first. 1 Samuel 30:7 — “Bring me hither the ephod”

The ephod was a priestly garment that represented access to God’s presence and God’s guidance.

David was doing something very deliberate.

He was saying,
Before I chase.
Before I fight.
Before I defend myself.
Before I answer my critics.
I want to stand in God’s presence and hear God’s word.

3. Walk where God leads.

We ask God what to do rather than assuming we know. 1 Samuel 30:8 — “And David enquired at the LORD”

Encouragement submits our instincts to God’s authority.

We act on God’s word even while the pain remains. 1 Samuel 30:8 — “And he answered him, Pursue”

Encouragement is complete when obedience begins.

At this point, some of us feel a tension we need to name.

“God told David to chase them down, so maybe I should too.”

We are not David.
Our enemies are not the Amalekites.
Our calling is not to recover stolen livestock and families by force.

Do not skip steps one through four.
The goal is not pursuit. The goal is obedience.

The Gospel does not call us to chase down our enemies.
It calls us to entrust justice to God and obey whatever He asks of us next.

Conclusion

Disappointment is inevitable.
Injustice is devastating.
Bitterness is possible.

But because of the gospel, it is not inevitable.

Invitation

For those who do not know Christ:
Bitterness is not your biggest problem. Unforgiven sin is. Today, God is not asking you to clean yourself up. He is offering you a Savior who has already carried the judgment you deserve. You can stop carrying what you were never meant to bear and trust in Christ today.

For those who belong to Christ:
Some of you are still holding a case God has already closed. Today is not about forgetting what happened. It is about releasing judgment back to the Lord and returning your heart to Him. Encourage yourself in the Lord. Lay it down. Trust Him again.

sermons.title: Desire needs Direction
sermons.speaker: Trent Cornwell
sermons.notesHtml:
FOUNDATIONAL TRUTH

  1. Desire is not sinful by default
  2. Desire is powerful by design
  3. Desire becomes shaped by who rules it

INTRODUCTION: DESIRE IS NEVER NEUTRAL

Life is shaped more by desire than by knowledge

We move toward what we want most

Desire moves us toward God or away from Him

Matthew 6:21 Where your treasure is, your heart follows

I. DESIRE AS GOD DESIGNED IT

A. Desire Is Part of God’s Good Creation

Desire existed before sin

Desire itself is not the enemy

B. Desire for God Is Good

We are commanded to long for God

  • Psalm 42:1–2
  • Psalm 73:25
  • Matthew 5:6

When God is the object, desire becomes worship

C. Desire Strengthens Covenant Love

Desire is celebrated within commitment

  • Song of Solomon 2:16
  • Proverbs 5:18–19
  • Hebrews 13:4

Biblical desire commits, it does not consume

D. Desire Can Drive Godly Purpose

Scripture affirms holy ambition

  • Philippians 3:13–14
  • 1 Timothy 3:1

Surrendered desire produces perseverance

II. WHAT HAPPENS TO DESIRE WITHOUT GOD

Ephesians 4:17–19

A. Desire First Corrupts Thinking

Vanity of mind precedes sinful behavior

Direction is lost before morality collapses

B. A Downward Pattern

Darkened mind

Distance from God

Hardened heart

C. Desire Escalates Without God

Desire intensifies rather than weakens

Sin grows out of unchecked longing

  • James 1:14–15
  • Romans 1:24–25

Sin begins with desire detached from God

III. LEARNING CHRIST REORDERS DESIRE

Ephesians 4:20–21

Christianity is not rule keeping

It is learning Christ

Truth is personal, not abstract

What we love shapes who we become

IV. PUTTING OFF AND PUTTING ON

Ephesians 4:22–24

A. Old Desires Must Be Put Off

Some desires lie and enslave

The heart needs correction, not trust

Jeremiah 17:9

B. Renewal Begins in the Mind

Change starts internally

God reshapes thinking to reshape desire

C. New Desires Are Created by God

God gives a new heart

Desire is redeemed, not erased

Ezekiel 36:26

V. THE THRONE QUESTION

Desire always serves something

If God does not rule desire, something else will

Self

Pleasure

Fear

Approval

Romans 6:16

TRANSITION TO SONG OF SOLOMON

Song of Solomon celebrates desire

Ephesians explains desire

Desire is safe when it is rightly ordered

Song of Solomon shows desire when:

God sets the boundaries

Covenant provides security

Love is intense but protected

sermons.title: Family Meeting 2026
sermons.speaker: Trent Cornwell
sermons.notesHtml:
1. Opening Hymn

Blest Be the Tie that Binds

Pastor Beau

John Fawcett wrote it in 1772 while serving as pastor of a small Baptist church in Wainsgate, Yorkshire, England. He and his wife were preparing to leave for a much larger church in London, but the deep love and attachment they felt for their humble congregation made them turn around and stay. Fawcett penned this hymn to express his gratitude for Christian fellowship, mutual love, shared burdens, and hope of reunion, emphasizing the spiritual bonds among believers over worldly opportunity.

Lyrics

Blest be the tie that binds Our hearts in Christian love The fellowship of kindred minds Is like to that above

Before our Father’s throne We pour our ardent prayers Our fears our hopes our aims are one Our comforts and our cares

We share our mutual woes Our mutual burdens bear And often for each other flows The sympathizing tear

When we asunder part It gives us inward pain But we shall still be joined in heart And hope to meet again

From sorrow toil and pain And sin we shall be free And perfect love and friendship reign Through all eternity

2. Prayer Across Generations

Pastor Greg

As we start tonight we want to recognize we are a church family made up of many generations.

We will ask three different generations to lead us in prayer.

3. Reading of the Church Covenant

Pastor Trent with the help of kids reading

Our Church Covenant

1. Having been led, as we believe, by the Spirit of God, to receive the Lord Jesus Christ as our Savior, and, on the profession of our faith, having been baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, we do now, in the presence of God, angels and this assembly, most solemnly and joyfully enter into covenant with one another as one body in Christ.

2. We engage, therefore, by the aid of the Holy Spirit, to walk together in Christian love, to strive for the advancement of this Church in knowledge, holiness and comfort; to promote its prosperity and spirituality; to sustain its worship, ordinances, discipline and doctrines; to contribute cheerfully and regularly to the support of the ministry, the expenses of the Church, and the spread of the Gospel through all nations.

3. We also engage to maintain family and personal devotions; to educate our children in the Christian faith; to seek the salvation of our kindred and acquaintances; to walk circumspectly in the world; to be just in our dealings, faithful in our engagements, and exemplary in our deportment, to avoid all tattling, backbiting and excessive anger; to seek God’s help in abstaining from all drugs, drink, and practices which bring unwarranted harm to the body or jeopardize our own or another’s faith.

4. We further engage to watch over one another in brotherly love; to remember one another in prayer; to aid one another in sickness and distress; to cultivate Christian sympathy in feeling and courtesy in speech; to be slow to take offense, but always ready for reconciliation and mindful of the rules of our Savior to secure it without delay.

5. We moreover engage that when we remove from this place, we will, if possible, unite with a church of like faith where we can carry out the articles of this confession and the spirit of this covenant.

4. Renewed Pastoral Dedication

Pastors with help from the deacons.

  • Pastors publicly reaffirm their calling to guard doctrine at all cost.
  • "We reaffirm our willingness to guard the truth of the Gospel, the purity, peace, and unity of the church, even unto the giving of our lives."
  • Prayed over by the deacons; active and inactive.

5. Changing of the Guard: Active Deacons

Pastors pray over the deacons.

  • Recognition of outgoing and incoming deacons
  • The ministry of the Word; give and guard
  • Acts 6:1–4 “1 And in those days, when the number of the disciples was multiplied, there arose a murmuring of the Grecians against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily ministration. 2 Then the twelve called the multitude of the disciples unto them, and said, It is not reason that we should leave the word of God, and serve tables. 3 Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business. 4 But we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word.”

6. Declaration of Continued Commitment to the Mission by the Congregation

The preparation, sending, and care for missionaries is vital to the mission of our church.

  • We must be willing to keep our eyes on the harvest.
  • We must never settle only for praying for those doing the work.
  • We cannot not allow a measure of success keep us from recognizing the growing need.

Read aloud together as a congregation:

  1. Wherewithal the Great Commission is still binding,  we refuse to live lives unaware of the great need in this world.
  2. Wherewithal there is still a great need in our community,  we will do what is needed to make sure that if there are still sinners in this community, there will be a seat for them beside us.

7. Explanation of the Annual Budget

Lead by Andrew Pearson / Treasurer

8. Family Ministry Update

Lead by Pastor Greg

Brief update with thanksgiving and statements to help with alignment for the new year.

9. Brief Sermon

What Heaven sees when we gather.

Grace changes what we love

I did not naturally love the church. God has taught me to love what He loves.

There was a time I thought of it as nice.. as long as I didn’t have a better option.

Love does not form accidentally. Love is shaped by what God opens our eyes to see.

We all begin somewhere

Most people do not begin loving the church deeply. They grow into it.

  • Some of us began indifferent.
  • Some of us began wounded.
  • Some of us began resistant.

Scripture shows us that journey clearly, because Paul lived it first.

Before Paul tells us what God is doing through the church, we must remember who Paul used to be.

Paul once hated the church. Paul once persecuted the church. And by grace, Paul learned to love the church.

Grace did not just forgive Paul. Grace reshaped what Paul loved.

Ephesians 3:10–11 “10 To the intent that now unto the principalities and powers in heavenly places might be known by the church the manifold wisdom of God, 11 According to the eternal purpose which he purposed in Christ Jesus our Lord:”

1. Grace doesn’t leave you neutral toward the church. It moves you toward it.

Ephesians 3:8 “8 Unto me, who am less than the least of all saints, is this grace given, that I should preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ;”

A. Paul’s humility grows out of his past.

  1. Paul never forgot that he once opposed the church.
  2. Paul remembered his sin so that grace would remain amazing.
  3. Paul knew he was changed, not self made.

B. Grace changed Paul’s relationship to the church.

  1. Paul went from hunting believers to serving them.
  2. Paul went from destroying the church to defending it.
  3. Paul went from standing outside to suffering within it.

C. Paul’s story explains why he values the church so deeply.

  1. Paul knew what the church cost Christ.
  2. Paul knew what grace rescued him from.
  3. Paul knew the church was not optional to faith.

Transition: Once grace changes what we love, it also changes how we see God’s design.

2. You don’t get to or need to redesign what God spent eternity revealing.

Ephesians 3:9 “9 And to make all men see what is the fellowship of the mystery, which from the beginning of the world hath been hid in God, who created all things by Jesus Christ:”

A. The church was hidden in God before it was revealed to people.

  1. The church was not invented by strategy.
  2. The church was not discovered by culture.
  3. The church was revealed by God in Christ.

B. The mystery is not only salvation, but shared life.

  1. God saves individuals into a people.
  2. God unites what sin divided.
  3. God forms one body through grace.

C. The Creator stands behind the church.

  1. The God who created all things formed the church.
  2. The authority behind the church is eternal.
  3. The church exists because God purposed it.

Transition: If the church comes from God’s eternal plan, then its purpose must be larger than we imagine.

3. God is displaying His wisdom to Heaven through the life of the church.

A. God has a watching audience.

  1. Paul points to principalities and powers.
  2. Heaven observes what God is doing on earth.
  3. The church is God’s chosen display.

B. God reveals wisdom through ordinary faithfulness.

  1. Love practiced over time shows wisdom.
  2. Forgiveness reveals grace.
  3. Commitment displays the gospel.

C. This display rests on God’s eternal purpose in Christ.

  1. The church is not Plan B.
  2. The church is not temporary.
  3. Christ stands at the center of it all.

Grace Is Still Doing This Work

If grace could turn Paul’s hatred into love, grace can reshape our indifference into devotion.

Distance from the church is not always rebellion. It is often fear, ignorance, or misplaced trust.

Grace invites us back into what God is doing.

A FAMILY COMMITMENT (THE CHAIR)

Tonight, there is a chair on this stage.

Right now, it is empty. But it will not stay that way.

That chair represents people like Paul once was. People who hate the church today but whom grace will transform tomorrow.

That chair represents people who are indifferent right now. Not hostile. Just unmoved. But one day, they will be here. Singing with us. Serving beside us.

That chair represents people who do not yet know there is a seat for them. They do not know they are welcome. They do not know grace has already made room.

And this time next year, they will be sitting here. And they will bring others with them.

So tonight, as a church family, we commit.

We commit to keeping a seat open.

  • A seat for the skeptic.
  • A seat for the wounded.
  • A seat for the indifferent.
  • A seat for the one grace is still pursuing.

Because God once made room for Paul. And God is still making room.

God is showing His wisdom through His church. And heaven is watching.

Let us love the church well. And let us always leave a seat open.

10. Closing Song and Offering Received

We must never settle only for praying for those doing the work.

We cannot not allow a measure of success keep us from recognizing the growing need. 

Read aloud together as a congregation:

Wherewithal the Great Commission is still binding,
 we refuse to live lives unaware of the great need in this world.

Wherewithal there is still a great need in our community,
 we will do what is needed to make sure that if there are still sinners in this community, there will be a seat for them beside us.

7. Explanation of the Annual Budget

Lead by Andrew Pearson / Treasurer

8. Family Ministry Update

Lead by Pastor Greg

Brief update with thanksgiving and statements to help with alignment for the new year. 

9. Brief Sermon 

What Heaven sees when we gather.

Grace changes what we love

I did not naturally love the church.
God has taught me to love what He loves.

There was a time I thought of it as nice.. as long as I didn’t have a better option. 

Love does not form accidentally.
Love is shaped by what God opens our eyes to see.

We all begin somewhere

Most people do not begin loving the church deeply.
They grow into it.

Some of us began indifferent.

Some of us began wounded.

Some of us began resistant.

Scripture shows us that journey clearly,
because Paul lived it first.

Before Paul tells us what God is doing through the church,
we must remember who Paul used to be.

Paul once hated the church.
Paul once persecuted the church.
And by grace, Paul learned to love the church.

Grace did not just forgive Paul.
Grace reshaped what Paul loved.

Ephesians 3:10–11 “10 To the intent that now unto the principalities and powers in heavenly places might be known by the church the manifold wisdom of God, 11 According to the eternal purpose which he purposed in Christ Jesus our Lord:” 

1. Grace doesn’t leave you neutral toward the church. It moves you toward it.

Ephesians 3:8 “8 Unto me, who am less than the least of all saints, is this grace given, that I should preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ;” 

A. Paul’s humility grows out of his past.

Paul never forgot that he once opposed the church.

Paul remembered his sin so that grace would remain amazing.

Paul knew he was changed, not self made.

B. Grace changed Paul’s relationship to the church.

Paul went from hunting believers to serving them.

Paul went from destroying the church to defending it.

Paul went from standing outside to suffering within it.

C. Paul’s story explains why he values the church so deeply.

Paul knew what the church cost Christ.

Paul knew what grace rescued him from.

Paul knew the church was not optional to faith.

Transition:
Once grace changes what we love, it also changes how we see God’s design.

2. You don’t get to or need to redesign what God spent eternity revealing.

Ephesians 3:9 “9 And to make all men see what is the fellowship of the mystery, which from the beginning of the world hath been hid in God, who created all things by Jesus Christ:” 

A. The church was hidden in God before it was revealed to people.

The church was not invented by strategy.

The church was not discovered by culture.

The church was revealed by God in Christ.

B. The mystery is not only salvation, but shared life.

God saves individuals into a people.

God unites what sin divided.

God forms one body through grace.

C. The Creator stands behind the church.

The God who created all things formed the church.

The authority behind the church is eternal.

The church exists because God purposed it.

Transition:
If the church comes from God’s eternal plan, then its purpose must be larger than we imagine.

3. God is displaying His wisdom to Heaven through the life of the church. 

A. God has a watching audience.

Paul points to principalities and powers.

Heaven observes what God is doing on earth.

The church is God’s chosen display.

B. God reveals wisdom through ordinary faithfulness.

Love practiced over time shows wisdom.

Forgiveness reveals grace.

Commitment displays the gospel.

C. This display rests on God’s eternal purpose in Christ.

The church is not Plan B.

The church is not temporary.

Christ stands at the center of it all.

Grace Is Still Doing This Work

If grace could turn Paul’s hatred into love,
grace can reshape our indifference into devotion.

Distance from the church is not always rebellion.
It is often fear, ignorance, or misplaced trust.

Grace invites us back into what God is doing.

A FAMILY COMMITMENT (THE CHAIR)

Tonight, there is a chair on this stage.

Right now, it is empty.
But it will not stay that way.

That chair represents people like Paul once was.
People who hate the church today
but whom grace will transform tomorrow.

That chair represents people who are indifferent right now.
Not hostile.
Just unmoved.
But one day, they will be here.
Singing with us.
Serving beside us.

That chair represents people who do not yet know
there is a seat for them.
They do not know they are welcome.
They do not know grace has already made room.

And this time next year,
they will be sitting here.
And they will bring others with them.

So tonight, as a church family, we commit.

We commit to keeping a seat open.

A seat for the skeptic.

A seat for the wounded.

A seat for the indifferent.

A seat for the one grace is still pursuing.

Because God once made room for Paul.
And God is still making room.

God is showing His wisdom through His church.
And heaven is watching.

Let us love the church well.
And let us always leave a seat open.

10. Closing Song and Offering Received

sermons.title: Talking to God When You Don’t Know What to Say
sermons.speaker: Trent Cornwell
sermons.notesHtml:
From Questions to Worship

Psalm 77

Introduction

Recently, I was deeply blessed by time spent with my cousin Talana. Being near her at the end of her life shaped how I think about faith, suffering, and honest prayer.

  1. She understood that death hurts because love is real, not because faith is weak. She did not pretend otherwise.
  2. She faced the honest questions about death that most of us spend our lives avoiding. She did not rush past them, deny them, or silence them.
  3. She showed us that taking our questions to God is not a lack of faith, but one of its clearest expressions.
  4. And her hope was never in who she was, but in what Jesus had done.

I pray I will never forget the sound of her voice as she looked at me and humbly said, “If Jesus dying for me is not enough, I have nothing else to offer.”

I do not know if I have ever witnessed a greater expression of faith.

Psalm 77 gives us language for moments like that. Moments when words feel hard to find, when silence presses in, and when faith does not collapse but leans toward God with trembling honesty.

This Psalm does not teach us how to escape pain. It teaches us how to talk to God inside it.

God invites hurting believers to talk to Him honestly and then trains their hearts to rest in what He has already done.

Psalm 77 shows us a simple but demanding rhythm of faith:

  1. Name the pain.
  2. Trust God with the questions.
  3. Anchor your heart in what He’s done.

Suffering exposes what we really believe about God, because pain always presses our faith to speak.

A. Asaph’s suffering drives him toward God rather than into silence.

  1. “I cried unto God with my voice… and he gave ear unto me.” (v.1)
  2. Loud prayer reveals urgency, not irreverence.
  3. Faith does not wait for emotional calm before it speaks.

Practice – Name the pain: Faith begins by saying out loud what hurts instead of pretending it does not.

B. Seeking God does not always produce immediate emotional relief.

  1. “In the day of my trouble I sought the Lord.” (v.2)
  2. “My soul refused to be comforted.”
  3. Scripture normalizes faithful people who still ache.

Permission: Seeking God while still hurting is not spiritual failure.

C. Remembering God can initially intensify the struggle.

  1. “I remembered God, and was troubled.” (v.3)
  2. Honest prayer often surfaces pain we have suppressed.
  3. Lament is faith choosing honesty over avoidance.

What pain have you learned to manage instead of bringing to God?

Transition: When suffering presses faith to speak, it often robs us of rest and exposes what we are trusting to hold us together.

Restlessness often reveals a heart that knows truth but is struggling to rest in it.

A. Asaph acknowledges God’s hand even in his sleeplessness.

  1. “Thou holdest mine eyes waking.” (v.4)
  2. Restlessness is addressed spiritually, not ignored.
  3. God is spoken to, not spoken about.

Practice – Name the pain: Tell God what keeps you awake instead of medicating the moment.

This is why you scroll at night instead of sleeping. Your body is tired, but your heart does not know where to rest.

B. Familiar spiritual language does not automatically produce peace.

  1. “I call to remembrance my song in the night.” (v.6)
  2. Truth remembered without trust does not calm the soul.
  3. Knowledge and rest are not the same thing.

C. Honest prayer gives unrest a place to go.

  1. Asaph does not distract himself.
  2. Silence becomes prayer instead of escape.
  3. Faith stays present even when comfort delays.

What do you reach for first when the house finally gets quiet?

Transition: As unrest lingers, the heart begins to ask questions that reveal what it truly believes about God’s character.

Lament is not the absence of faith, but faith trusting God with questions it cannot yet answer.

A. Asaph asks questions that cut to the core of God’s character.

  1. “Will the Lord cast off for ever?” (v.7)
  2. “Is his mercy clean gone for ever?” (v.8)
  3. These are theological questions, not emotional outbursts.

Practice – Trust God with the questions: Bring your hardest questions into God’s presence instead of hiding them.

Lament sounds like praying, “Lord, I know what I believe, but I don’t feel it right now. Help me stay.”

B. These questions assume covenant faith.

  1. Only believers question God’s promises.
  2. Only faith wonders if mercy has failed.
  3. Lament stays relational.

C. Prayer keeps pain from becoming godless.

  1. Asaph refuses silent despair.
  2. He keeps talking to God even without answers.
  3. Faith remains engaged.

What question about God have you decided not to ask because you are afraid of the answer?

Transition: After exhausting his questions, Asaph does not wait for his emotions to change. He chooses a discipline that reshapes the heart.

Faith grows when the heart anchors itself in what God has already done, not in what it feels right now.

A. Asaph names his weakness without excusing it.

  1. “This is my infirmity.” (v.10)
  2. Weakness is acknowledged, not indulged.
  3. Honest self-awareness precedes spiritual recalibration.

B. Remembering becomes an intentional act of obedience.

  1. “I will remember the works of the Lord.” (v.11)
  2. “I will meditate… and talk of thy doings.” (v.12)
  3. Memory is disciplined, not accidental.

Practice – Anchor your heart in what He’s done: Faith rehearses God’s past faithfulness when present emotions resist trust.

This is why you write things down. Your heart forgets faster than your circumstances change.

C. Truth-filled solitude protects the heart.

  1. Solitude without Scripture leaves us alone with ourselves.
  2. God’s Word anchors remembrance.
  3. Truth steadies the soul when feelings drift.

What clear work of God’s faithfulness have you stopped rehearsing?

Transition: As remembrance retrains the heart, Asaph’s questions shift from confusion to worship.

Worship happens when suffering narrows our focus from unanswered questions to the greatness of God Himself.

A. The Psalm ends without resolution but not without hope.

  1. No explanation is offered.
  2. No circumstances are resolved.
  3. Faith matures without closure.

B. A better question replaces the earlier ones.

  1. “Who is so great a God as our God?” (v.13)
  2. God’s character eclipses unanswered pain.
  3. Worship reframes suffering without denying it.

C. Lament fulfills its purpose in re-centered worship. (Heading 2)

  1. The goal of lament is not relief.
  2. The goal is restored vision of God.
  3. Faith survives because God remains supreme.

If nothing changes this week, is God still enough for you?

Guided Closing Practice

Before we leave, practice Psalm 77 once.

  1. Name the pain: Silently tell God one thing that is heavy right now.
  2. Trust God with the questions: Ask one honest question you have been carrying.
  3. Anchor your heart in what He’s done: Call to mind one clear way God has been faithful.

That is lament. That is faith staying present.

Conclusion

Psalm 77 does not teach us how to fix pain. It teaches us how to stay with God inside it.

  1. Name the pain.
  2. Trust God with the questions.
  3. Anchor your heart in what He’s done.

And keep talking to God, even when you do not know what to say.

He is still listening.

sermons.title: Your Words
sermons.speaker: Trent Cornwell
sermons.notesHtml:
Introduction

We had plans but not a map.

Twenty years ago, we did not know what the next twenty would hold.

  • We did not know the funerals.
  • We did not know the salvations.
  • We did not know the hard conversations.
  • We did not know the victories or the valleys.

But every week, we opened the Book.

Not because we saw the whole road. Because we needed the next step.

God gave us a lamp.

And looking back, I can say this with confidence:

We did not carry the Word. The Word carried us.

Psalm 119:105 (KJV)
105 NUN. Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.

We Have Walked by a Lamp

In David’s day, a lamp was small. A clay vessel. A small flame. Held close to the ground.

It did not eliminate all darkness. It gave just enough light to keep you from stumbling.

That is how the Word has worked among us.

  • It gave enough light to forgive.
  • Enough light to repent.
  • Enough light to endure.
  • Enough light to obey.

Not answers to every curiosity. Light for the next act of faithfulness.

Over twenty years:

  • The light met us in hospital rooms.
  • The light met us in parenting decisions.
  • The light met us in leadership moments.
  • The light met us in private conviction.

The Word works close to where we actually live.

It shines at ground level.

How God Works Through His Word

1. God gives light for obedience, not speculation.

A. The Word shows what is directly in front of us.

  1. It exposes sin we would step into.
  2. It clarifies the next right action.

B. The Word trains us to trust Him for what we cannot see.

  1. We walk before we understand.
  2. We obey before we see outcomes.
  3. God does not satisfy our curiosity. He forms our character.

2. God uses His Word to shape real life, not just church life.

A. The light reaches ordinary places.

  1. Marriage.
  2. Parenting.
  3. Work and leadership.

B. The light confronts hidden places.

  1. Pride.
  2. Idols.
  3. Compromise.

The Word is not decorative. It is vital.

3. God proves His faithfulness every time we walk in the light.

A. The Word stands steady when everything else shifts.

  1. Culture changes.
  2. Emotions fluctuate.
  3. Circumstances shake.

B. The Word produces fruit over time.

  1. Wisdom grows.
  2. Character forms.
  3. Confidence deepens.

For twenty years we have tested the Word in real life. It has never contradicted the character of the God who gave it.

If it was enough then, it is enough now.

The Light Only Helps the One Who Walks

The lamp does not help the man who refuses to move.

The light only helps the one who walks.

  • What step did the Word call you to take that changed your life?
  • What verse steadied you in your darkest season?
  • What obedience felt costly but proved faithful?

The Word works when we step where it shines.

  • It corrects.
  • It comforts.
  • It directs.
  • It anchors.

But only if we walk.

The Next Twenty Years

For twenty years, we have walked by a lamp.

  • Not perfectly.
  • Not without questions.
  • But consistently.

We are not celebrating that we finished a study. We are celebrating that God has been faithful.

His Word has been enough.

  • We will not trade that lamp for the glow of culture.
  • We will not exchange it for trends.
  • We will not dim it to fit the room.

We will keep opening the Book. We will keep taking the next step. We will keep trusting the light.

Because God’s Word has given us enough light for every faithful step.

And it will be enough for the next twenty years too.

Testimonies from Psalm 119

Psalm 119:9 God’s Word straightens us out. It gets into our habits, our attitudes, our patterns. When we start drifting, the Bible pulls us back to a clean path.

9 BETH. Wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way? by taking heed thereto according to thy word.

Psalm 119:11 When we hide the Word in our heart, it guards us. The verses we memorize become the brakes when temptation accelerates.

11 Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee.

Psalm 119:18 The Bible opens our eyes. It helps us see what we would normally miss. We begin to notice God’s hand in ordinary days.

18 Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law.

Psalm 119:24 God’s Word advises us. When we do not know what to do as parents, leaders, husbands, wives, we sit under Scripture and let it speak.

24 Thy testimonies also are my delight and my counsellors.

Psalm 119:50 The Word meets us in sorrow. In hospital rooms. In hard seasons. It breathes life back into tired hearts.

50 This is my comfort in my affliction: for thy word hath quickened me.

Psalm 119:72 The Bible resets what we value. It reminds us that knowing God is richer than anything we can earn.

72 The law of thy mouth is better unto me than thousands of gold and silver.

Psalm 119:89 God’s Word does not wobble. When culture shifts and opinions rage, the Bible stands steady. We build our lives on something that does not move.

89 LAMED. For ever, O LORD, thy word is settled in heaven.

Psalm 119:103 The Word satisfies us. It is not dry duty. It feeds the soul. There is joy in hearing from God.

103 How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth!

Psalm 119:130 God’s Word makes ordinary people wise. You do not have to be impressive. You just have to be teachable.

130 The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.

That is what we have seen for twenty years.

The Word corrected us. The Word guarded us. The Word guided us. The Word comforted us. The Word fed us. The Word anchored us.

The Word meets us in sorrow. In hospital rooms. In hard seasons. It breathes life back into tired hearts.

50 This is my comfort in my affliction: for thy word hath quickened me.

Psalm 119:72
The Bible resets what we value. It reminds us that knowing God is richer than anything we can earn.

72 The law of thy mouth is better unto me than thousands of gold and silver.

Psalm 119:89
God’s Word does not wobble. When culture shifts and opinions rage, the Bible stands steady. We build our lives on something that does not move.

89 LAMED. For ever, O LORD, thy word is settled in heaven.

Psalm 119:103
The Word satisfies us. It is not dry duty. It feeds the soul. There is joy in hearing from God.

103 How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth!

Psalm 119:130
God’s Word makes ordinary people wise. You do not have to be impressive. You just have to be teachable.

130 The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.

That is what we have seen for twenty years.

The Word corrected us.
The Word guarded us.
The Word guided us.
The Word comforted us.
The Word fed us.
The Word anchored us.

sermons.title: Jesus Made Sure We Knew
sermons.speaker: Trent Cornwell
sermons.notesHtml:
SERVICE FLOW

Greeting → Bible Reading (Luke 24:41–53) → Prayer by a missionary

Premise

God wrote Himself into our story, paid what we owed, and made sure we knew — He left the tomb empty.

This is Sunday evening, the same day Jesus rose from the dead. Earlier that morning, the tomb was found empty.

  • The women had gone to the tomb and heard the message.
  • Later, a couple walking on the road encountered Him. And now, Jesus appears again.

You could almost think of this as the third Easter sermon —

  1. first to the women,
  2. then to the travelers on the road,
  3. and now to the disciples gathered together.

This is not morning anymore. This is late in the day. The sun is going down on Resurrection Sunday, and Jesus appears again. I want you to think about this moment as the sun sets on this day.

It shows how good and gracious our God is. Not only in dying on the cross, but in spending time with them afterward so they would have understanding.

That is my prayer today, that we would receive understanding and leave here with joy.

INTRODUCTION

Tonight when the sun starts to go down I want you to consider the evening of the Resurrection.

· I want you to think about that room.

· Locked doors. Frightened people. A movement that looked finished three days earlier.

· And then someone walked in.

· Not a vision. Not a feeling. A person. With wounds you could touch and fish he could eat.

· What happened in that room changed everything. And this morning I want to show you why it still does.

  • Re-entry: Four Words From What You Just Heard

SCREEN: Luke 24:41 “41 And while they yet believed not for joy, and wondered, he said unto them, Have ye here any meat?”

• Not disbelieved from doubt — disbelieved for joy

• The thing happening in front of them was too good to process as real.

• Jesus in the flesh. Sitting, eating, alive!

• Being overwhelmed is understandable. The implications of the empty tomb are huge.

Before I tell you what Jesus says next — I need to answer a question that sits underneath all of this for a lot of people in the room.

The Question Underneath the Story

The question is not whether the resurrection is historically credible. The question is more basic than that. It is this: why would God show up in human history at all? Why would the author of the universe be findable on a dusty road in Galilee or eating fish in a locked room in Jerusalem?

Here is the answer. He made us. Not as an experiment. Not as a project. In his image. Which means from the very beginning, we were made for relationship with him. The distance between God and man was never his idea. We created that. And everything from Genesis 3 forward is the story of God closing it.

With the lauch of Artemis last week. I was reminded of a story I heard about the first person to orbit the earth.

• Artemis is going 240k miles and should be near the moon

• In 1961 the Soviet Union sent a man into space — Yuri Gah-GAR-in 108 minutes orbiting the earth

• The only way Hamlet ever knows anything about Shakespeare is if Shakespeare writes himself into the play

And that — is precisely what Christianity claims happened.

• The author wrote Himself into the story — not as a concept or a force, as a person

• Born in Bethlehem. Walking the roads of Galilee. Standing trial before Pontius Pilate.

• Nailed to a cross outside Jerusalem. And on the third day — standing in a locked room eating fish.

• That is the claim. And everything about Easter rises or falls on whether it is true.

1 In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

14 And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.

SCREEN: The story you are telling yourself may not be complete.

A. Dealing with unmet expectations by God.

• Not just grief but a conclusion.

• The narrative is built. The story is over.

• They are preaching that narrative to themselves every hour behind that door.

• I am not the only who has prepared to preach an Easter sermon. We all have one we have created.

• In that room they were created a timeline – and that time line there was a break in it.

• We had hoped. I had believed. I used to think God was good.

• We have all heard this sermon. Some of you may be preaching it to yourself this morning.

SCREEN: Luke 24:21 But we trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel. — Luke 24:21

▶ At Chick-Fila this week I heard some men talking about what they wanted to do on Sunday, but couldn’t because Easter was important to their mom, wife, or kids.

  • Maybe it was hardship?
  • Maybe it was a lack of understanding?
  • Maybe God always disappoints the person who wants to live exclusively for themselves?

But we trusted…

That sentence — in whatever form it has taken in your life — is the reason this morning matters.

B. Jesus shows up uninvited but very much needed

• Friday — six hours on the cross, darkness at noon, It is finished, He dies

• The disciples — scattered, hidden, behind locked doors

• If or when they heard “it is finished” they must have interpreted it as “we are finished.”

Jesus Himself stood among them.

• Doors still locked. He did not knock. Simply — present.

• Touch Me. Flesh and bones. He shows them the wounds.

• He asks for something to eat. Broiled fish. He takes it. He eats it. In front of all of them.

• Not a vision. Not a metaphor. A body. Wounds visible. A room full of witnesses.

Jesus doesn’t rebuke the narrative they have been preaching. He doesn’t argue with the pain. He opens their minds to the Scriptures and replaces the sermon with the one that was always true.

Four words that complete the story the locked room could not finish.

SCREEN: "Thus it is written."

So many confusing, unfinished stories in our lives are not finished until they are framed by, “Thus it is written.”

SCREEN: The message that left that tomb has arrived in this room today.

A. The Cross Was Scripture Arriving at Its Destination

• Thus it is written — not “I know that looked bad.”

• The cross was always the plan.

• Psalm 22:1 — My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me — written 1,000 years before

• Psalm 22:16 — they pierced my hands and my feet — written before crucifixion existed as a form of execution

• Isaiah 53:5 — wounded for our transgressions, bruised for our iniquities — written 700 years before

• Zechariah 11:12 — thirty pieces of silver — the exact price Judas was paid, written 500 years before

“Thus it is written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer, and to rise from the dead the third day: and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations.” Luke 24:46–47

Not might. Not perhaps.

It was written. It would be done.

The sooner you accept this the better off you will be.

B. What is the message Christ shared that must be shared?

..should be preached in his name among all nations.” (sounds pretty important huh)

• Preached — not suggested, not one perspective among many.

• Proclaimed. Announce. Say.. “it is written”

SCREEN: Repentance and Forgiveness

1. Repentance: Repentance — not feeling bad, not trying harder. An actual turning from self-rule toward Christ.

a. The reversal of the original Genesis 3 choice

b. I will no longer sit on the throne of my own life

2. Forgiveness: Forgiveness — complete, permanent, not maintained by your performance.

a. Grounded entirely in what He did — not what you do

b. The debt paid. The separation bridged. The fracture healed.

SCREEN: "This is what was written. God did not leave our story. He walked out of the tomb and now offers forgiveness for sin."

• God wrote Himself into our story — we didn’t climb up to Him

• Christ suffered — the payment was made. Christ rose — the receipt was issued.

• Pentecost confirmed — the Spirit sent because the Son’s work was complete

  • The message that left that tomb has arrived in this room today.

C. The Empty Tomb Is the Proof the Payment Cleared

▶ Costco asks for a receipt at the door

• Declaration — debt cleared, case closed, separation over

SCREEN: Who was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification. Romans 4:25 “25 Who was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification.”

• The raising is the verdict the death was sufficient

• If the death had not been sufficient — there would be no resurrection

And God didn’t just leave an empty tomb. He made sure we knew.

  1. The veil tore. The earth shook.
  2. He walked among us for forty days. Five hundred people saw him.
  3. Fifty days later, Peter stood in Jerusalem — three minutes from the tomb — and said he was alive.
  4. He said it to people who were there. People who could walk over and check.
  5. If the tomb wasn't empty, the movement dies in Jerusalem before it starts.
  6. The Roman soldiers were paid to lie about it. You don't bribe guards to cover up something that didn't happen.
  7. These men were hiding behind locked doors on Friday. By Sunday they were willing to die for what they saw.
  8. And when Peter finished preaching, three thousand people believed in a single day.
  9. God didn't just give them a sermon. He gave them his Spirit.
  10. He preserved it in his Word.
  11. And he sent someone to tell you. Today, that's me. And that can be you for someone else tomorrow!

Jesus Made Sure We Knew

And here is what that message does to a person when they actually receive it. Look at how Luke ends the chapter.

The same people hiding behind locked doors — by the end of Luke 24 they are not hiding anymore. Something happened between verse 41 and verse 52 that is the most important thing that can happen to any person in this room today.

SCREEN: You have seen too much to walk out of here unchanged.

A. The Empty Tomb Has a Meaning and the Meaning Produces Joy

  1. •The resurrection is not just a miracle — it is the Father’s verdict on the cross
  2. The cross was the payment. The empty tomb is the receipt.
  3. You will never allow truth to shape your life unless you are certain of it.
  4. Most people are not joyless because life is hard. They are joyless because they are not certain of anything beneath them.

The tomb is empty because the verdict is final. That is what makes the joy not just great but safe and secure.

B. What Understanding Produced

SCREEN: Luke 24:52–53 “52 And they worshipped him, and returned to Jerusalem with great joy: 53 And were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God. Amen.”

  1. And they worshipped him, and returned to Jerusalem with great joy: and were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God. — Luke 24:52–53
  2. Same people — locked doors, past tense hope, disbelieving for joy in verse 41
  3. End of the chapter — worshipping, great joy, continually in the temple

What made the difference?

Luke 24:45 “45 Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures,”

Joy sent them out.

• Not duty. Not obligation.

• Joy. Unshakeable. Not fragile.

• Would say not because of circumstances. But certainly, due to the circumstance. The tomb is empty.

• Luke doesn’t give instructions at the end of the chapter — he gives a picture. Let the picture be enough.

This is what a sufficient death and an empty tomb produce in people who receive it.

C. You Have Seen Too Much

  1. You came in today carrying a narrative — possibly past tense hope, honest doubt, or disbelieving for joy
  2. The tomb is either empty or it isn’t. The verdict is either final or it isn’t.

Conclusion

We are really only left with 3 choices.

1. Accept it. Turn from yourself toward Christ. Walk out the way they walked out; with great joy.

2. Reject it. That is your choice. But know what you are rejecting. Not a rumor. Not a feeling. Evidence. And the quiet work of the Holy Spirit in your life that brought you to this room.

3. Ignore it. That was possible before this morning. We pray it is harder now.

The Invitation

• The same God who walked through that locked door is present in this room today. That day through the person or Jesus Christ, and today through the work of the Holy Spirit.

• Jesus made sure they knew the tomb was empty and what that meant for them.

My prayer is that we have done the same today — for every person in this room.

sermons.title: Good Friday \ Proven at the Cross
sermons.speaker: Trent Cornwell
sermons.notesHtml:
The way Jesus died proves he is exactly who he claimed to be. [Read Luke 23:33–46 & Pray]

Introduction

I want to ask you something honest. Have you ever looked at the crucifixion and felt not inspired but unsettled? A man nailed to a cross, mocked, bleeding out.

  • It doesn’t look like victory.
  • It doesn’t look like a king.
  • It looks like the end of something.

WE

We all have a category for failure. And if we’re honest, the cross fits that category on the surface.

The people standing there thought it did.

  • The rulers laughed.
  • The soldiers gambled.
  • One of the criminals joined in.

Everything about that scene was trying to communicate one thing.

This man was wrong about himself.

What looks like defeat is actually a display of victory.

A. The crucifixion scene is designed to humiliate.

Nailed, mocked, stripped. Everything about it says this man has lost.

But the first thing Luke shows you is Jesus interceding. “Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.” (v. 34)

That’s not a defeated man. That’s a man in complete control of who He is.

B. You don’t produce forgiveness under torture unless it’s already in you.

The cross didn’t break his character. It put it on display.

What looks like his worst moment is actually his clearest self revelation.

C. Luke wants you to see this clearly.

The cross is not the undoing of Jesus.

It’s the unveiling of him. — His nature is clear. — But what about his authority? — The crowd’s argument was simple. A real king would come down. — Luke answers that next and not the way you’d expect.

What looks like the end of his reign is actually the exercise of it.

A. Three groups mock him with identical logic. (v. 35–38)

Save yourself. If you’re really the king, come down.

The rulers sneer.

The soldiers taunt.

The sign above his head was written to humiliate.

But Luke lets every word stand. As unintentional testimony.

B. One man cuts through all of it.

The criminal doesn’t ask Jesus to come down. He asks to be taken with him. “Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.” (v. 42)

That’s not wishful thinking. That’s the only clear eyed faith in the entire scene.

And Jesus answers him like a king. “Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” (v. 43)

C. This defines his kingship.

A king who saves himself saves no one.

A king who stays saves everyone who asks. — So he dies forgiving. — He dies reigning. — But the next three hours raise a harder question. — Does he die alone? — What happens in the darkness matters more than most people realize.

What looks like the end of the story is actually the beginning of ours.

A. Three hours of darkness. The veil of the temple tears from top to bottom. (v. 44–45)

  1. This isn’t just backdrop. It’s an announcement.
  2. The veil had one job for fifteen hundred years. To keep humanity out of God’s presence.
  3. It was the architectural statement of the problem. You cannot come in here.
  4. It doesn’t tear from the bottom up. As if a man pulled it.
  5. It tears from the top down. God is the one opening the door.

B. That tearing is not the end of a system.

It’s the start of an era.

  • One priest.
  • One day a year.
  • Behind a curtain.
  • For a people who could not come close.

What Jesus accomplishes collapses that distance permanently. Hebrews 10:19–20 “Having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus…”

His body was the veil. His death was the tearing. His cross is the door.

C. His final words seal it.

“Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit.” (v. 46)

He is quoting Psalm 31. A man surrounded, near death, trusting God.

Jesus dies with a script. He knows how this ends.

The criminal got it in real time. “Remember me.” And Jesus handed him access. “Today with me paradise.”

D. His story doesn’t end at the cross.

  1. And because it doesn’t yours doesn’t have to start with you.
  2. Every human story before the cross began the same way. Outside.
  3. Separated. Distant from God.
  • By sin.
  • By the veil.
  • By the weight of everything we’ve done and everything we are.
  1. The cross ends that story. And starts a new one. • Not distance but access. • Not performance but trust. • Not death but the Father’s hands.

Conclusion

You know this story. But knowing the story and being in the story are two different things.

A. Think about what that man could see.

  1. The same darkness.
  2. Every reason to sneer.
  3. Every reason to give up.

But something in him saw past it.

Not a failed messiah. A king.

C. And in the worst moment of his life.

  1. Nothing to offer.
  2. Nothing to trade.
  3. He made the only move available.

D. He didn’t clean himself up.

  1. He didn’t negotiate.
  2. He just turned his head and said five words.
  3. “Remember me when you come.”

E. That posture is still available tonight.

  1. To the one who knows the Bible.
  2. To the one carrying something heavy.

F. Have you ever gotten to the end of yourself and said I cannot fix this. I cannot earn this. But remember me.

G. That is the door.

  1. It is open because of the cross.
