sermons.notesText:
The way Jesus died proves he is exactly who he claimed to be.
[Read Luke 23:33–46 & Pray]

Introduction

I want to ask you something honest.
Have you ever looked at the crucifixion and felt not inspired but unsettled?
A man nailed to a cross, mocked, bleeding out.

It doesn’t look like victory.

It doesn’t look like a king.

It looks like the end of something.

WE

We all have a category for failure.
And if we’re honest, the cross fits that category on the surface.


The people standing there thought it did.

The rulers laughed.

The soldiers gambled.

One of the criminals joined in.


Everything about that scene was trying to communicate one thing.

This man was wrong about himself.

What looks like defeat is actually a display of victory.

A. The crucifixion scene is designed to humiliate.

Nailed, mocked, stripped.
Everything about it says this man has lost.

But the first thing Luke shows you is Jesus interceding.
“Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.” (v. 34)

That’s not a defeated man.
That’s a man in complete control of who He is.

B. You don’t produce forgiveness under torture unless it’s already in you.

The cross didn’t break his character.
It put it on display.

What looks like his worst moment
is actually his clearest self revelation.

C. Luke wants you to see this clearly.

The cross is not the undoing of Jesus.

It’s the unveiling of him.
— His nature is clear.
— But what about his authority?
— The crowd’s argument was simple.
A real king would come down.
— Luke answers that next and not the way you’d expect.

What looks like the end of his reign is actually the exercise of it.

A. Three groups mock him with identical logic. (v. 35–38)

Save yourself.
If you’re really the king, come down.

The rulers sneer.

The soldiers taunt.

The sign above his head was written to humiliate.

But Luke lets every word stand.
As unintentional testimony.

B. One man cuts through all of it.

The criminal doesn’t ask Jesus to come down.
He asks to be taken with him.
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.” (v. 42)

That’s not wishful thinking.
That’s the only clear eyed faith in the entire scene.

And Jesus answers him like a king.
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” (v. 43)

C. This defines his kingship.

A king who saves himself saves no one.

A king who stays saves everyone who asks.
— So he dies forgiving.
— He dies reigning.
— But the next three hours raise a harder question.
— Does he die alone?
— What happens in the darkness matters more than most people realize.

What looks like the end of the story is actually the beginning of ours.

A. Three hours of darkness. The veil of the temple tears from top to bottom. (v. 44–45)

This isn’t just backdrop. It’s an announcement.

The veil had one job for fifteen hundred years. To keep humanity out of God’s presence.

It was the architectural statement of the problem. You cannot come in here.

It doesn’t tear from the bottom up. As if a man pulled it.

It tears from the top down. God is the one opening the door.

B. That tearing is not the end of a system.

It’s the start of an era.

One priest.

One day a year.

Behind a curtain.

For a people who could not come close.

What Jesus accomplishes collapses that distance permanently.
Hebrews 10:19–20
“Having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus…”

His body was the veil.
His death was the tearing.
His cross is the door.

C. His final words seal it.

“Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit.” (v. 46)

He is quoting Psalm 31.
A man surrounded, near death, trusting God.

Jesus dies with a script.
He knows how this ends.

The criminal got it in real time.
“Remember me.”
And Jesus handed him access.
“Today with me paradise.”

D. His story doesn’t end at the cross.

And because it doesn’t yours doesn’t have to start with you.

Every human story before the cross began the same way.
Outside.

Separated. Distant from God.

By sin.

By the veil.

By the weight of everything we’ve done and everything we are.

The cross ends that story.
And starts a new one.
• Not distance but access.
• Not performance but trust.
• Not death but the Father’s hands.

Conclusion

You know this story.
But knowing the story and being in the story are two different things.


A. Think about what that man could see.

The same darkness.

Every reason to sneer.

Every reason to give up.

But something in him saw past it.

Not a failed messiah. A king.


C. And in the worst moment of his life.

Nothing to offer.

Nothing to trade.

He made the only move available.


D. He didn’t clean himself up.

He didn’t negotiate.

He just turned his head and said five words.

“Remember me when you come.”


E. That posture is still available tonight.

To the one who knows the Bible.

To the one carrying something heavy.


F. Have you ever gotten to the end of yourself and said
I cannot fix this.
I cannot earn this.
But remember me.


G. That is the door.

It is open because of the cross.

You don’t need more information.

Ask.

sermons.title: The Gift That Made No Sense
sermons.speaker: Trent Cornwell
sermons.notesHtml:
Text: John 12:1–8

Big Idea

“There is someone in this story who understood something about Jesus that nobody else in the room did. She never said a word.”

Opening Scripture Reading

13 Verily I say unto you, Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached in the whole world, there shall also this, that this woman hath done, be told for a memorial of her.

Is the gospel preached here?

Then the story must be told.

And today there are stories in this room that must be told too.

Introduction

Six days before Passover, during the most important week in history, Jesus reclines at the table.

In the first century meal posture, guests reclined on low couches around a low table with their feet extended away from the food. That detail matters because His feet are already accessible, already pointing toward her.

Martha is serving. Lazarus is at the table. It is a quiet evening among friends.

Then someone stops the room.

Key Truth

The world measures everything by what it produces. We calculate. We evaluate return. What happens when love refuses to do that math?

1. She Gave What Could Not Be Replaced

3 Then took Mary a pound of ointment of spikenard, very costly, and anointed the feet of Jesus, and wiped his feet with her hair: and the house was filled with the odour of the ointment.

Story of the Ointment

A. “Then took Mary” — She acted with full intention

  1. “Took” implies deliberate action.
  2. She moved toward it.
  3. Love had nowhere left to go but out.

B. “Spikenard, very costly” — She gave the irreplaceable thing

  1. Pure. Unadulterated.
  2. One pound. John records the weight because it mattered.
  3. A year’s wages, and she broke the seal anyway.

C. “Anointed the feet… wiped with her hair” — She spent her dignity along with her treasure

  1. Jesus is reclining with His feet already extended into the room.
  2. Head anointing belonged to kings. She went to the floor.
  3. Unbound hair carried social cost in that culture.
  4. She gave the jar, then gave herself with it.

This act declared:

“I will go as low as love requires.”

D. “The house was filled with the odour” — Extravagant love changes every room it enters

  1. Not just His corner. The whole house.
  2. Some things fill a room and you do not know the source until you stop.
  3. Love poured out completely always fills more than the immediate space around it.

E. The Silence of Mary

  1. Mary never speaks in any Gospel account.
  2. She never explains.
  3. Never defends.
  4. Never asks for credit.
  5. The perfume was her sermon. She preached with the alabaster box.
  6. An act so complete it required no words.

2. The World Always Has a Better Idea

4 Then saith one of his disciples, Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, which should betray him, 5 Why was not this ointment sold for three hundred pence, and given to the poor? 6 This he said, not that he cared for the poor; but because he was a thief, and had the bag, and bare what was put therein.

A. “Then saith Judas Iscariot” — John names him before quoting him

  1. “Which should betray him” is intentional.
  2. Read his logic knowing where it led.
  3. The man committed to redirecting love from Jesus would soon sell Him for thirty pieces of silver.

B. “Three hundred pence” — He already ran the numbers

  1. He did not guess.
  2. He knew the exact price.
  3. The thief knew down to the penny what she surrendered.

C. “Given to the poor” — The criticism wrapped itself in righteousness

  1. Sounded responsible.
  2. Sounded wise.
  3. Sounded moral.
  4. That is what made it dangerous.
  5. The world’s most reasonable arguments against devotion almost always protect something other than what they claim.

D. “Not that he cared for the poor” — John pulls back the curtain

  1. He objected to losing control, not to the waste.
  2. A thief steals more than money. He steals meaning.
  3. He could not tolerate what he could not profit from.

E. She was criticized every time she appeared

Luke 10 — Martha criticized her for sitting instead of serving.

John 12 — Judas criticized her for wasting.

  1. Every scene involving Mary ends with someone telling her she got it wrong.
  2. Extravagant devotion to Jesus always attracts criticism from people who appear to have a point.
  3. If nobody has ever told you your devotion to Christ is excessive, examine whether it actually is.

Illustration

Judas is not a cartoon villain.

  • He is practical. Responsible. Organized around what things are worth.
  • Most people in this room are Judas in that sense. Trained since childhood to ask whether something is worth it.
  • That is wisdom until it meets Jesus.
  • Then it becomes the most dangerous posture in the world.

The criticism of extravagant love almost always sounds reasonable. That is what makes it dangerous.

3. Jesus Defends What the World Dismisses

7 Then said Jesus, Let her alone: against the day of my burying hath she kept this. 8 For the poor always ye have with you; but me ye have not always.

A. “Let her alone” — Jesus shut it down before she said a word

  1. He did not ask her to explain herself.
  2. He did not open the floor for discussion.
  3. Two words. Case closed.
  4. She did not need to speak because the right person spoke for her.

B. “Against the day of my burying” — This is where the gospel opens up

  1. Six days from now there will be a cross.
  2. He knew what was coming, and He went anyway.
  3. Mary had been sitting at His feet long enough to hear what others refused to understand.
  4. The disciples heard His death predictions and missed them.
  5. Mary may have understood what they dismissed.
  6. Or perhaps she understood nothing fully, but love moved her to do the right thing before her mind caught up.

What does someone have to believe to do what Mary did?

  • She is not pouring out to get something.
  • She already received something nobody could take away.
  • She knows she is loved. She knows she belongs.
  • She gives like a daughter of the house, not a servant earning a seat.
  • Slaves give to earn. Children give because they already belong.

C. This was an act of courage, not just love — Spurgeon

  1. This happened publicly.
  2. Religious leaders were already plotting to kill Jesus.
  3. To anoint Him openly was to take a side when taking sides carried a cost.
  4. Mary was not merely worshipping. She was identifying herself with Him.

D. “Me ye have not always” — He declared this moment irreplaceable

  1. Some moments do not come twice.
  2. Mary recognized this one.
  3. Judas missed it.
  4. The difference was not personality. It was what each believed about Jesus.

E. What she poured out could never be recovered — Spurgeon

  1. Once the seal broke, the perfume could not be gathered back.
  2. True sacrifice cannot be reclaimed or hedged.
  3. She broke it, and when it was broken it was all His.

F. Jesus doesn’t want us to miss what others despise

“Be told for a memorial of her.”
  1. She never defended herself because she never had to.
  2. Jesus does not forget what is poured out for Him.
  3. Nothing given to Christ is ever truly lost.

Key Truth

  1. You do not always get credit for what you pour out.
  2. The world may call it foolish.
  3. But Jesus sees it. Names it. Honors it.

The Gospel

Mary poured out perfume.

Six days later Jesus poured out Himself.

He did not merely receive sacrifice. He became the sacrifice.

  • He did not calculate. Did not redirect. He broke the seal and poured it all out.

The reason any love like this exists is because there is a God who loved first.

  • Gave first.
  • Went lowest first.
  • You do not work your way up to this love.
  • You receive it.

The perfume filled the house because the seal broke.

  • The gospel fills a life the same way.
  • If you have never let that happen, today is the day.

Conclusion

Preached this whole sermon and never mentioned mothers.

But many people have been thinking about one the entire time.

A face. A name. A memory.

Reapplication

Point 1 — She gave what could not be replaced

  • A mother pours herself out day after day.
  • Time she cannot recover.
  • Energy she cannot renew.
  • Some things fill a room and you do not know the source until you stop.

Question

What did she pour out for you that she can never get back?

She never asked you to notice.

Point 2 — The world always has a better idea

Someone in her life ran the numbers too.

Ambition redirected.

The world told her she was wasting herself.

The criticism always sounded reasonable.

Martha had a point. Judas had a point.

They were all looking at the wrong thing.

Question

Who told her she was wasting herself, and did you ever push back?

Sometimes Judas is not a stranger. Sometimes he is the voice we never corrected.

Point 3 — Jesus defends what the world dismisses

Illustration

Every mother who quietly poured herself out without explanation or recognition:

  • Jesus sees it.
  • Jesus saw Mary.
  • Jesus named it.
  • Jesus made the world remember her.

He will not forget what your mother gave either.

Question

Have you ever looked her in the eye and said:

“I see what it cost you.”

She has never asked you to say it.

That is exactly why you should.

Final Application

Maybe she is here today. Tell her.

Maybe she is gone. Carry it like it matters because it does.

Maybe you are a mother and you are tired and wondering if it matters.

Maybe you have never truly said thank you.

Maybe you always wanted to be a mother and it never happened.

This room sees you.

And so does Jesus.

Closing Statement

The lie most people believe is that a small life is a wasted life.

  • Picking up the same toys.
  • Driving the same carpool.
  • Making the same lunches.
  • Answering the same questions.

Judas would agree.

Spreadsheet ready. Hours counted. Certain you could have done more.

But Judas never understood this:

Mary was not on the floor because her life was small.

She was on the floor because she knew Jesus who was in the room.

sermons.title: YOU CAN TRUST GOD WITH BOTH HANDS
sermons.speaker: Trent Cornwell
sermons.notesHtml:
Introduction:

  • give out dollar coins
  • speak about something i have not often spoke to you about; money

I. THE MAN GOD USED WAS NOT WHO YOU WOULD EXPECT

(George Müller — Bristol, England — 1805–1898)

Born in Prussia, 1805 By his own admission: a liar, thief, drunkard, and womanizer his mother died while he was drunk in the streets Stole from his father — landed in prison at age 20

The turning point: At 20, attended a Bible study and was converted

He was moved simply by watching other people kneel to pray Settled in Bristol, England — and found the streets filled with orphaned children

Thousands of children orphaned by cholera. Those children either starved or were forced into workhouses — essentially slave labor. Müller felt the call of God to do something

Principle: God does not call the qualified. He qualifies the called.

II. THE MISSION HE BUILT ON NOTHING BUT PRAYER

He had roughly two shillings — about fifty cents — when he started He made three commitments that sounded impossible:

  1. He would never ask another human being for money.
  2. He would never take out a loan or go into debt
  3. He would tell no one about his needs — except God

The results over his lifetime:

  • Cared for 10,024 orphans
  • Never asked for a single cent directly
  • Never took a salary for the last 68 years of his ministry
  • Never took a loan — never went into debt
  • Neither he nor the orphans were ever hungry

III. THE GOD WHO SHOWED UP EVERY TIME

(Müller's faith was not theoretical — it was proven at the table)

The morning the pantry was empty:

300 children — no food in the house Müller sat the children at the table anyway and prayed out loud, thanking God for what He was about to send

A baker arrived: he could not sleep the night before — felt impressed by God to bake bread for the orphanage

Minutes later: a milkman — his cart had broken down directly in front of the orphanage He unloaded all his milk just to lighten the cart The children ate that morning They always did

Principle: Müller's faith was not the absence of need. It was the presence of God in the middle of need.

IV. THE MOMENT AT THE DOOR

(The scene that defines his entire ministry)

Every child who grew up at Ashley Down eventually came of age. When that day arrived, Müller did not simply send them out. He prayed with each child individually — one by one He placed a Bible in their right hand He placed a coin in their left hand

Each child also received:

  • A complete new outfit
  • A tin trunk
  • Two full changes of clothing
  • An umbrella
  • A copy of Müller's published Narratives of God's faithfulness
  • Their accumulated savings
  • A train ticket
  • A job already arranged before they walked out the door
  • A dollar
  • A Bible

Then he said:

"Hold onto what is in your right hand — and God will always make sure there is something in your left."

He did this more than ten thousand times

  • The same man who arrived with nothing
  • The same man who never asked for a cent
  • The same man who sat children at empty tables and prayed
  • Was now placing ten thousand children into the world with the same conviction he had built his life on

V. THE WORD BEHIND THE MOMENT

Müller never had to quote Matthew 6:33 “33 But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.”

This was not a verse Müller had just memorized

It was a verse Müller had proven He read his Bible end to end nearly 200 times He preached at least 10,000 sermons At age 70 he began seventeen years of missionary travel — preaching until age 87 He died in 1898 — a poor man with few possessions At his funeral: over 100 carriages in procession — thousands lined the streets

Principle: The man who held the Bible in both hands his whole life died with nothing — and left everything.

CLOSING CHARGE

You can trust God with both hands.

The man who proved it is buried in Bristol. The God who proved it through him is still on the throne.

He had roughly two shillings — about fifty cents — when he started He made three commitments that sounded impossible:

He would never ask another human being for money. 

He would never take out a loan or go into debt 

He would tell no one about his needs — except God   

The results over his lifetime:

Cared for 10,024 orphans 

Never asked for a single cent directly 

Never took a salary for the last 68 years of his ministry 

Never took a loan — never went into debt 

Neither he nor the orphans were ever hungry

III. THE GOD WHO SHOWED UP EVERY TIME

(Müller's faith was not theoretical — it was proven at the table)

The morning the pantry was empty:

300 children — no food in the house Müller sat the children at the table anyway and prayed out loud, thanking God for what He was about to send 

A baker arrived: he could not sleep the night before — felt impressed by God to bake bread for the orphanage 

Minutes later: a milkman — his cart had broken down directly in front of the orphanage He unloaded all his milk just to lighten the cart The children ate that morning They always did

Principle: Müller's faith was not the absence of need. It was the presence of God in the middle of need.


IV. THE MOMENT AT THE DOOR

(The scene that defines his entire ministry)

Every child who grew up at Ashley Down eventually came of age. When that day arrived, Müller did not simply send them out. He prayed with each child individually — one by one He placed a Bible in their right hand He placed a coin in their left hand 

Each child also received:

A complete new outfit 

A tin trunk 

Two full changes of clothing 

An umbrella 

A copy of Müller's published Narratives of God's faithfulness 

Their accumulated savings 

A train ticket 

A job already arranged before they walked out the door   

A dollar

A Bible

Then he said:

"Hold onto what is in your right hand — and God will always make sure there is something in your left."


He did this more than ten thousand times 

The same man who arrived with nothing 

The same man who never asked for a cent 

The same man who sat children at empty tables and prayed 

Was now placing ten thousand children into the world with the same conviction he had built his life on

V. THE WORD BEHIND THE MOMENT

Müller never had to quote Matthew 6:33 “33 But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.” 

This was not a verse Müller had just memorized 

It was a verse Müller had proven   He read his Bible end to end nearly 200 times He preached at least 10,000 sermons At age 70 he began seventeen years of missionary travel — preaching until age 87 He died in 1898 — a poor man with few possessions At his funeral: over 100 carriages in procession — thousands lined the streets

Principle: The man who held the Bible in both hands his whole life died with nothing — and left everything.


CLOSING CHARGE

You can trust God with both hands.

The man who proved it is buried in Bristol. The God who proved it through him is still on the throne.

sermons.notesHtml:
THE RENEWED MIND

Romans 12:1–2 and the Life the Gospel Makes Possible

The daily presenting of your body to God — refusing the world's shaping pressure and submitting to the Word — is the natural, reasonable response to a mercy you have already received.

Bible Reading & Prayer

Turn to about three-quarters of the way through Romans.

Note: the chapter and verse numbers were not in Paul's original letter — they were added centuries later. They are helpful, but sometimes the chapter break works against us. Watch the very first word of the next section.

Romans 11:33-12:2

Introduction

Kentucky Drive — The Self-Esteem Club

  • Driving through Kentucky — passed my old school. Remembered something I haven't told many people.
  • I stayed after school for the self-esteem club.
  • I didn't know what self-esteem was until they told me. Which was not great for my self-esteem.
  • It was the first time I realized someone cared about more than math and speech. They cared about my mind — what was happening inside, the part nobody could see.
  • I expected it to fix me. Nobody in that room could get outside their own mind long enough to fix someone else's.

Everyone in this room has been shaped by something they didn't choose:

• A parent's voice you still hear when you fail.

• Shame so old you think it is just personality.

• Anxiety that shows up at 2am and calls itself reason.

• The belief that you are behind — and everyone else somehow is not.

• A loss that reorganized everything and never fully let go.

We are all being formed. The question is: by what? And is there a way out?

  • "Paul says yes. But it is not a self-esteem club."

Genesis — The Mind That Sin Shapes

Every major turn in Genesis begins not with an action — with a thought. The serpent does not attack Eve physically. He raises a question: "Yea, hath God said?" He changes the way she sees the fruit before she ever reaches for it.

The battle was won in the mind before it was acted out in the body. Every character who falls in Genesis falls first in their thinking.

  • "Every character who falls in Genesis, falls first in their thinking. Every character who is renewed is renewed from the outside in."

Adam — Genesis 3

God gave him everything. The serpent raised one question. Adam's thinking shifted.

Before he reached for the fruit — a thought: God is withholding. I can be more.

The moment he ate, the next thought hit:

  • "I am exposed. I am not enough. I need to hide."
  • "I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself." — Genesis 3:10

Then a third thought: it is not my fault. (Genesis 3:12)

One lie produced shame. Shame produced hiding. Hiding produced blame. The mind was the first casualty and the last thing to heal.

• Clinical: shame response, social withdrawal, blame attribution.

• Scripture: sin. The clinical term names the shape of the damage. The Bible names the root.

Jacob — Genesis 37

His sons brought him Joseph's coat, dipped in blood. He formed a conclusion instantly:

  • "My son is dead. I will never recover. This grief is all I have left of him."

His sons came to comfort him. His daughters came. All of them. He refused every one.

  • "And he refused to be comforted; and he said, For I will go down into the grave unto my son mourning." — Genesis 37:35

The thought became a vow. Grief became identity. To accept comfort felt like betraying Joseph.

  • "Joseph was alive. God was already working. Jacob refused comfort from a loss that was not final — because his mind had decided it was."

• Clinical: complicated grief disorder, treatment-resistant mourning — grief that hardens into identity.

• Scripture: the disordered mind cannot see what God is already doing. Only renewal from the outside breaks it open.

Brain vs. Mind

The brain is the physical organ — the instrument the mind uses.

The mind in Scripture is the seat of will, loyalty, and worship — what decides what is worth having and who is worth trusting.

  • "A pill can change brain chemistry. It cannot replace a false belief with a true one. For that you need something no self-esteem club could supply."

The World's Mold

Paul says the world is pressing a pattern into your thinking. Specifically. In a culture like ours, that pattern says:

• Your worth is what you have achieved — visible in your house, your children's school, your title. Fall behind and something is wrong with you.

• Your body is a project to be managed, optimized, and performed — not a vessel to be offered.

• If you find the right system — the right discipline, the right therapist, the right routine — you can fix yourself from the inside.

  • "That last one is the most dangerous. Because it is the closest to true. And the furthest from the gospel."

The Press Is Not Accidental — Someone Is Being Paid For It

Social media platforms pay creators based on how many minutes of your attention they can capture. Not per post. Not per follow. Per minute watched.

YouTube, TikTok, Instagram Reels — all built around watch time. The algorithm is not designed to show you what is true. It is designed to show you what keeps you watching.

What keeps people watching longest is emotional — outrage, fear, comparison, desire, anxiety. The exact categories that bend the mind away from God.

• The average person gives social media more than two hours every day.

• That attention is worth roughly fifty dollars a year per user to the platforms — across billions of users.

  • "Paul wrote "be not conformed" before any of this existed. Every minute you give to the feed is a minute someone is being paid to shape the way you see yourself, others, and God. That is not neutral. That is the mold."
  • "Your mind is being shaped by something right now. The only question is whether it is the world or the Word."

What I Have Preached — And What the Text Says Instead

What many churches have preached: real spiritual growth begins with a decisive, once-for-all act of surrender. Consecrate yourself and sanctification begins.

Different delivery. Same problem — it puts the solution in your hands and makes your sincerity the key.

Gospel

  • Paul is about to describe a life built on mercies already received. Before we talk about the response, we need to talk about the offer. Some of you are carrying the weight of things God has not yet forgiven — because you have never asked Him to. That can change right now. In your seat. A simple prayer: "God, I know I am a sinner. I believe Jesus died for me and rose again. I receive your mercy. I am yours." That prayer, meant honestly, is the beginning of everything Paul is about to describe. For those who have received these mercies — this is what Paul says you do next.

The Text — Romans 12:1–2

Paul just finished the greatest argument about God's mercy in the letter — and erupts into doxology. (Romans 11:33)

That is not a conclusion. That is a man undone by what he just wrote. The chapter break makes it look like he stopped. He did not. Watch the first word:

  • "Therefore. That word is picking up everything Paul has argued since page one — justification, peace, union with Christ, the Spirit, adoption, the unbreakable promise of Romans 8:38-39. That is what "the mercies of God" means. Eleven chapters of specific, named, accomplished mercy. Now he says: therefore."
  • "I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service. And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God." — Romans 12:1–2 (KJV)

Three movements: the basis for the offering. The nature of the offering. The mechanism that sustains it.

I. Before Paul asks anything of you, he wants to make sure you understand what has already been done for you.

The Word Beseech

"I beseech you" — Paul does not command here. He pleads.

This is a man so undone by what he just finished writing that he cannot bring himself to issue an order. He appeals. The tone is pastoral before it is propositional.

  • "He is not standing over you with a requirement. He is standing beside you, pointing at what God has done, and saying: given all of that — here is what I am asking."
  • "Therefore" and "by the mercies of God" — the offering is grounded entirely in what God has already done.

• The offering is a response to grace already received — not a condition for grace to be given.

  • ""The gospel is precisely God's mercy to inexcusable and undeserving sinners." — John Stott"

What Are We Bringing?

Paul says: your bodies. Not your feelings. Not your sincerity. Not your intentions.

  • "Your bodies. Everything you do in skin — your hands, your tongue, your time, your habits, your choices."
  • In the animal sacrifice the priest brought someone else's body. The animal had no idea what was happening to it.
  • "Paul says: bring your own. He calls this your "reasonable service" — the worship of a rational being who comprehends what they are doing. You cannot consecrate an emotion. You can consecrate a body that shows up."

Holy, Acceptable Unto God

These words follow "living sacrifice" and are easy to skip. Don't.

In the OT the animal brought to the altar had to be without blemish — spotless, fit for the altar. Paul says your body, offered in response to mercy, is exactly that.

  • "Not because of what you brought. Because of whose altar it lands on. Justification does not just change your standing before God in the future — it makes your offering fit right now."

• A common misreading turns this into two-tier Christianity — carnal vs. dedicated — verse 1 as the door between them.

• Paul writes to people already justified, already alive in Christ. The offering is not the key that unlocks grace. It is the natural response of a person who understands grace already given.

Gospel Call

  • Paul has just named the mercies. Before we talk about the response, we need to talk about the offer. Some of you are carrying the weight of things God has not yet forgiven — because you have never asked Him to. That can change right now. In your seat. A simple prayer: "God, I know I am a sinner. I believe Jesus died for me and rose again. I receive your mercy. I am yours." That prayer, meant honestly, is the beginning of everything Paul is about to describe. For those who have received these mercies — Point II is for you.

II. Mercy this costly deserves more than one emotional night. It deserves every ordinary morning that follows.

How a Body Stays on the Altar — The Two Commands of Verse 2

Verse 2 tells us what it looks like for a body to stay on the altar. Two commands — one negative, one positive. Together they are the mechanism of consecration.

Command 1: Be Not Conformed to This World

• "Conformed" — a mold pressing its shape into something pliable.

• "This world" means this present age — the age before Christ returns, the age that is already passing away.

  • "The press of the mold is temporary. The transformation is eternal. You are being asked to resist something that is already fading in order to become something that will never fade."
  • "Your worth is your achievement. Your body is a project. You are your own solution. That is the mold. And it is pressing right now, today, in this room."

– Present tense: ongoing, continuous, never-stopping resistance. Not a gate you walk through once.

Command 2: Be Ye Transformed by the Renewing of Your Mind

• The transformation is passive — you are being transformed. God is the agent. The instrument is the renewing of the mind.

• Present tense: ongoing, never-finished. The mind reshaped from the inside so it sees differently, wants differently, chooses differently.

What the Text Just Disproved — A Misunderstanding I Have Preached

On many occasions I have preached: real spiritual growth begins with a decisive, once-for-all act of surrender. Consecrate yourself and sanctification begins.

  • ""The sacrifice Paul urges in verse 1 is no one-time act. The present-tense verbs stress the progressive, ongoing nature of the believer's participation." — William Combs"
  • "The consecrated life is not a feeling. It is a body submitted to a mind being renewed — daily, through the Word, against the press of the world."
  • "A dead sacrifice is already done. Paul is not asking for something you finish. He is asking for something you live."

Illustration — Bonfire Summer

One summer — Friday night bonfires, week after week. Invitation every night. Kids responded. Some burned CDs.

I still believe dedication is real and necessary. But here is what I had not yet seen:

  • "Those kids needed a body that showed up the next morning, and a mind being renewed so that body knew what to do with the day."

The fire dies. The summer ends. If all a person has is the memory of a decision, they have very little when November comes.

  • "Mercy that forgave your sin, adopted you as a child, and secured your eternity is not honored by one emotional Friday night. It is honored by a body. Showing up. Every ordinary day. The whole life."
  • "Your mind is being shaped by something right now. The only question is whether it is the world or the Word."

III. The mind that sin bent out of shape will not fix itself. But the Word, working from the inside out, can rebuild what grace has already redeemed.

"Renewing" — same word as Titus 3:5: "the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost."

• Mind-renewal begins at the new birth but does not end there.

• Thinking patterns, desires, default orientations — not instantly rewritten. Being rewritten.

Romans 1 contrast: the "reprobate" mind — consistently misidentifies what is good and what is God.

• Adam believed a lie and hid. Jacob refused comfort while Joseph was alive.

• In every case the renewal came from outside — God opening eyes, God working while someone wept.

  • ""The mind is renewed by the Word and Spirit of God; then we are able to discern and desire the will of God; and then we are increasingly transformed by it." —
  • "The self-improvement culture says: find the right system. The gospel says: you cannot get outside your own mind with your own mind. The Word has to come in."

That Ye May Prove

The word "prove" means to test something and find that it holds — like testing metal for quality.

The renewed mind does not merely obey the will of God. It tests it, examines it, puts it to the proof — and finds it genuinely good.

  • "That is a completely different posture than reluctant compliance. Paul is not promising that the Christian life becomes easier. He is promising that the renewed mind begins to recognize the will of God as something it actually wants."

Good and Acceptable and Perfect

• "Good" — morally excellent, truly beneficial. Not just permitted. Actually good.

• "Acceptable" — pleasing, well-received, fitting. Not something God tolerates from you. Something He is pleased with in you.

• "Perfect" — complete, lacking nothing, mature. The will of God does not leave you short. It is the fullest version of the life you were made for.

  • "The renewed mind does not find the will of God merely tolerable. It finds it good. And acceptable. And perfect. All three at once."

Reasonable Service and the Renewed Mind

Paul calls the offering in verse 1 "reasonable service" — logical, rational, intelligent worship.

Then immediately in verse 2 he names the mechanism: the renewing of the mind.

  • "He is saying: the offering flows from comprehension. As your mind is renewed you understand more fully what the mercies of God actually mean — and the offering becomes more natural, not more forced. Glad response. The more you understand what was given for you, the more reasonable it becomes to give everything back."

This is the answer to every person who feels the Christian life is duty without joy. The problem is not the will. The problem is a mind that has not yet been renewed enough to see what it is responding to.

The Destination — What the Renewed Mind Begins to See

The person whose mind is being renewed begins to want differently. The things the world said would satisfy start to feel thin. The things God says are good start to feel true.

  • "The voice that said your worth is your achievement begins to lose its authority — not because you silenced it, but because something truer has been growing louder."

The One Ask

  • "Give the Word access to your mind every day."

Not to earn what you do not have. Not to impress God. Not because guilt demands it.

  • "Because your mind is being shaped by something right now — and the Word is the only thing that comes from outside, works from the inside, and can rebuild what sin bent out of shape."

Application

The Person Who Has Tried Everything

You believe the gospel. You have made decisions — real ones. Maybe more than once.

You have read the books. Done the therapy — it helped, the same patterns came back. Resolution in January, lasted until March. Built the habit. Watched it unravel.

  • "You can describe your problem with remarkable precision. You just cannot seem to fix it."

Somewhere underneath is a question you are afraid to ask out loud:

  • "Is something wrong with me that cannot be fixed?" "Paul's answer is: yes. And also — that is not the end of the sentence."
  • Yes — the mind bent by sin will not fix itself. Every system you have tried has been run by the same mind that needs renewing.
  • But the Word of God comes from outside. The Spirit works from within. What you cannot do from the inside, God has been doing patiently — every time you opened your Bible, every time you brought your body back after a failure.
  • "The question is not whether you can fix yourself. The question is whether you are giving the Word access to your mind every day."

Not to earn what you do not have. The mercy is already yours. But the renewal happens through the Word. And it has to be daily.

  • "Your mind is being shaped by something right now. The only question is whether it is the world or the Word."

Conclusion

  • ""The matter of personal consecration is reduced to the simple element of honesty." — Hubert Brooke, Personal Consecration (1897)"
  • "Not intensity. Not drama. Not a big enough fire. Honesty. Is there a body being offered — day by day — to the God who gave everything to make the offering possible?"
  • "Combs, after a full study of this text: what Paul means by dedication has too often been understood to mean a decisive, often one-time decision. It is not. It is a life." — William Combs"

The Mercy That Makes It Possible

God did not ask you to offer yourself so He could love you.

  • "He loved you — comprehensively, at infinite cost — and says: in light of all that, what else would make sense?"

• Adam hid with nothing to bring but shame. The gospel says: bring the shame. That is the altar. That is where mercy meets you.

• Hagar wept with nothing left. The gospel says: God opens eyes. He saw her then. He sees you now.

• Jacob refused comfort while the answer was already on its way. The gospel says: your mind does not have to stay where it decided to go.

  • "This mercy is not fragile. It is not revoked when you fail. It is the only ground on which a life of offering becomes possible at all."

Back to Jacob

Jacob sat in his grief. Mind closed. Convinced of what was true. Refusing every comfort.

And Joseph was alive. The answer was already on its way. God was already working.

  • "Jacob's mind had decided what was possible. And it was wrong. Your mind does not have to stay where it decided to go."

The Word comes from outside. The Spirit works from within. You cannot get there alone.

  • "Give the Word access to your mind every day. That is the ask. That is the whole ask."

Go Live In Response To This

You are not leaving to try harder. You are leaving to respond — to mercy already given, love already demonstrated, grace that has already secured your standing before God.

• Open the Word tomorrow morning — the mind being renewed needs the Word the way a field needs rain.

• When the world presses its mold — name it. Bring your mind back to what is true.

• When you sin — do not hide the way Adam hid. Bring the body back. A living sacrifice comes back.

• When your mind closes around despair the way Hagar's did — ask God to open your eyes. He will.

• Find people who will press the Word into your life when you would rather reach for something easier.

  • "Walk out of here and live like someone who has been shown that kind of mercy. That is the reasonable thing to do."

The renewed mind. Not once. Every day.

  • "Be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God." — Romans 12:2

Holy, Acceptable Unto God

These words follow "living sacrifice" and are easy to skip. Don't.

In the OT the animal brought to the altar had to be without blemish — spotless, fit for the altar. Paul says your body, offered in response to mercy, is exactly that.

"Not because of what you brought. Because of whose altar it lands on. Justification does not just change your standing before God in the future — it makes your offering fit right now."

• A common misreading turns this into two-tier Christianity — carnal vs. dedicated — verse 1 as the door between them.

• Paul writes to people already justified, already alive in Christ. The offering is not the key that unlocks grace. It is the natural response of a person who understands grace already given.

Gospel Call 

Paul has just named the mercies. Before we talk about the response, we need to talk about the offer. Some of you are carrying the weight of things God has not yet forgiven — because you have never asked Him to. That can change right now. In your seat. A simple prayer: "God, I know I am a sinner. I believe Jesus died for me and rose again. I receive your mercy. I am yours."  That prayer, meant honestly, is the beginning of everything Paul is about to describe. For those who have received these mercies — Point II is for you.


II. Mercy this costly deserves more than one emotional night. It deserves every ordinary morning that follows.

How a Body Stays on the Altar — The Two Commands of Verse 2

Verse 2 tells us what it looks like for a body to stay on the altar. Two commands — one negative, one positive. Together they are the mechanism of consecration.

Command 1: Be Not Conformed to This World

• "Conformed" — a mold pressing its shape into something pliable.

• "This world" means this present age — the age before Christ returns, the age that is already passing away.

"The press of the mold is temporary. The transformation is eternal. You are being asked to resist something that is already fading in order to become something that will never fade."

"Your worth is your achievement. Your body is a project. You are your own solution. That is the mold. And it is pressing right now, today, in this room."


– Present tense: ongoing, continuous, never-stopping resistance. Not a gate you walk through once.

Command 2: Be Ye Transformed by the Renewing of Your Mind

• The transformation is passive — you are being transformed. God is the agent. The instrument is the renewing of the mind.

• Present tense: ongoing, never-finished. The mind reshaped from the inside so it sees differently, wants differently, chooses differently.

What the Text Just Disproved — A Misunderstanding I Have Preached

On many occasions I have preached: real spiritual growth begins with a decisive, once-for-all act of surrender. Consecrate yourself and sanctification begins.

""The sacrifice Paul urges in verse 1 is no one-time act. The present-tense verbs stress the progressive, ongoing nature of the believer's participation." — William Combs"

"The consecrated life is not a feeling. It is a body submitted to a mind being renewed — daily, through the Word, against the press of the world."

"A dead sacrifice is already done. Paul is not asking for something you finish. He is asking for something you live."


Illustration — Bonfire Summer

One summer — Friday night bonfires, week after week. Invitation every night. Kids responded. Some burned CDs.

I still believe dedication is real and necessary. But here is what I had not yet seen:

"Those kids needed a body that showed up the next morning, and a mind being renewed so that body knew what to do with the day."


The fire dies. The summer ends. If all a person has is the memory of a decision, they have very little when November comes.

"Mercy that forgave your sin, adopted you as a child, and secured your eternity is not honored by one emotional Friday night. It is honored by a body. Showing up. Every ordinary day. The whole life."

"Your mind is being shaped by something right now. The only question is whether it is the world or the Word."

III. The mind that sin bent out of shape will not fix itself. But the Word, working from the inside out, can rebuild what grace has already redeemed.

"Renewing" — same word as Titus 3:5: "the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost."

• Mind-renewal begins at the new birth but does not end there.

• Thinking patterns, desires, default orientations — not instantly rewritten. Being rewritten.

Romans 1 contrast: the "reprobate" mind — consistently misidentifies what is good and what is God.

• Adam believed a lie and hid. Jacob refused comfort while Joseph was alive.

• In every case the renewal came from outside — God opening eyes, God working while someone wept.

""The mind is renewed by the Word and Spirit of God; then we are able to discern and desire the will of God; and then we are increasingly transformed by it." — 

"The self-improvement culture says: find the right system. The gospel says: you cannot get outside your own mind with your own mind. The Word has to come in."


That Ye May Prove

The word "prove" means to test something and find that it holds — like testing metal for quality.

The renewed mind does not merely obey the will of God. It tests it, examines it, puts it to the proof — and finds it genuinely good.

"That is a completely different posture than reluctant compliance. Paul is not promising that the Christian life becomes easier. He is promising that the renewed mind begins to recognize the will of God as something it actually wants."


Good and Acceptable and Perfect

• "Good" — morally excellent, truly beneficial. Not just permitted. Actually good.

• "Acceptable" — pleasing, well-received, fitting. Not something God tolerates from you. Something He is pleased with in you.

• "Perfect" — complete, lacking nothing, mature. The will of God does not leave you short. It is the fullest version of the life you were made for.

"The renewed mind does not find the will of God merely tolerable. It finds it good. And acceptable. And perfect. All three at once."


Reasonable Service and the Renewed Mind

Paul calls the offering in verse 1 "reasonable service" — logical, rational, intelligent worship.

Then immediately in verse 2 he names the mechanism: the renewing of the mind.

"He is saying: the offering flows from comprehension. As your mind is renewed you understand more fully what the mercies of God actually mean — and the offering becomes more natural, not more forced.  Glad response. The more you understand what was given for you, the more reasonable it becomes to give everything back."


This is the answer to every person who feels the Christian life is duty without joy. The problem is not the will. The problem is a mind that has not yet been renewed enough to see what it is responding to.

The Destination — What the Renewed Mind Begins to See

The person whose mind is being renewed begins to want differently. The things the world said would satisfy start to feel thin. The things God says are good start to feel true.

"The voice that said your worth is your achievement begins to lose its authority — not because you silenced it, but because something truer has been growing louder."


The One Ask

"Give the Word access to your mind every day."


Not to earn what you do not have. Not to impress God. Not because guilt demands it.

"Because your mind is being shaped by something right now — and the Word is the only thing that comes from outside, works from the inside, and can rebuild what sin bent out of shape."


Application

The Person Who Has Tried Everything

You believe the gospel. You have made decisions — real ones. Maybe more than once.

You have read the books. Done the therapy — it helped, the same patterns came back. Resolution in January, lasted until March. Built the habit. Watched it unravel.

"You can describe your problem with remarkable precision. You just cannot seem to fix it."


Somewhere underneath is a question you are afraid to ask out loud:

"Is something wrong with me that cannot be fixed?"
"Paul's answer is: yes. And also — that is not the end of the sentence."


Yes — the mind bent by sin will not fix itself. Every system you have tried has been run by the same mind that needs renewing.

But the Word of God comes from outside. The Spirit works from within. What you cannot do from the inside, God has been doing patiently — every time you opened your Bible, every time you brought your body back after a failure.

"The question is not whether you can fix yourself. The question is whether you are giving the Word access to your mind every day."


Not to earn what you do not have. The mercy is already yours. But the renewal happens through the Word. And it has to be daily.

"Your mind is being shaped by something right now. The only question is whether it is the world or the Word."


Conclusion

""The matter of personal consecration is reduced to the simple element of honesty." — Hubert Brooke, Personal Consecration (1897)"

"Not intensity. Not drama. Not a big enough fire. Honesty. Is there a body being offered — day by day — to the God who gave everything to make the offering possible?"

"Combs, after a full study of this text: what Paul means by dedication has too often been understood to mean a decisive, often one-time decision. It is not. It is a life." — William Combs"


The Mercy That Makes It Possible

God did not ask you to offer yourself so He could love you.

"He loved you — comprehensively, at infinite cost — and says: in light of all that, what else would make sense?"

• Adam hid with nothing to bring but shame. The gospel says: bring the shame. That is the altar. That is where mercy meets you.

• Hagar wept with nothing left. The gospel says: God opens eyes. He saw her then. He sees you now.

• Jacob refused comfort while the answer was already on its way. The gospel says: your mind does not have to stay where it decided to go.

"This mercy is not fragile. It is not revoked when you fail. It is the only ground on which a life of offering becomes possible at all."


Back to Jacob

Jacob sat in his grief. Mind closed. Convinced of what was true. Refusing every comfort.

And Joseph was alive. The answer was already on its way. God was already working.

"Jacob's mind had decided what was possible. And it was wrong. Your mind does not have to stay where it decided to go."

The Word comes from outside. The Spirit works from within. You cannot get there alone.

"Give the Word access to your mind every day. That is the ask. That is the whole ask."


Go Live In Response To This

You are not leaving to try harder. You are leaving to respond — to mercy already given, love already demonstrated, grace that has already secured your standing before God.

• Open the Word tomorrow morning — the mind being renewed needs the Word the way a field needs rain.

• When the world presses its mold — name it. Bring your mind back to what is true.

• When you sin — do not hide the way Adam hid. Bring the body back. A living sacrifice comes back.

• When your mind closes around despair the way Hagar's did — ask God to open your eyes. He will.

• Find people who will press the Word into your life when you would rather reach for something easier.

"Walk out of here and live like someone who has been shown that kind of mercy. That is the reasonable thing to do."

The renewed mind. Not once. Every day.

"Be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God." — Romans 12:2

sermons.title: DEVOTION: FREEDOM TO TELL — July 4, 250th Anniversary
sermons.speaker: Trent Cornwell
sermons.notesHtml:
For 250 years this nation has protected the freedom to share Christ without fear — the greatest freedom we have is not found in our founding documents, but in the One who makes us free indeed.

INTRODUCTION — A Moment Before the Sky Lights Up

These are the moments in life I hope to always remember. Coop and Avery on the grill. Andrew and group of pyromaniacs ready to blow things up. People expressing gratitude.

  • Tonight we do not worship this country. That would be idolatry.
  • But we do express our gratitude to God for it.
  • God bless America. Land that I love.

Transition: tonight, before the fireworks, is a night to notice it

1. THE COMMAND — GIVE THANKS FIRST

Let’s do more than observe a day on the calendar.

Let’s be live out Scripture.

1 Timothy 2:1–2 — "I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men; for kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty."

"First of all" — before anything else, give thanks

Illustration: George Washington, First Thanksgiving Proclamation (1789)

Called it a "duty" to be "grateful for His benefits" Not for a perfect country. Not for leaders who get it right. Just thanks.

2. THE FREEDOM I CHERISH MOST

Many blessings could be named tonight — this is the one that matters most

For 250 years, someone has always had the freedom to tell me about Jesus

No whispering. No looking over the shoulder. That freedom has belonged to every person in this country, without fear

Application: this is our 250th year — use the freedom, don't just enjoy it

3. THE GOSPEL — WHY THIS FREEDOM MATTERS

Sin — the international problem

  • Romans 3:23 — "For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God."
  • Not just "bad people out there." Us.

Death — the wage

Romans 6:23 — "For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord."

The worst news and the best news in one verse

Christ — the gift

Died on the cross for sinners, buried, rose the third day

Romans 10:9 — "That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved."

True freedom — the point

You can have every American freedom and still be in chains to sin

John 8:36 — "If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed."

“While we are zealously performing the duties of good citizens and soldiers, we certainly ought not to be inattentive to the higher duties of religion. To the distinguished character of Patriot, it should be our highest glory to add the more distinguished character of Christian.” George Washington

Do not just celebrate tonight be a freedom livng America. Let us most importantly be Jesus loving Christians.

CALL TO RESPONSE

Tonight, before the fireworks, you can be free indeed

Not by what your country gave you — by what Christ did for you

If you've never trusted Him: right now, quietly, where you're sitting

  • Confess you're a sinner
  • Believe He died and rose for you
  • Ask Him to save you

The Founders gave us a Declaration of Independence. Christ offers a declaration of pardon. One gives freedom under a Constitution. The other gives freedom under the cross.
